cpsa.title: Hypotension Hours After Bowel Surgery / Blame the Epidural Last
cpsa.mlaTheme: Recognition of the acutely unwell patient
cpsa.contentMap: Surgery / Acute and emergency · early postoperative hypotension with an epidural in situ: NEWS2 escalation, ABCDE, haemorrhage until proven otherwise, fluid resuscitation and reassessment, holding anticoagulant prophylaxis, senior surgical and anaesthetic involvement
cpsa.capabilities: Calculating NEWS2 and triggering an emergency response; assessing a deteriorating postoperative patient with ABCDE; recognising that a tachycardia and worsening abdominal pain do not fit an epidural explanation; treating postoperative shock as bleeding until proven otherwise; obtaining wide-bore access, crossmatch, clotting and a venous gas; giving a crystalloid bolus and reassessing; adjusting the epidural only through the local protocol and the anaesthetic team; holding scheduled prophylactic heparin pending senior review; escalating early to the surgical registrar for a return-to-theatre decision.
cpsa.setting: Surgical ward, 17:30. You are the FY1. A role-player speaks for the patient and the nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Desmond Oakhurst, 67, is 5 hours after an open right hemicolectomy. The nurse has called you because his blood pressure has fallen. Assess him, ask the examiner for the findings you need, and tell the nurse your plan.
cpsa.scenario: Mr Oakhurst had an open right hemicolectomy for caecal cancer this morning and returned from recovery at 13:00 with a thoracic epidural infusion and a urinary catheter; no abdominal drain. Weight 80 kg. He takes ramipril for hypertension; no anticoagulants. Observations now: RR 24, SpO₂ 96% on air, BP 86/52 (128/76 in recovery), HR 118 regular, temperature 36.8 °C, alert. On request: pale and clammy, capillary refill 4 seconds, cool hands; abdomen more distended and more tender than at 15:00 despite the epidural; wound dressing dry. Urine output 15 mL/h for the last 2 hours. Epidural: bilateral sensory block to T6, unchanged since recovery; no motor block. Venous gas on request: Hb 92 g/L (128 g/L pre-op), lactate 3.6 mmol/L. One 20G cannula. His first dose of prophylactic enoxaparin is due at 18:00. The nurse says: 'It'll be the epidural — they always drop their pressure. Shall I just turn it down and run the bag a bit faster?'

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Yes, that sounds sensible. Epidurals often drop the pressure.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: I feel a bit faint, doctor, and my tummy's sore.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's normal after a big operation. I'll write up some more painkillers.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: And his heparin at six?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Give it as prescribed. Recheck the obs in an hour and call me if he's worse.

fail.examinerNote: Accepted the epidural explanation without examining him, calculating NEWS2 or noticing the tachycardia, falling urine output and worsening pain. No bloods, no crossmatch, no bolus with reassessment and no senior help. Allowed anticoagulant prophylaxis into a patient who may be bleeding.
fail.summary: Anchored on the epidural; NEWS2 7 not recognised; no assessment, bloods or escalation; heparin given.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Let me assess him first. (To examiner.) RR 24, BP 86, pulse 118 — that's a NEWS2 of 7. May I have his capillary refill, abdomen and urine output?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Pale and clammy, refill 4 seconds. Abdomen more distended and tender than earlier. Urine 15 mL an hour for two hours.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: This is shock five hours after bowel surgery, so I'm treating it as bleeding until proven otherwise. I'll put in a second large cannula, send FBC, clotting and a crossmatch, do a venous gas and give 500 mL of crystalloid over 15 minutes, then reassess.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) Please put out an emergency call for the surgical registrar and outreach now.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: And the heparin at six?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Hold it until the registrar has seen him.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To patient.) Mr Oakhurst, your blood pressure is low and we need to find out why. More doctors are coming now.

pass.examinerNote: Calculated NEWS2, assessed circulation, named haemorrhage, sent the right bloods including crossmatch, gave a measured bolus with reassessment, escalated as an emergency and held the heparin. Did not explain why the epidural does not account for the picture, involve the anaesthetic team in managing the epidural, or anticipate major haemorrhage and theatre.
pass.summary: NEWS2 7 recognised; haemorrhage named; access, crossmatch, bolus and reassessment; emergency surgical call; heparin held.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: It'll be the epidural. Shall I turn it down and run the bag faster?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Maybe, but I want to rule out the dangerous cause first. (To examiner.) Airway patent, RR 24, sats 96 on air, BP 86/52 from 128/76, pulse 118: NEWS2 is 7. Capillary refill, abdomen, urine output and the block height, please?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Refill 4 seconds, clammy. Abdomen more distended and more tender than at 15:00. Urine 15 mL an hour. Block T6, unchanged.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) An epidural can lower the pressure, but it wouldn't usually make his pulse 118, stop his urine or make his tummy more painful while the block hasn't changed. I'm treating this as bleeding until the surgeons prove otherwise. Please make an emergency call for the surgical registrar and outreach, and bleep the anaesthetist about the epidural.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) I'm putting in a second wide-bore cannula and sending FBC, clotting, fibrinogen, U&E and a crossmatch, with the number of units per the transfusion policy. I'll do a venous gas and give 500 mL of crystalloid over less than 15 minutes, then reassess. High-flow oxygen through a reservoir mask while he is shocked, then titrate to 94–98%, and please hold the 18:00 enoxaparin.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Venous gas: Hb 92, down from 128 pre-op; lactate 3.6. After the bolus: BP 88/54, pulse 116.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's a falling haemoglobin and a transient response at best. I'll tell the registrar: 'Five hours post right hemicolectomy, NEWS2 7, BP 88 after 500 mL, Hb down 36, lactate 3.6 — I think he's bleeding and needs you now, and he may need the major haemorrhage protocol and theatre.' Any changes to the epidural are for the anaesthetist, using our protocol.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To patient.) Mr Oakhurst, your blood pressure is low and I'm worried you may be bleeding inside. We're giving you fluid and the surgical team is on the way.

distinction.examinerNote: Gave a structured ABCDE with a correct NEWS2, explained why the epidural did not fit using the pulse, urine output, pain and unchanged block, and treated it as haemorrhage. Delivered access, crossmatch, a measured bolus with reassessment and an SBAR-quality escalation, held the prophylactic heparin, left the epidural to the anaesthetist and anticipated major haemorrhage and theatre.
distinction.summary: Correct NEWS2; epidural explanation challenged with reasons; haemorrhage bundle; bolus and reassessment; SBAR escalation; heparin held; theatre anticipated.

cpsa.hook: An epidural can lower a blood pressure, but it does not usually cause a pulse of 118, stop the urine or make abdominal pain worse. Hypotension after surgery is bleeding until a surgeon proves otherwise; blame the epidural last.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The nurse offers a familiar, comfortable explanation and a plan that sounds active. The observations give a NEWS2 of 7 — an emergency response under the RCP NEWS2 chart — and the Faculty of Pain Medicine's epidural guidance says other causes of hypotension, including bleeding, must be considered and excluded. Turning the epidural down and running a maintenance bag faster treats a number, not the cause. NICE CG174 sets resuscitation as a 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes followed by reassessment, and the scheduled prophylactic heparin should be held until a surgeon has seen him. The marks are for recognition, the haemorrhage bundle, reassessment and early surgical escalation; the decision to return to theatre is the surgeon's.

cpsa.title: A Positive Blood Culture After Discharge / The Result Belongs to the Team That Sent It
cpsa.mlaTheme: Readiness for safe practice / Acute and emergency care
cpsa.contentMap: Infection / Acute and emergency · Gram-negative bacteraemia found after discharge: closed-loop result handling, telephone risk assessment for sepsis, antibiotic adequacy for upper urinary tract infection, recall to hospital, documentation and system learning
cpsa.capabilities: Taking a critical result from the laboratory with a read-back; recognising Gram-negative bacilli in blood cultures as a likely bacteraemia needing prompt action; reviewing the admission notes and discharge prescription; recognising that nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis or bacteraemia; contacting a discharged patient by telephone with identity and consent checks; assessing sepsis risk remotely using NICE NG253 criteria and collateral history; arranging an emergency return when high-risk features are present; seeking senior and microbiology advice on antibiotics; documenting, informing the GP and reporting the missing pending-result plan.
cpsa.setting: Medical ward, Saturday 10:00. You are the FY1 covering the ward. The examiner plays the laboratory, the registrar and the patient's daughter on the telephone.
cpsa.yourRole: The microbiology laboratory phones with a positive blood culture for Mrs Irene Quarmby, 79, who was discharged from your ward yesterday. Take the result, decide what needs to happen, and speak to the patient's family on the telephone.
cpsa.scenario: Laboratory: 'Blood cultures taken on admission three days ago: Gram-negative bacilli in both bottles. Identification and sensitivities to follow.' Notes (on request): admitted with fever 38.7 °C, rigors and dysuria; right loin tenderness documented in the clerking; urine dip positive for leucocytes and nitrites; eGFR 38. Coded as 'lower UTI', treated with IV antibiotics for 24 hours, then discharged yesterday on oral nitrofurantoin for 5 days. The discharge summary does not mention pending blood cultures. No clinician has contacted the patient. On the telephone, her daughter answers; Mrs Quarmby is beside her and agrees to her daughter speaking for her. Mrs Quarmby says she is 'fine, just tired'. Only if asked directly, the daughter says her mother has been muddled since she woke — she called her by her sister's name — had another shivering episode overnight and has passed very little urine since yesterday evening. No home observations available. The registrar is in the emergency department and reachable by phone.

markingGrid.domain: Reads back the result to the laboratory and records who called and when
Recognises Gram-negative bacilli in blood cultures as a serious result needing same-day action
Reviews the notes and identifies loin tenderness and the nitrofurantoin discharge prescription
Recognises that nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis or bacteraemia, and is a poor choice with an eGFR of 38
Checks identity and consent before discussing the result with the daughter
Asks about confusion, rigors, urine output and breathing rather than accepting 'fine'
Recognises new confusion as a high-risk sepsis feature and arranges an emergency ambulance
Informs the registrar and the emergency department, and seeks microbiology advice on antibiotics
Documents the result, the call, the advice and the plan, and informs the GP
Reports the absent pending-result plan as an incident for learning

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Laboratory here: Gram-negative bacilli in both bottles for Irene Quarmby. Sensitivities to follow.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks. She went home yesterday on antibiotics, so that should cover it.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Will you contact her?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'll ring her. (On phone.) Hello, is that Mrs Quarmby's house? Is she okay?

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: She says she's fine, just tired.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Good. Tell her to finish the antibiotics and see her GP on Monday.

fail.examinerNote: Assumed the discharge antibiotic was adequate without checking it, did not confirm identity or consent, and accepted 'fine' without asking about confusion, rigors or urine output. Missed new confusion, a high-risk sepsis feature, and reduced urine output in a bacteraemic 79-year-old on nitrofurantoin. No senior, microbiology or documentation.
fail.summary: Result not owned; nitrofurantoin not questioned; 'fine' accepted; high-risk features missed; deferred to GP.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Laboratory here: Gram-negative bacilli in both bottles for Irene Quarmby. Sensitivities to follow.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Let me read that back: Irene Quarmby, Gram-negative bacilli in both bottles, sensitivities to follow. Thank you. (To examiner.) May I see her notes and discharge prescription?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Fever and rigors on admission, right loin tenderness, eGFR 38. Discharged yesterday on nitrofurantoin.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: This looks like a pyelonephritis with bacteraemia, and nitrofurantoin won't treat that. I need to contact her today. (On phone.) Hello, I'm the doctor from the medical ward. Could I check who I'm speaking to and that Mrs Quarmby is happy for me to talk to you?

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: I'm her daughter. She says yes — she says she's fine, just tired.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Has she been confused at all, shivery, or passing less urine?

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: Actually, she's been muddled since she woke up, and she shivered a lot overnight.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's worrying. Her blood test shows an infection in the bloodstream, and she needs to come back to hospital now. Please call 999 and say she has sepsis; I'll let the emergency department know she's coming. (To examiner.) I'll call the registrar and microbiology, and document it.

pass.examinerNote: Read the result back, reviewed the notes, recognised bacteraemic pyelonephritis on an inadequate antibiotic, checked identity and consent, elicited confusion and rigors from the daughter, and arranged an emergency return with ED and senior notification. Did not ask about urine output, record the time and caller, explain the eGFR issue, inform the GP, or report the missing pending-result plan.
pass.summary: Read-back; nitrofurantoin recognised as inadequate; consent checked; confusion elicited; 999 and ED alerted; registrar and microbiology informed.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Laboratory here: Gram-negative bacilli in both bottles for Irene Quarmby. Sensitivities to follow.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Reading back: Irene Quarmby, date of birth on the request, blood cultures from three days ago, Gram-negative bacilli in both bottles. Could I take your name? I'm noting the time now. (To examiner.) Notes and discharge prescription, please.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Fever 38.7, rigors, right loin tenderness, eGFR 38. Coded as lower UTI; discharged yesterday on nitrofurantoin. No mention of pending cultures.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: So this is pyelonephritis with a Gram-negative bacteraemia. Nitrofurantoin doesn't reach useful levels in the kidney or the blood, and with an eGFR of 38 it's a poor choice anyway. She's still our patient. I'll phone her now.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (On phone.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors from the medical ward. Who am I speaking to? Is Mrs Quarmby with you, and is she happy for me to talk to you about her results?

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: I'm her daughter, and yes. She says she's fine, just tired.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'm glad she's talking to you. Can I ask you a few questions too? Has she seemed muddled at all, had any shivering, passed less urine, or been breathless?

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: She called me by my sister's name this morning. She shivered a lot overnight and has hardly been to the toilet since last night.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you, that's really important. The blood test shows a bacterial infection in her bloodstream, and the new confusion and low urine worry me. She needs treatment in hospital now. Please call 999, say she's 79 with suspected sepsis from a blood infection, and call back if she becomes harder to wake. I'll tell the emergency department she's coming.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll phone the registrar in ED with an SBAR and ask microbiology for advice on the antibiotic while we await sensitivities, so treatment starts within the hour of arrival. I'll document the result, the call and the plan, update her GP, and complete an incident report because the discharge summary didn't flag pending cultures.

distinction.examinerNote: Ran a closed loop from laboratory to patient: read-back with caller and time, notes review, a reasoned rejection of nitrofurantoin, identity and consent, a structured collateral sepsis screen that overcame 'fine', a clear 999 instruction with interim safety-netting, ED and senior notification, microbiology input, GP update and an incident report for the system gap.
distinction.summary: Closed-loop result handling; antibiotic inadequacy explained; consent; collateral NG253 screen; 999 recall; ED, registrar, microbiology, GP; incident report.

cpsa.hook: A positive blood culture is still your patient's result after they have gone home. Read it back, check whether the discharge antibiotic actually treats it, and ask the family the questions the patient will not answer — 'fine' is not an assessment.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Three reassurances are built in: she is already on an antibiotic, she says she is fine, and the result has arrived on a weekend with no plan. Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate kidney or blood levels and is not recommended for pyelonephritis (NICE NG111), and her eGFR of 38 makes it unsuitable anyway. Only collateral history reveals new confusion — a high-risk criterion in NICE NG253 — and reduced urine output adds to the concern, so she needs an emergency return, not a GP appointment. The candidate is not marked on naming an antibiotic: that is for the senior and microbiology. Marks are for owning the result, identifying the inadequate treatment, a structured remote risk assessment with consent, an emergency recall and closing every loop.

cpsa.title: Paediatric Basic Life Support / Five Breaths Before You Push — and Gasping Is Not Breathing
cpsa.mlaTheme: Readiness for safe practice / Acute and emergency care
cpsa.contentMap: Paediatrics / Acute and emergency · in-hospital paediatric basic life support on a child manikin (RCUK 2025 paediatric BLS): hypoxic arrest, five initial rescue breaths, 15:2, defibrillator, agonal breathing
cpsa.capabilities: Recognising a child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally; calling for help and activating the emergency team (2222) early; opening a child's airway without over-extending the neck; giving five initial rescue breaths with a bag-valve-mask and oxygen and checking that the chest rises; recognising that the absence of signs of life, not a pulse check, triggers compressions; delivering good-quality compressions for a child at 15:2; attaching a defibrillator as soon as it arrives and keeping everyone clear; recognising agonal gasping as a sign of arrest, not recovery; speaking honestly and briefly to a frightened parent; handing over to the paediatric resuscitation team.
cpsa.setting: Paediatric ward, 03:10. You are the FY1. A child resuscitation manikin, a paediatric bag-valve-mask with oxygen, a resuscitation trolley and a defibrillator with paediatric pads are available; the role-player speaks for the parent and the examiner for the nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Alfie Kitteridge, 4, was admitted yesterday with a right lower lobe pneumonia and needed increasing oxygen overnight. His mother has pressed the emergency buzzer. You are the first doctor to arrive. Manage the situation on the manikin, talking through your actions, until the paediatric resuscitation team takes over.
cpsa.scenario: Alfie, 4, weight about 17 kg on his chart, was on 2 L/min of nasal oxygen with SpO₂ 93% at the 02:00 observations, RR 46, HR 150. His mother, Ms Jodie Kitteridge, says: 'He went quiet and floppy and I can't wake him.' On arrival he is pale and limp on the bed and does not respond to voice or touch. When the airway is opened and breathing is checked (examiner gives findings): no normal breathing, no movement, no cough. The nasal cannula has slipped off his face. A nurse arrives within 30 seconds of the call for help and can fetch equipment, put out the 2222 call and squeeze the bag if asked. After the five rescue breaths the examiner says: 'The chest rose with each breath. There are still no signs of life.' At about 4 minutes, during compressions, the examiner says: 'He is making an occasional gasping breath — about one every 15 seconds.' His mother shouts: 'He's breathing! Stop, you're hurting him!' The defibrillator, when attached, advises: 'No shock advised. Continue CPR.' At about 7 minutes the paediatric resuscitation team arrives.

markingGrid.domain: Checks for danger, assesses responsiveness and shouts for help, pressing the emergency buzzer
Asks for a 2222 paediatric arrest call and the defibrillator early, as soon as a second person arrives
Opens the airway (head tilt–chin lift without over-extension) and looks, listens and feels for breathing for no more than 10 seconds
Gives five initial rescue breaths with a bag-valve-mask and high-flow oxygen, checking for chest rise, before compressions
Starts compressions immediately when there are no signs of life — does not wait for or rely on a pulse check
Compresses on the lower half of the sternum to at least one third of the chest depth at 100–120 per minute, with full recoil
Uses a 15:2 ratio and keeps interruptions to a minimum
Recognises occasional gasping as agonal breathing and continues CPR, explaining briefly to the mother
Attaches the defibrillator with paediatric pads as soon as it arrives, keeps everyone clear for analysis and resumes CPR immediately after 'no shock advised'
Hands over to the resuscitation team concisely: probable hypoxic arrest, time of collapse, breaths and CPR given, rhythm advice, mother present

dialogue.speaker: MOTHER
dialogue.text: He went floppy — I can't wake him!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Alfie? Alfie! (Shakes him.) Let me feel for a pulse. (Spends 20 seconds at the neck.) I'm not sure.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Right, starting CPR. (Starts compressions straight away.) Thirty… two breaths… (Gives two breaths mouth-to-mouth with no bag or oxygen.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He is making an occasional gasping breath — about one every 15 seconds.

dialogue.speaker: MOTHER
dialogue.text: He's breathing! Stop, you're hurting him!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Oh — OK, he's breathing. (Stops CPR.) Let's put him in the recovery position and get the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: You are the doctor. What now?

fail.examinerNote: Used the adult sequence on a child in a hypoxic arrest: no five rescue breaths, 30:2, and no oxygen. Spent 20 seconds on an uncertain pulse check instead of acting on the absence of signs of life. Never asked for a 2222 call or the defibrillator. Then stopped CPR for agonal gasps because the mother called them breathing — the most dangerous error in the station.
fail.summary: Adult sequence on a child; no rescue breaths; prolonged pulse check; no 2222 call; CPR stopped for agonal gasps.

dialogue.speaker: MOTHER
dialogue.text: He went floppy — I can't wake him!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Alfie? Alfie! (Taps him.) Help! I need help in here! (Presses the buzzer. Opens the airway and checks breathing.) Not breathing normally.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) Please put out a 2222 paediatric arrest call and bring the defibrillator.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Five rescue breaths first — his arrest is almost certainly from lack of oxygen. (Bag-valve-mask on oxygen.) One… two… three… four… five.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The chest rose with each breath. There are still no signs of life.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Starting compressions. Fifteen compressions, two breaths. (One hand, lower half of the sternum, a third of the chest depth.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He is making an occasional gasping breath — about one every 15 seconds.

dialogue.speaker: MOTHER
dialogue.text: He's breathing! Stop, you're hurting him!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Those aren't normal breaths — I need to keep going. (Continues 15:2.)

pass.examinerNote: Correct paediatric sequence: help and 2222 call, airway, five rescue breaths with oxygen, then compressions at 15:2 with good technique. Recognised the gasps as agonal and kept going. Did not attach the defibrillator when it arrived or explain to the mother why CPR was continuing, and gave no handover to the team.
pass.summary: Help called; five rescue breaths; 15:2 with good technique; agonal gasps recognised; defibrillator and handover not addressed.

dialogue.speaker: MOTHER
dialogue.text: He went floppy — I can't wake him!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Alfie? Alfie! (Taps him and speaks loudly.) Help, please! (Presses the emergency buzzer.) Ms Kitteridge, I'm a doctor — stay with me, you're in the right place.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Head tilt, chin lift — not over-extended. Looks, listens, feels for up to 10 seconds.) No normal breathing, no movement. The cannula's off his face.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) 2222, paediatric arrest, Ward 4, bed 6 — then the defibrillator and the trolley, please.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: This is a breathing problem that has stopped his heart, so oxygen first. (Bag-valve-mask, 15 litres.) Five rescue breaths — watching the chest rise. One… two… three… four… five.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The chest rose with each breath. There are still no signs of life.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: No signs of life — I'm not wasting time hunting for a pulse. Compressions now: one hand, lower half of the breastbone, at least a third of the chest depth, 100 to 120 a minute. Fifteen to two. (To nurse.) Can you take the bag? Two breaths after every fifteen.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He is making an occasional gasping breath — about one every 15 seconds.

dialogue.speaker: MOTHER
dialogue.text: He's breathing! Stop, you're hurting him!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Keeps compressing.) Ms Kitteridge, I know it's frightening. Those slow gasps happen when the heart isn't pumping — they're not proper breathing, so we have to keep going. His heart needs us to push for it right now.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Defibrillator arrives.) Pads on while we keep compressing — paediatric pads — one on the front just left of the breastbone, one on the back between the shoulder blades. Analysing — everybody off. (Hands clear.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: No shock advised. Continue CPR.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Straight back on — fifteen, two.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Team arrives.) This is Alfie, 4, 17 kilos, day 2 of a right lower lobe pneumonia on 2 litres. Found unresponsive at about 03:08, cannula off; probable hypoxic arrest. Five rescue breaths with oxygen, CPR 15:2 since about 03:10, one analysis, no shock advised. Agonal gasps only. Mum is here.

distinction.examinerNote: Ran in-hospital paediatric BLS exactly as RCUK 2025 sets it out, and said why: a hypoxic arrest needs oxygen first. Acted on the absence of signs of life, not an uncertain pulse. Delegated the bag so compressions were not interrupted, handled the agonal gasps and the mother's distress in one sentence without stopping, used the defibrillator safely with minimal pauses, and gave a handover the team could act on — including the slipped cannula as the likely cause.
distinction.summary: Hypoxic arrest recognised; five oxygenated breaths; 15:2 with minimal interruptions; agonal gasps explained to mother; safe defibrillator use; structured handover.

cpsa.hook: Children rarely arrest from the heart first — they arrest from lack of oxygen. That is why paediatric BLS starts with five rescue breaths, runs at 15:2, and why a few slow gasps are a sign of arrest, not recovery.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The adult habit is the trap: going straight to compressions at 30:2, or spending precious seconds on a carotid pulse. RCUK 2025 in-hospital paediatric BLS is: check responsiveness and call for help (2222), open the airway, give five rescue breaths (bag-mask with oxygen for competent providers), start compressions if there are no signs of life, continue at 15:2, attach a defibrillator as soon as possible (paediatric pads or mode under 25 kg, front-and-back placement). One or two hands may be used for a child — what is marked is depth (at least one third of the chest), rate and recoil, not the number of hands. The second trap is the mother's shout: agonal gasping is not normal breathing, and stopping CPR because 'he's breathing' would be a critical error. The defibrillator is likely to advise no shock in a hypoxic arrest — the candidate must get straight back on the chest.

thinkSayDo.think: A floppy child on oxygen with the cannula off — this is a breathing problem that has become an arrest.
thinkSayDo.say: Help, please — 2222 paediatric arrest, and bring the defibrillator.
thinkSayDo.do: Buzzer · 2222 call · airway open · look, listen, feel ≤10 seconds

thinkSayDo.think: Oxygen first, then the heart.
thinkSayDo.say: Five rescue breaths — watching the chest rise.
thinkSayDo.do: Bag-valve-mask with 15 L oxygen · five breaths · no signs of life → compressions

thinkSayDo.think: Child technique and ratio, not adult.
thinkSayDo.say: Fifteen compressions, two breaths.
thinkSayDo.do: Lower half of sternum · at least one third depth · one or two hands · 100–120/min · full recoil · minimal pauses

thinkSayDo.think: Slow gasps are agonal — the heart still isn't pumping.
thinkSayDo.say: Those aren't proper breaths, so we keep going.
thinkSayDo.do: Continue CPR · pads on during compressions · clear for analysis · resume immediately · hand over

markTriggers: Shouts for help and presses the emergency buzzer
Requests a 2222 paediatric arrest call and the defibrillator
Opens the airway without over-extension and checks breathing for up to 10 seconds
Gives five initial rescue breaths with bag-valve-mask and oxygen
Starts compressions on no signs of life without a prolonged pulse check
Compresses lower half of sternum, one third depth, 100–120 per minute
Uses 15:2
Identifies occasional gasping as agonal and continues CPR
Keeps everyone clear for analysis and resumes CPR straight after 'no shock advised'
Hands over with probable cause and timings

cpsa.title: Snoring, Pinpoint and Slowing / Open the Airway, Size the Guedel, Then Breathe for Him
cpsa.mlaTheme: Recognition of the acutely unwell patient
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Acute and emergency · basic airway management on a manikin: airway manoeuvres, suction, oropharyngeal airway sizing and insertion, bag-valve-mask ventilation; post-operative opioid-induced respiratory depression
cpsa.capabilities: Recognising partial airway obstruction from snoring and a falling conscious level; calling for help early; opening the airway with head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust; suction under direct vision; choosing an oropharyngeal airway only when airway reflexes are absent, sizing it from the incisors to the angle of the jaw and inserting it without force; recognising hypoventilation and supporting breathing with a bag-valve-mask and oxygen rather than a face mask alone; withholding further opioid and sedative doses and asking for naloxone per protocol; removing the airway the moment the patient gags; reassessing after every intervention and handing over clearly.
cpsa.setting: Surgical ward, 05:30. You are the FY1. An airway manikin, oropharyngeal airways of several sizes, a Yankauer sucker, a non-rebreathe mask, a bag-valve-mask with oxygen and monitoring are available; the examiner gives findings and speaks for the nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Clifford Aynsley, 67, is day 1 after a right total knee replacement. The nurse has called you because he is 'very sleepy and snoring loudly' and his saturations have fallen. Assess and manage his airway and breathing on the manikin, talking through your actions and asking the examiner for findings.
cpsa.scenario: Since surgery he has been on modified-release oxycodone twice daily and pregabalin; the drug chart shows two extra doses of immediate-release oral oxycodone overnight for breakthrough pain, the last at 03:00. No known allergies; no history of COPD; eGFR 52 (baseline 75). Observations: RR 7, SpO₂ 85% on room air, HR 64, BP 118/70, temperature 37.0 °C. He groans to a trapezius squeeze but does not open his eyes (responds to pain). Loud snoring, worse when the head falls forward; pupils pinpoint; no vomit, a little saliva in the mouth. Capillary glucose 6.8 mmol/L if checked. When an oropharyngeal airway is inserted correctly, the examiner says: 'The airway is tolerated. Snoring stops, but he is still breathing 7 times a minute and SpO₂ is 87% on a non-rebreathe mask at 15 litres.' If bag-valve-mask ventilation is started: 'Chest rising, SpO₂ climbing to 95%.' At about 5 minutes, after naloxone is given per protocol by the outreach nurse, the examiner says: 'He opens his eyes, coughs and starts to gag on the airway.'

markingGrid.domain: Recognises snoring with a reduced conscious level as partial airway obstruction and calls for urgent help (outreach or medical emergency team) early
Opens the airway with head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust and suctions the mouth under direct vision
Gives high-flow oxygen and assesses breathing rate, depth and saturation, and conscious level (AVPU/GCS) and pupils
Explains that an oropharyngeal airway is appropriate only because he is not responding to voice and has no gag, and sizes it from the incisors to the angle of the jaw
Inserts the airway correctly (inverted, rotated 180° at the soft palate) without force, and reassesses patency
Recognises that a clear airway with RR 7 is still hypoventilation and starts bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen
Identifies opioid toxicity, withholds further opioid and pregabalin doses and asks for naloxone per protocol, titrated
Removes the oropharyngeal airway immediately when he gags and reassesses the airway
Anticipates re-sedation because naloxone is shorter-acting than modified-release oxycodone — continuous monitoring, analgesia review and senior plan for repeat doses or infusion
Hands over in SBAR, documents, and raises the stacked opioid doses, the gabapentinoid and impaired renal function as contributors

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: He's snoring and his sats are 85%. Can you have a look?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: He's probably just asleep after the surgery. Let's sit him up and put a mask on.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Non-rebreathe at 15 litres. RR still 7, SpO₂ 87%, still snoring.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'll put an airway in. (Picks the largest oropharyngeal airway and pushes it in the right way up.) It's a bit stiff… (Pushes harder.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The airway is in. He is still breathing 7 times a minute.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Good, the airway's in, so he's safe now. I'll write him up for a chest X-ray and ask the team to review on the ward round.

fail.examinerNote: Called the snoring sleep, did not call for help, and did not open the airway manually first. Chose an airway without sizing it and forced it in the wrong orientation, risking trauma and pushing the tongue back. Took a patent airway as the end point while the respiratory rate was 7 — no ventilation support, no recognition of opioid toxicity, no naloxone and the next opioid dose left on the chart.
fail.summary: Obstruction not recognised; no help; unsized airway forced in; hypoventilation ignored; opioid cause missed.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: He's snoring and his sats are 85%. Can you have a look?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Aynsley? (Trapezius squeeze.) Responds to pain only. Snoring means his airway is partly blocked. Please call outreach urgently. (Head tilt, chin lift — snoring eases.) Yankauer, please. (Suctions under direct vision.) Fifteen litres on a non-rebreathe.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: He isn't responding to voice, so an oropharyngeal airway is reasonable. Sizing it — incisor to the angle of the jaw. (Inserts upside down, rotates 180°.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The airway is tolerated. Snoring stops, but he is still breathing 7 times a minute and SpO₂ is 87% on a non-rebreathe mask at 15 litres.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Pinpoint pupils, RR 7, on regular and extra oxycodone — this is opioid toxicity. Please hold any further opioid doses. I'd like naloxone given per the protocol.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He opens his eyes, coughs and starts to gag on the airway.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Taking the airway out now. (Removes it.) Mr Aynsley, you're in hospital — you've been very sleepy. Keeping the oxygen on.

pass.examinerNote: Recognised obstruction, called for help, used manual manoeuvres and suction first, then sized and inserted the airway correctly and removed it promptly when he gagged. Identified opioid toxicity and held further opioid doses. However, with a clear airway and a respiratory rate of 7 the patient needed bag-valve-mask ventilation before naloxone arrived, and the candidate did not anticipate re-sedation or hand over.
pass.summary: Obstruction recognised; manoeuvres, suction, correct OPA technique; opioid toxicity named; ventilation support and re-sedation plan missing.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: He's snoring and his sats are 85%. Can you have a look?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Aynsley? Can you open your eyes? (Trapezius squeeze.) Responds to pain only. Snoring at a reduced conscious level is a partly blocked airway. Please call outreach urgently — say a post-op patient with airway and breathing compromise.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Head tilt, chin lift.) Snoring eases. Yankauer — (suctions saliva under direct vision). Fifteen litres non-rebreathe and full monitoring. Breathing rate?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: RR 7, shallow. SpO₂ 85% before the mask. Pupils pinpoint.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: He's not responding to voice and has no gag at the moment, so a Guedel is appropriate. Sizing incisor to angle of jaw — this one. In upside down, rotate at the back of the palate — no force.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The airway is tolerated. Snoring stops, but he is still breathing 7 times a minute and SpO₂ is 87% on a non-rebreathe mask at 15 litres.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The airway is open but he isn't breathing enough — an open airway isn't the end point. I'm going to support his breathing with the bag-valve-mask on oxygen. (To nurse.) Can you squeeze while I hold a two-handed seal? One breath every 6 seconds, timed with his own.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Chest rising, SpO₂ climbing to 95%.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Pinpoint pupils, RR 7, regular oxycodone plus two extra doses overnight and pregabalin, and his kidneys are worse than baseline — opioid toxicity. Please hold the next oxycodone and pregabalin doses. Naloxone IV per protocol in small titrated doses, aiming for adequate breathing, not full reversal of his pain relief. Glucose?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: 6.8. Naloxone is given by the outreach nurse. He opens his eyes, coughs and starts to gag on the airway.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Airway out now. (Removes it.) Mr Aynsley, you've been very drowsy from the painkillers; you're safe. RR and sats please.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To outreach.) Naloxone wears off before modified-release oxycodone does, especially with his kidney function — he needs continuous monitoring, his analgesia reviewed by the pain team with the pregabalin dose checked against his renal function, and a senior plan for repeat doses or an infusion. I'll document and call the registrar.

distinction.examinerNote: Worked in the right order — recognise, call for help, manual manoeuvres, suction, oxygen — then justified the adjunct by the absent airway reflexes, sized and inserted it correctly, and reassessed. Recognised that a patent airway with a respiratory rate of 7 still needs ventilation and gave it. Named and treated the cause with titrated naloxone, removed the airway the moment he gagged, and anticipated re-sedation with a plan the team could act on.
distinction.summary: Airway opened stepwise; OPA justified, sized and inserted; ventilation supported; opioid toxicity treated with titrated naloxone; OPA removed on gag; re-sedation planned.

cpsa.hook: A Guedel airway opens the airway — it does not breathe for the patient. Size it, use it only when the gag has gone, take it out the moment it comes back, and look at the respiratory rate before you feel safe.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The station has three steps where weak candidates stop early. First, snoring is labelled as sleep rather than partial obstruction. Second, the airway adjunct is treated as the goal: once the snoring stops, the respiratory rate of 7 and SpO₂ of 87% on 15 litres are ignored — but an open airway with hypoventilation needs bag-valve-mask ventilation, not just a mask. Third, the gag: when naloxone works and he wakes, a tolerated oropharyngeal airway becomes a cause of vomiting and laryngospasm and must come out immediately. Sizing is from the incisors to the angle of the jaw, and in adults the airway is inserted inverted and rotated 180°. Naloxone is given titrated per protocol; the mark is for the decision, and for recognising that its effect is shorter than that of modified-release oxycodone.

thinkSayDo.think: Snoring plus responds only to pain is a partly blocked airway, not sleep.
thinkSayDo.say: Outreach, please, urgently — airway and breathing compromise.
thinkSayDo.do: Head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust · suction under direct vision · 15 L oxygen · monitoring

thinkSayDo.think: No gag, not responding to voice — an oropharyngeal airway is safe to try.
thinkSayDo.say: Sizing incisor to angle of jaw; in inverted, rotate, no force.
thinkSayDo.do: Size · insert · reassess snoring, chest movement, saturation

thinkSayDo.think: Open airway, but RR 7 — he isn't breathing enough.
thinkSayDo.say: I'm going to support his breathing with the bag.
thinkSayDo.do: Two-person bag-valve-mask with oxygen · hold further opioid doses · naloxone per protocol, titrated

thinkSayDo.think: He is waking and gagging — the airway is now the hazard.
thinkSayDo.say: Taking the airway out now.
thinkSayDo.do: Remove OPA · reassess · continuous monitoring for re-sedation · SBAR · document

markTriggers: Names snoring with reduced consciousness as partial airway obstruction
Calls for urgent help early
Head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust before any adjunct
Suctions under direct vision
Justifies the OPA by absent response to voice and absent gag
Sizes from incisors to angle of jaw and inserts inverted, rotating 180°
Starts bag-valve-mask ventilation for RR 7 despite a patent airway
Holds further opioid doses and requests titrated naloxone per protocol
Removes the OPA immediately when he gags
Plans for re-sedation as naloxone wears off

cpsa.title: Choking on the Stroke Unit / Judge the Cough, Then Back Blows and Thrusts — and the Job Isn't Over When It Comes Out
cpsa.mlaTheme: Recognition of the acutely unwell patient
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Acute and emergency · adult foreign-body airway obstruction (RCUK 2025 adult choking algorithm) in a patient with post-stroke dysphagia; after-care following abdominal thrusts; diet-texture safety incident
cpsa.capabilities: Recognising choking and grading it by the effectiveness of the cough; encouraging an effective cough without interfering; calling for help as soon as the cough becomes ineffective; giving up to five back blows then up to five abdominal thrusts, checking after each, and repeating; never performing a blind finger sweep; knowing that if the patient becomes unresponsive CPR starts; after relief, arranging medical examination for abdominal-thrust injury and assessing for aspiration; keeping the patient nil by mouth pending speech and language therapy review; reporting the wrong-texture food as a patient safety incident without blaming the relative.
cpsa.setting: Hyperacute stroke unit, 12:40. You are the FY1. A seated choking manikin or role-player is used; the examiner gives findings and speaks for the nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Walter Pengelly, 79, is day 3 after a left middle cerebral artery infarct with dysphagia. You are passing his bay when his daughter calls: 'Dad's choking!' Manage the situation, talking through what you do, and deal with what follows.
cpsa.scenario: Mr Pengelly is on a speech and language therapy (SALT) plan for a pureed diet and mildly thick fluids, with supervision at meals. His daughter, Mrs Tamsin Pengelly-Ward, brought in a ham sandwich because 'he was desperate for proper food'. He is sitting in his chair. Stage 1 (examiner): he is coughing forcefully, red-faced, able to say 'stuck'. Stage 2 (about 1 minute later): 'His cough has become silent, he cannot speak, he is clutching his throat and his lips are turning dusky.' If up to five back blows are given correctly: 'No relief.' If up to five abdominal thrusts are given correctly: 'A piece of bread comes out. He takes a big breath and coughs.' After relief (examiner gives on request): RR 26, SpO₂ 91% on air, HR 112, BP 156/88, alert; coarse crackles at the right base; he complains of pain in the upper abdomen. The daughter is tearful: 'This is my fault, isn't it?'

markingGrid.domain: Recognises choking and asks 'Are you choking?', grading the obstruction by the cough
With an effective cough, encourages coughing and stays with him — no back blows yet
Recognises the change to an ineffective cough as severe obstruction and calls for help immediately (nurse, emergency team)
Gives up to five back blows correctly (leaning forward, heel of the hand between the shoulder blades), checking after each
Gives up to five abdominal thrusts correctly (fist between umbilicus and xiphisternum, inward and upward), checking after each, and states he would repeat the cycle
Avoids a blind finger sweep and states that if he becomes unresponsive he would call 2222 and start CPR
After relief, reassesses ABCDE, gives oxygen titrated to target and recognises possible aspiration (crackles, SpO₂ 91%)
Arranges medical examination for abdominal-thrust injury given his epigastric pain
Keeps him nil by mouth, asks for SALT reassessment and a chest X-ray, and escalates to the registrar
Reports the incident, reinforces the diet plan with the daughter without blame and checks the bay's mealtime supervision

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: Dad's choking!

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He is coughing forcefully, red-faced, able to say 'stuck'.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Immediately starts hard back blows.) Come on, get it out! (Reaches into his mouth with a finger.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: His cough has become silent, he cannot speak, he is clutching his throat and his lips are turning dusky.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Keep coughing, Mr Pengelly, keep coughing! (Waits.) Can someone get a doctor?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: You are the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Gives several back blows, then stops.) I'll try the Heimlich. (One abdominal thrust.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: A piece of bread comes out. He takes a big breath and coughs.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Great, it's out. He's fine now. Let's get him back to his lunch — maybe something softer.

fail.examinerNote: Intervened while the cough was effective and did a blind finger sweep, risking pushing the food deeper. Then, when the obstruction became severe, told him to keep coughing and did not call for help. Once the bread came out, ignored the hypoxia, crackles and abdominal pain, and returned a dysphagic patient to oral food without SALT review.
fail.summary: Graded the cough wrongly at both stages; blind sweep; no help; no after-care for aspiration or thrust injury; restarted food.

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: Dad's choking!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Pengelly, are you choking?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He is coughing forcefully, red-faced, able to say 'stuck'.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Good strong cough — keep coughing, I'm right here. (Stays beside him.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: His cough has become silent, he cannot speak, he is clutching his throat and his lips are turning dusky.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Help, please — choking in bay 2! (Leans him forward, supports his chest.) Back blows. (Gives up to five, checking after each.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: No relief.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Abdominal thrusts. (Stands behind, fist above the umbilicus, inward and upward, up to five, checking after each.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: A piece of bread comes out. He takes a big breath and coughs.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Well done, Mr Pengelly. I'm going to check your breathing. Oxygen, please. (To examiner.) If he'd gone unresponsive, I'd have called 2222 and started CPR.

pass.examinerNote: Graded the cough correctly at both stages, called for help as soon as it became ineffective and gave correctly performed back blows then abdominal thrusts with checks. Knew the unresponsive pathway. After relief, started oxygen but did not identify the aspiration signs, did not arrange examination for thrust injury despite his abdominal pain, and did not address diet, SALT or the incident.
pass.summary: Correct choking sequence with help called; after-care incomplete — aspiration, thrust injury and SALT not addressed.

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: Dad's choking!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Pengelly, are you choking?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He is coughing forcefully, red-faced, able to say 'stuck'.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's a strong cough — keep coughing, it's the best thing. I'm staying right with you. (To daughter.) Could you press the buzzer, please?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: His cough has become silent, he cannot speak, he is clutching his throat and his lips are turning dusky.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The cough has stopped working — this is now severe. (Loudly.) Help — choking in bay 2, bring the emergency trolley! (Leans him well forward, one hand on his chest.) Up to five back blows, checking each time. (Heel of hand between the shoulder blades.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: No relief.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Abdominal thrusts. (Behind him, fist between navel and breastbone, other hand over it, sharp inward and upward pulls — checking after each.) If this fails I'll go back to five back blows. If he becomes unresponsive, I'll lower him safely, call 2222 and start CPR — no finger in the mouth unless I can see the food.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: A piece of bread comes out. He takes a big breath and coughs.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Well done. Let's get you comfortable. Observations, please, and oxygen.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: RR 26, SpO₂ 91% on air, HR 112, BP 156/88, alert. Coarse crackles at the right base. He says his upper tummy hurts.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Oxygen to keep him in his normal target range. With crackles at the right base he may have aspirated — chest X-ray and a sepsis screen if he becomes febrile. And anyone who has had abdominal thrusts needs examining for internal injury — I'll examine his abdomen now and ask the registrar to review. He stays nil by mouth until SALT reassess his swallow.

dialogue.speaker: DAUGHTER
dialogue.text: This is my fault, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: You brought him something he loves — that came from caring about him. The stroke has affected his swallow, so food has to be a very particular texture for now. Let's ask the speech therapist to talk you through what's safe to bring. I'll report what happened so we can make sure the whole ward's mealtime checks are working — that's about the system, not about you.

distinction.examinerNote: Graded the cough out loud at each stage and acted on the change, called for help at the right moment, and delivered back blows and abdominal thrusts correctly with checks and the plan to repeat. Stated the unresponsive pathway and the rule on finger sweeps. After relief, recognised probable aspiration, arranged examination for thrust injury as RCUK advises, kept him nil by mouth pending SALT and escalated. Supported the daughter without blame and reported the incident as a system issue.
distinction.summary: Cough graded at each stage; correct back blows and thrusts with help called; aspiration and thrust injury addressed; NBM and SALT; incident reported; daughter supported.

cpsa.hook: In choking, the cough decides everything: if it works, leave it alone; if it fails, back blows then abdominal thrusts; if he goes unresponsive, CPR. And when the food comes out, the patient still needs a doctor.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The first trap is acting too early — slapping the back of a man who is coughing effectively, or sweeping a finger blindly into his mouth. The second is acting too late — telling him to keep coughing once the cough has gone silent. The RCUK 2025 adult choking algorithm is: effective cough, encourage cough and watch for deterioration; ineffective cough in a conscious patient, call for help and give up to five back blows then up to five abdominal thrusts, repeating; unconscious, call for help and start CPR. The third trap comes after relief: abdominal thrusts can cause internal injury, so the patient needs medical examination, and in a stroke patient with crackles and SpO₂ 91% aspiration must be considered. The sandwich is a safety incident, not a family failing.

thinkSayDo.think: He can cough and speak — the airway is only partly blocked.
thinkSayDo.say: Keep coughing — I'm right here.
thinkSayDo.do: Encourage cough · stay with him · no back blows yet

thinkSayDo.think: Silent cough, can't speak, going dusky — severe obstruction.
thinkSayDo.say: Help — choking in bay 2!
thinkSayDo.do: Up to 5 back blows → up to 5 abdominal thrusts · check after each · repeat · no blind sweep

thinkSayDo.think: If he goes floppy, choking becomes cardiac arrest.
thinkSayDo.say: If he becomes unresponsive, I'll call 2222 and start CPR.
thinkSayDo.do: Lower safely · 2222 · CPR

thinkSayDo.think: Out is not over — aspiration and thrust injury.
thinkSayDo.say: He needs his chest and abdomen checking, and nothing by mouth until SALT see him.
thinkSayDo.do: Oxygen to target · examine abdomen · CXR · NBM · SALT · registrar · incident report

Encourages an effective cough without intervening
Calls for help when the cough becomes ineffective
Up to five back blows with the patient leaning forward
Up to five abdominal thrusts, inward and upward, checking after each
No blind finger sweep
States CPR and 2222 if he becomes unresponsive
Recognises possible aspiration after relief

cpsa.title: Digital Rectal Examination / The Haemorrhoid Is Not the Answer
cpsa.contentMap: Clinical examination / Colorectal surgery · Digital rectal examination on a manikin for rectal bleeding: inspection, systematic palpation, describing a rectal mass and referral without waiting for FIT
cpsa.capabilities: Explaining an intimate examination and obtaining consent; offering a chaperone and recording their identity; positioning in the left lateral position with dignity; inspecting the perianal area before palpation; gentle lubricated insertion with warning; assessing tone, all rectal walls and the prostate; inspecting the glove; describing a rectal mass by distance from the anal verge, wall, size, consistency and fixity; not attributing bleeding to an incidental haemorrhoid; urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for a palpable rectal mass without waiting for a FIT result; honest explanation without diagnosing; documentation
cpsa.setting: GP surgery. You are the FY1 on a GP placement. A rectal examination manikin is provided; the role-player speaks for the patient and the examiner gives findings.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Desmond Quarrell, 69, has had 6 weeks of rectal bleeding. Your GP supervisor has asked you to perform a digital rectal examination before deciding the next step. Explain, obtain consent and examine on the manikin. Tell the examiner your findings and explain the plan to the patient.
cpsa.scenario: Mr Quarrell is a retired bus driver. For 6 weeks he has passed dark red blood mixed in with the stool, with some mucus, looser stools than usual and a feeling of not having fully emptied; he has lost about 3 kg without trying. He had 'piles' treated with cream 10 years ago. He takes amlodipine; no anticoagulants. A FIT kit was given to him last week and is still at home, unused. A healthcare assistant is available to chaperone. When the candidate inspects, the examiner says: 'Two small external skin tags at the anal margin and a small, non-tender external haemorrhoid. No fissure, no fistula opening, no blood at the margin.' On palpation (only for the findings asked about): normal anal tone and squeeze; on the posterior rectal wall, about 6 cm from the anal verge, a hard, irregular, ulcerated mass about 3 cm across, fixed, with its upper edge just reachable; prostate smooth, moderately enlarged, median sulcus palpable, non-tender. Glove: dark blood and mucus. After the examination he says: 'It's the piles again, isn't it? Can't I just do the poo test and wait?'

markingGrid.domain: Explains why the examination is needed, what it involves and that it may be uncomfortable; tells him he can ask to stop; obtains consent
Offers a chaperone, provides privacy and covering, and records the chaperone's identity
Hand hygiene and gloves; positions him in the left lateral position with knees drawn up
Inspects the perianal area before inserting a finger and reports the skin tags and haemorrhoid
Warns before insertion, uses adequate lubrication and inserts gently
Assesses anal tone and squeeze, sweeps all walls of the rectum, and assesses the prostate
Inspects the glove for blood, mucus and stool colour, then restores dignity and offers tissues
Describes the mass precisely: distance from the anal verge, wall, size, consistency, surface, fixity and whether the upper edge is reachable
Does not attribute the bleeding to the haemorrhoid; arranges an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral and tells his GP supervisor the same day

Explains that a palpable rectal mass is referred directly and the FIT result does not change that decision; explains honestly that cancer is possible without stating a diagnosis; documents findings, chaperone and plan

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I need to do a back passage exam. Can you lie on your side?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Right now? Okay.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Inserts the finger without inspecting or warning.) Sorry. (Withdraws after a few seconds.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: There's a haemorrhoid at the anal margin, so that's probably the source of the bleeding.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: It's the piles again, isn't it? Can't I just do the poo test and wait?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Yes, do the FIT test and we'll go from there. Some cream should help the piles.

fail.examinerNote: No explanation, consent or chaperone offer for an intimate examination, no inspection, no warning and an incomplete palpation that never felt the rectal walls. The candidate attached the bleeding to an incidental haemorrhoid and endorsed waiting for a FIT result, missing a hard, fixed rectal mass in a 69-year-old with weight loss — a delayed cancer diagnosis.
fail.summary: No consent or chaperone; no inspection; incomplete palpation; mass missed; bleeding blamed on a haemorrhoid; FIT used as a reason to wait.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Quarrell, I'm one of the FY1 doctors. To help find the cause of the bleeding, I'd like to examine your back passage with a gloved, lubricated finger. It's uncomfortable but shouldn't be painful, and you can ask me to stop at any time. A healthcare assistant will be here as a chaperone. Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Fine, let's get it done.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, gloves, left lateral position, sheet over.) I'm going to look first. (Inspects.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Two small external skin tags at the anal margin and a small, non-tender external haemorrhoid. No fissure, no fistula opening, no blood at the margin.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Now my finger — a cold feeling. (Lubricates, inserts gently, checks tone, sweeps the walls, feels the prostate.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Normal tone. Posterior wall, about 6 cm in: a hard, irregular, ulcerated mass about 3 cm across, fixed. Prostate smooth, moderately enlarged. Dark blood and mucus on the glove.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To patient, after covering him.) There's an area inside the back passage that feels abnormal, so I need you to see the bowel specialists urgently. I'll speak to my supervisor and make that referral today.

pass.examinerNote: Good explanation, consent and chaperone; correct position; inspected first; warned, lubricated, systematic palpation and glove inspection. Found the mass and arranged an urgent referral. The description lacked consistency of reporting (surface, fixity, upper edge), the request to wait for the FIT test was not addressed, and the explanation did not prepare him for the possibility of cancer.
pass.summary: Consented, chaperoned, systematic examination; mass found; urgent referral; FIT question and honest framing not addressed.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Quarrell, I'm one of the FY1 doctors. With the bleeding you've described, an examination of the back passage is an important part of finding the cause. I'll look at the skin around it, then feel inside with a gloved, lubricated finger for about a minute. It can be uncomfortable but shouldn't hurt, and you can ask me to stop at any time. A healthcare assistant, Mo, will be in the room as a chaperone. Any questions? Are you happy to go ahead?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, go on.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Privacy to undress, left lateral, knees up, sheet over. Hand hygiene, gloves.) I'm going to lift your buttock to look first. (Inspects.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Two small external skin tags at the anal margin and a small, non-tender external haemorrhoid. No fissure, no fistula opening, no blood at the margin.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) A haemorrhoid is common at his age, so I won't let that explain the bleeding until I've felt inside. (To patient.) Now my finger — cool and slippery, take a slow breath out. (Inserts gently.) Squeeze my finger, please. (Sweeps through 360 degrees, then feels the prostate anteriorly.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Normal tone and squeeze. Posterior wall, about 6 cm in: a hard, irregular, ulcerated mass about 3 cm across, fixed, upper edge just reachable. Prostate smooth, moderately enlarged, sulcus present. Dark blood and mucus on the glove.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Withdraws gently, inspects glove, offers tissues, covers him.) (To examiner.) Summary: a hard, irregular, ulcerated, fixed mass on the posterior rectal wall, about 6 cm from the anal verge and about 3 cm across, upper edge reachable; dark blood and mucus on the glove; incidental skin tags and a small haemorrhoid; smooth benign-feeling prostate.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: It's the piles again, isn't it? Can't I just do the poo test and wait?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I can see why you'd hope so, and you do have a small pile, but it isn't the explanation. I felt a firm, irregular area inside the back passage. I can't tell you what it is from a finger examination, but one possibility is a bowel cancer, and that's why I don't want you to wait. When a lump can be felt, we don't need the poo test to decide — I'm referring you urgently to the bowel team on the suspected cancer pathway, so you're seen quickly for a camera test and biopsies, with the aim of an answer within four weeks. I'll check a blood count today too.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll tell my GP supervisor now, document the consent, Mo as chaperone, the findings and the urgent referral, and make sure Mr Quarrell knows to call us if he hasn't heard within a week or if the bleeding becomes heavy or he feels faint.

distinction.examinerNote: Thorough consent with a named chaperone, dignified positioning, inspection first, a gentle and systematic palpation with tone, all walls and the prostate, and glove inspection. Explicitly refused to let the incidental haemorrhoid explain the bleeding. Described the mass in reportable terms (distance, wall, size, consistency, surface, fixity, upper edge). Answered the request to wait for FIT correctly — a palpable rectal mass goes straight to an urgent suspected cancer pathway — and was honest about cancer as a possibility without diagnosing it. Documentation and safety-netting complete.
distinction.summary: Complete, respectful DRE; haemorrhoid not accepted as the cause; mass described precisely; FIT not used to delay; honest explanation; urgent referral and safety-net.

cpsa.hook: Inspection finds the distractor; the finger finds the diagnosis. A haemorrhoid at 69 is a finding, not an explanation — and once a rectal mass is felt, the referral is urgent and does not wait for a FIT result.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The station places a small external haemorrhoid where every candidate will see it. Weak candidates stop there, blame it for the bleeding, and agree with the patient that a FIT test at home can decide. With dark blood mixed in the stool, mucus, tenesmus and weight loss at 69, the history already points beyond piles, and palpation finds a hard, fixed, ulcerated mass. NICE NG12 supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for a rectal mass, and BSG/ACPGBI guidance on FIT advises that people with a rectal mass are referred on the suspected cancer pathway without waiting for FIT. The technique marks are for the order and the dignity: explanation, consent, chaperone with identity recorded, left lateral, inspection before palpation, warning, lubrication, tone, all walls, prostate, glove. Describe position by wall (anterior, posterior, left, right) and distance from the anal verge rather than a clock face, which depends on how the patient is lying.

thinkSayDo.think: Intimate examination: he needs to know what, why and that he can stop.
thinkSayDo.say: A gloved, lubricated finger for about a minute — tell me to stop at any time.
thinkSayDo.do: Consent · chaperone named · privacy · left lateral · hand hygiene and gloves

thinkSayDo.think: Look before I feel — but what I see may not be the answer.
thinkSayDo.say: I'll look first, then feel inside.
thinkSayDo.do: Inspect · warn · lubricate · gentle insertion · tone · 360-degree sweep · prostate · glove

thinkSayDo.think: A hard, fixed mass must be described so the next doctor can find it.
thinkSayDo.say: Posterior wall, 6 cm from the verge, 3 cm, hard, irregular, ulcerated, fixed.
thinkSayDo.do: Report distance, wall, size, consistency, surface, fixity, upper edge

thinkSayDo.think: The haemorrhoid and the FIT kit are both reasons to wait — neither applies.
thinkSayDo.say: When a lump can be felt, we don't need the poo test to decide.
thinkSayDo.do: Urgent suspected cancer referral · FBC · tell supervisor · document · safety-net

Inspects before inserting a finger
