cpsa.title: Bimanual Pelvic Examination in Pelvic Pain / Pregnancy Test First, and the Coil Is Not the Emergency
cpsa.contentMap: Clinical examination / Sexual health and gynaecology · Bimanual pelvic examination on a manikin in lower abdominal pain: pregnancy excluded first, cervical motion and adnexal tenderness, PID with a copper coil in place
cpsa.capabilities: Checking a pregnancy test before a pelvic examination in a woman with pelvic pain; explaining an intimate examination and obtaining consent; offering a chaperone and recording their identity; positioning with dignity; inspecting the vulva; performing a gentle bimanual examination assessing cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, position and tenderness, and both adnexa; stopping if pain is significant; interpreting findings in context as pelvic inflammatory disease; starting empirical treatment without waiting for swab results; recognising that a copper coil does not routinely need removing in PID and that removal would require attention to recent unprotected sex; criteria for admission; documentation
cpsa.setting: GP surgery. You are the FY1 on a GP placement. A pelvic examination manikin is provided; the role-player speaks for the patient and the examiner gives findings.
cpsa.yourRole: Ms Jodie Mallinson, 27, has 5 days of lower abdominal pain. Your GP supervisor has taken the history and asked you to perform a bimanual pelvic examination. Prepare, obtain consent and examine on the manikin, tell the examiner your findings, and explain the next steps to the patient.
cpsa.scenario: Ms Mallinson works in a call centre. She has 5 days of aching pain low in both sides of her abdomen, pain deep inside during sex, a new yellowish discharge and some bleeding between periods. A copper coil was fitted 2 years ago. She has had a new partner for 2 months; they last had sex 2 days ago, without a condom. Last period 3 weeks ago. No vomiting, no shoulder-tip pain, no fainting, no urinary symptoms. No allergies. Observations: temperature 37.8 °C, HR 92, BP 118/74, RR 16. A urine pregnancy test has been done by the nurse; the result is given only if the candidate asks: negative. A practice nurse is available to chaperone. Findings on request: abdomen — tender in both lower quadrants, no guarding, no rebound, no mass. Vulva — normal; yellow discharge at the introitus. Speculum (if the candidate says they would perform one): mucopurulent discharge at the os, coil threads visible; swabs taken. Bimanual: marked cervical motion tenderness; uterus normal size, anteverted, mobile, mildly tender; tenderness in both adnexa, no adnexal mass. When the findings are given, the patient says: 'It's the coil, isn't it? Can you just take it out now?'

markingGrid.domain: Checks the pregnancy test result before examining
Explains the purpose and what the examination involves, that it may be uncomfortable and that she can stop at any time; obtains consent
Offers a chaperone, provides privacy and covering, positions her comfortably and records the chaperone's identity
Hand hygiene and gloves; inspects the vulva; lubricates and warns before inserting two fingers gently
Assesses cervical motion tenderness and the cervix
Uses the abdominal hand to assess uterine size, position, mobility and tenderness
Assesses both adnexa for tenderness or a mass, watching her face and stopping if pain is significant
Withdraws, inspects the glove, restores dignity, and states the findings in order and the working diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease
Plans swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea and starts empirical antibiotics per the national or local guideline today, without waiting for results, with early review

Explains that the coil does not routinely need removing and that, if it were removed, sex 2 days ago would create a pregnancy risk needing emergency contraception; states admission criteria, partner notification and HIV and syphilis testing

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'm going to do an internal examination now, if you could lie back.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Okay… is it going to hurt?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: A bit. (Inserts fingers without lubrication or warning, presses firmly.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Marked cervical motion tenderness. Uterus normal size, mildly tender. Both adnexa tender, no mass.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Ow! It's the coil, isn't it? Can you just take it out now?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Probably the coil, yes. I'll take it out and you can have some antibiotics once the swabs are back.

fail.examinerNote: No pregnancy test checked, no consent, no chaperone offer, no lubrication or warning, and continued pressing through obvious pain. Blamed the coil and planned to remove it without asking about recent sex, leaving her at risk of pregnancy, and delayed antibiotics until swab results — the delay that leads to tubal damage.
fail.summary: Pregnancy not excluded; no consent or chaperone; rough technique; coil removed reflexively without contraceptive thought; antibiotics delayed.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Before I examine, may I have the pregnancy test result?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Negative.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Mallinson, I'm one of the FY1 doctors. I'd like to examine inside with two gloved, lubricated fingers, with my other hand on your tummy, to find where the pain is coming from. It may be uncomfortable; tell me to stop at any time. The nurse will be here as a chaperone. Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, gloves, positions, covers, inspects, lubricates, warns, inserts gently. Moves the cervix, then the uterus, then each side.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Marked cervical motion tenderness. Uterus normal size, anteverted, mildly tender. Both adnexa tender, no mass.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) With a negative pregnancy test, a low-grade fever, discharge, and cervical motion and bilateral adnexal tenderness, this is most likely pelvic inflammatory disease. I'd take swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea and start antibiotics per the guideline today, without waiting for results, and review her in a few days.

pass.examinerNote: Excluded pregnancy first, consented with a chaperone and examined gently and systematically. Correct interpretation and the key decision to treat empirically today. The request to remove the coil was not answered, so the contraceptive consequence of removal and recent unprotected sex was not considered; admission criteria and partner management were not mentioned.
pass.summary: Pregnancy excluded; consent and chaperone; systematic gentle examination; PID recognised; empirical treatment; coil question not addressed.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Before any pelvic examination for pain, I need the pregnancy test — an ectopic pregnancy changes everything. May I have it?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Negative.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Mallinson, I'm one of the FY1 doctors. To work out where the pain is coming from, I'd like to examine you internally: two gloved, lubricated fingers inside, my other hand on your tummy, about a minute. It may be uncomfortable, and you can tell me to stop at any time. The practice nurse will be with us as a chaperone. Do you have any questions? Are you happy for me to go ahead?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Okay. Go gently.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Privacy to undress, sheet over, lying back, heels together, knees apart. Hand hygiene, gloves. Inspects the vulva.) I'm going to touch your thigh, then insert my fingers. (Lubricates, inserts gently.) I'm going to move the neck of the womb slightly side to side. (Then abdominal hand above the pubic bone to bring the uterus down; then each side in turn, watching her face.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Marked cervical motion tenderness. Uterus normal size, anteverted, mobile, mildly tender. Both adnexa tender, no mass.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Withdraws, checks the glove, covers her.) (To examiner.) Marked cervical motion tenderness, bilateral adnexal tenderness without a mass, uterus normal size, anteverted, mobile and mildly tender. With a negative pregnancy test, temperature 37.8, mucopurulent discharge and a new partner, the working diagnosis is pelvic inflammatory disease. She is not severely unwell, has no peritonism and no mass to suggest an abscess, so she can be treated as an outpatient. I'd take swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, offer HIV and syphilis testing, and start antibiotics per the BASHH-based local guideline today — waiting for results risks damage to the tubes.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: It's the coil, isn't it? Can you just take it out now?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The coil isn't the cause of the infection, and it doesn't usually need to come out — the antibiotics work with it in place. We'll review you in two to three days, and if you're not clearly better by then, we'd take it out. One important point: you had sex two days ago, and if the coil came out today you could get pregnant from that, so we'd need to talk about emergency contraception first. I'd rather keep it in and treat you now.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To patient.) Please avoid sex until you and your partner have both been treated; the sexual health team can help contact him. If the pain gets much worse, you vomit and can't keep tablets down, or you feel faint or feverish, come back the same day — that would mean hospital treatment. (To examiner.) I'll document consent, the chaperone's name, findings, treatment and a review within 72 hours.

distinction.examinerNote: Made the pregnancy test the gate to the examination. Consent, chaperone and dignity were excellent; the bimanual was gentle and systematic, with her face watched throughout. Interpreted the findings in context, judged severity for outpatient care, and started empirical treatment without waiting for swabs. Handled the coil request correctly: no routine removal in PID, removal if no significant improvement at 48–72 hours, and — the hidden hazard — removal two days after unprotected sex would need emergency contraception. Partner notification, wider STI testing, safety-netting and documentation complete.
distinction.summary: Pregnancy excluded first; exemplary consent and technique; PID recognised and treated empirically; coil kept with reasons; contraceptive risk spotted; admission criteria and partner care.

cpsa.hook: In a woman with pelvic pain, the first instrument is the pregnancy test, not the hand. And when the findings point to PID, the emergency is the antibiotics today — not pulling out the coil she relies on for contraception.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Two reflexes are tested. The first is examining without checking pregnancy: cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness also occur in ectopic pregnancy, so the result must be known before the findings are interpreted. The second is the coil. Patients and doctors often assume an intrauterine device must come out in PID. UK sexual health guidance does not require routine removal: treatment starts with it in place, she is reviewed at 48–72 hours, and it is removed if there has not been significant improvement. If it is removed, sex in the preceding 7 days creates a pregnancy risk that needs emergency contraception — she had sex 2 days ago. Swab results must not delay antibiotics: BASHH advises a low threshold for empirical treatment because delay increases the risk of infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain. Antibiotic regimens are left to the guideline; the marks are for the order, the technique and the decisions.

thinkSayDo.say: I'm going to move the neck of the womb slightly — tell me if that hurts.
thinkSayDo.do: Inspect · lubricate · cervix and motion tenderness · uterus with abdominal hand · each adnexum

thinkSayDo.think: Cervical motion and bilateral adnexal tenderness with fever and discharge: PID until proven otherwise.
thinkSayDo.say: This looks like an infection of the womb and tubes; I'd like to start treatment today.
thinkSayDo.do: Swabs · empirical antibiotics per guideline · HIV and syphilis offer · early review

thinkSayDo.think: The coil is not the emergency; removing it creates a new risk.
thinkSayDo.say: It doesn't usually need to come out — and if it did, sex two days ago would mean emergency contraception.
thinkSayDo.do: Keep coil · review at 48–72 hours, remove if not improving · partner notification · safety-net

cpsa.title: Glasgow Coma Scale on the Surgical Ward / Score the Parts, Then Find the Cause
cpsa.mlaTheme: Recognition of the acutely unwell patient
cpsa.contentMap: Clinical examination / Acute and perioperative care · Structured GCS assessment on a role-player with correct stimuli and component reporting; postoperative opioid toxicity from a PCA pressed by a relative, with acute kidney injury
cpsa.capabilities: Assessing conscious level with the Glasgow Coma Scale using a structured approach (check, observe, stimulate, rate); choosing appropriate stimuli (speech, fingertip pressure, trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure) and applying them safely; reporting eye, verbal and motor components as well as the total; examining pupils; moving straight from a reduced GCS to ABCDE; recognising opioid toxicity (drowsiness, slow breathing, small pupils) and its causes, including PCA activation by someone other than the patient and accumulation in acute kidney injury; stopping the opioid, calling for help, supporting breathing and giving titrated naloxone per protocol; checking capillary glucose; planning frequent reassessment; incident reporting and documentation
cpsa.setting: Surgical ward, 16:00. You are the FY1. A role-player plays the patient and acts out the responses; do not apply real painful pressure — demonstrate the stimulus and the examiner will tell you the response.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Howard Brackley, 74, is on day 2 after an open right hemicolectomy, with a morphine PCA. The nurse is worried he has become very drowsy. Assess his conscious level using the Glasgow Coma Scale, tell the examiner the score and what it means, and start management.
cpsa.scenario: Nurse: 'He was GCS 15 this morning. He's very sleepy now — his son says he's just catching up on sleep after a bad night, but I'm not happy.' On assessment: eyes closed; no eye opening to voice; eyes open to fingertip pressure (E2). Speaks in single words — 'leave… tired… what' — not conversation (V3). Does not obey commands; with trapezius pinch, his hand comes up across the midline towards the stimulus (M5). Total GCS 10 (E2 V3 M5). Pupils 2 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Snoring intermittently; airway clears with a head tilt and chin lift. RR 8, SpO₂ 89% on air, HR 64, BP 112/70, temperature 36.9 °C. Capillary glucose (if asked) 6.4 mmol/L. PCA chart (if asked): 14 boluses in the last 6 hours, compared with 4 overnight. His son, when asked, says he 'pressed the button for him while he slept so he wouldn't wake in pain'. This morning's bloods (if asked): creatinine 168 micromol/L (88 before surgery); urine output 15 mL/h for the last 4 hours. No focal neurological signs. Abdomen soft, wound clean.

markingGrid.domain: Checks for factors affecting the assessment (hearing, sedation, language) and observes spontaneous eye opening, speech and movement before stimulating

Escalates stimulus correctly: speech first, then a safe physical stimulus — fingertip pressure for eye opening, trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure for localising — demonstrated, not applied hard
Scores each component correctly and reports it as E2 V3 M5, total 10, compared with 15 this morning
Examines pupil size and reaction and records them separately from the GCS
Moves immediately to ABCDE: opens the airway with head tilt and chin lift, notes RR 8 and SpO₂ 89%, gives oxygen
Recognises opioid toxicity, stops the PCA and calls for urgent help (registrar, outreach or acute pain team)

Gives naloxone IV in small titrated doses per the BNF or local protocol, aiming to restore breathing and responsiveness rather than reverse analgesia, and supports ventilation with a bag-valve-mask if needed
Checks capillary glucose and asks for the PCA chart and the renal function
Identifies both causes of the overdose — PCA pressed by the son and morphine accumulation in acute kidney injury — and explains to the son kindly that only the patient presses the button

Plans repeat GCS and observations frequently because naloxone wears off before morphine, alternative analgesia with the pain team, AKI management, an incident report and documentation of the components, not just the total

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: He was GCS 15 this morning. He's very sleepy now — his son says he's just catching up on sleep.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Brackley? Can you open your eyes? (Pause.) (Rubs his sternum hard.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: He opens his eyes briefly, mumbles a word, his hand comes up towards your hand.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: So GCS is about 10. That's not too bad — he's had a big operation and a bad night.

dialogue.speaker: COLLEAGUE
dialogue.text: Shall I leave the PCA running?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Yes, he'll need it for the pain. Let's recheck him in four hours.

fail.examinerNote: Shouted and then applied a hard sternal rub to a role-player instead of a structured, graded assessment; gave a rough total with no components and never looked at the pupils, breathing or saturations. A respiratory rate of 8, SpO₂ 89% and pinpoint pupils on a morphine PCA were missed, the opioid was left running and the patient was left for four hours — potentially fatal.
fail.summary: Unstructured assessment; harmful stimulus; no components or pupils; no ABCDE; opioid toxicity missed; PCA continued; no escalation.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: He was GCS 15 this morning. He's very sleepy now — his son says he's just catching up on sleep.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Brackley, it's one of the doctors. Can you open your eyes? (No response.) I'm going to press on your fingertip. (Demonstrates.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Eyes open to fingertip pressure. Single words only. Doesn't obey commands; with trapezius pinch his hand comes up across his body towards it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Eyes 2, verbal 3, motor 5 — GCS 10, down from 15. Pupils?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: 2 mm, equal, sluggish. RR 8, SpO₂ 89% on air.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Small pupils and a respiratory rate of 8 on a morphine PCA — this is opioid toxicity. Stop the PCA, please. Head tilt, chin lift, oxygen on. Could you put out an urgent call to the registrar and outreach and bring the naloxone? (To examiner.) I'd give small IV doses of naloxone per protocol, titrated to his breathing, check his glucose and recheck GCS every 15 minutes.

pass.examinerNote: Structured, graded stimuli with correct component scoring and pupil assessment; recognised opioid toxicity, stopped the PCA, opened the airway, gave oxygen, escalated and planned titrated naloxone and glucose. Did not look for why it happened — the bolus count, the son pressing the button and the acute kidney injury — so the cause would recur, and did not mention that naloxone wears off before morphine.
pass.summary: Correct GCS with components and pupils; opioid toxicity recognised; PCA stopped; airway, oxygen, naloxone, escalation; causes not explored.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: He was GCS 15 this morning. He's very sleepy now — his son says he's just catching up on sleep.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks — you're right to be worried. (Checks: no hearing aid, English-speaking, no sedatives charted except the PCA. Observes: eyes closed, no speech, no movement.) Mr Brackley, it's one of the doctors — can you open your eyes? (Louder.) Mr Brackley! (Nothing.) I'm going to press on your fingertip. (Demonstrates lateral fingertip pressure.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Eyes open to fingertip pressure and close again. He says 'leave… tired… what.' He doesn't squeeze your hand when asked.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Demonstrates a trapezius pinch.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: His hand comes up across his body towards the stimulus.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Eyes to pressure, 2; words, not conversation, 3; localising, 5 — E2 V3 M5, GCS 10, from 15 this morning. Pupils, please — and breathing.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Pupils 2 mm, equal, sluggish. Snoring. RR 8, SpO₂ 89% on air. HR 64, BP 112/70.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: This is opioid toxicity until proven otherwise. Please stop the PCA now. (Head tilt, chin lift — snoring settles.) Oxygen through a mask to keep his saturations up. Can you put out an urgent call for the registrar and outreach, and bring the naloxone and a bag-valve-mask? Capillary glucose too, please.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) If his breathing doesn't pick up with airway support, I'd ventilate with the bag-valve-mask. I'll give naloxone IV in small increments per the BNF and our protocol, titrated to his breathing and responsiveness — the aim is not to wake him in agony. Then I'll check the PCA chart and his kidney function.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Glucose 6.4. Fourteen boluses in six hours, four overnight. Creatinine 168, was 88. The son says he pressed the button for him while he slept.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To son.) Thank you for telling me — you were trying to keep him comfortable. The button is designed so that only your dad presses it: if he's too sleepy to press it, he doesn't need more. Pressing it for him gave him more morphine than his body could clear, especially as his kidneys are struggling. We're reversing it now.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Two causes: PCA by proxy and accumulation in acute kidney injury. Naloxone wears off before morphine, so he needs GCS, pupils and respiratory rate every 15 minutes initially and may need repeat doses or an infusion. I'll ask the acute pain team to plan analgesia that doesn't depend on the PCA, manage the AKI — fluids, catheter for hourly urine output, stop nephrotoxins — complete an incident report, and document the components and the times.

distinction.examinerNote: A model GCS: checked for confounders, observed before stimulating, escalated stimuli safely and in the right order, scored and reported each component and the trend, and examined the pupils separately. Moved without pause to airway, breathing, oxygen, escalation and titrated naloxone with ventilatory back-up, and checked glucose. Then found the two causes — PCA activation by the son and morphine accumulation in AKI — explained them to the son without blame, and planned close reassessment because naloxone is shorter-acting than morphine, alternative analgesia, AKI care, an incident report and documentation.
distinction.summary: Structured GCS with components, trend and pupils; immediate ABCDE; PCA stopped; titrated naloxone; both causes found; son counselled kindly; reassessment, AKI care and incident report.

cpsa.hook: A GCS is a description, not a diagnosis. E2 V3 M5 with small pupils and a respiratory rate of 8 on a PCA is opioid toxicity — and the next question is who pressed the button, and why his kidneys could not clear it.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Candidates fail this station in three ways. First, technique: a shout and a hard sternal rub, then a single number. The Glasgow structured approach is check, observe, stimulate, rate, with a physical stimulus only after speech fails — fingertip pressure for eye opening, trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure for localising — and the result reported as components (E2 V3 M5) because the total alone hides what changed. Pupils are recorded separately. Second, treating the score as the end point: a GCS of 10 with RR 8 and SpO₂ 89% demands ABCDE now. Third, the cause: PCA safety depends on only the patient pressing the button — sedation should stop them — so 'PCA by proxy' by a well-meaning relative bypasses that safeguard, and morphine metabolites accumulate in acute kidney injury. Naloxone is given in small titrated IV doses per the BNF or local protocol, and because it is shorter-acting than morphine, the patient is re-observed closely. The opioid reversal is marked as a decision; no dose is required.

thinkSayDo.think: Observe before I touch; escalate the stimulus only as far as needed.
thinkSayDo.say: Mr Brackley, can you open your eyes? I'm going to press on your fingertip.
thinkSayDo.do: Check confounders · observe · speech · fingertip pressure · trapezius pinch

thinkSayDo.think: Components, trend, pupils — then stop scoring and start treating.
thinkSayDo.say: E2 V3 M5, GCS 10, from 15 this morning. Pupils 2 mm, RR 8.
thinkSayDo.do: Report components · pupils · ABCDE · airway manoeuvre · oxygen

thinkSayDo.think: Small pupils, slow breathing, PCA: opioid toxicity.
thinkSayDo.say: Stop the PCA. Urgent call for the registrar and outreach. Naloxone, please.
thinkSayDo.do: Stop opioid · call for help · titrated IV naloxone · bag-valve-mask ready · glucose

thinkSayDo.think: Find the cause or it happens again tonight.
thinkSayDo.say: Only your dad presses the button — if he's too sleepy to press it, he doesn't need more.
thinkSayDo.do: PCA chart · renal function · counsel son · 15-minute obs · pain team · AKI care · incident report

markTriggers: Observes before stimulating and checks for confounders
Uses speech, then fingertip pressure, then a central stimulus — no hard sternal rub
Reports E2 V3 M5 and the fall from 15
Examines pupils and records them separately
Opens the airway and gives oxygen
Stops the PCA and calls for urgent help
Gives titrated IV naloxone per protocol
Checks capillary glucose
Identifies PCA by proxy and acute kidney injury as causes
Plans frequent reassessment because naloxone wears off first

cpsa.title: Fluid Balance Chart / Positive on Paper, Dry in the Bed
cpsa.contentMap: Acute medicine / Renal · interpreting a 12-hour fluid balance chart: totals, urine output per kg per hour, unmeasured losses; hypovolaemia with oliguria and AKI (NICE CG174 IV fluids, NICE NG148 AKI)
cpsa.capabilities: Totalling intake and output and stating the recorded balance; calculating urine output in mL/kg/hour and recognising oliguria; identifying what the chart does not capture — unmeasured diarrhoea, discarded vomit, an infusion that stopped, insensible losses; judging fluid status from the patient (observations, perfusion, mucous membranes, trend in blood pressure) rather than the arithmetic; staging AKI by creatinine and by urine output; giving a crystalloid bolus with reassessment per NICE CG174; withholding antihypertensives in hypovolaemia and AKI; making the chart reliable going forward; escalating a NEWS2 of 5.
cpsa.setting: Medical ward, 20:15. You are the FY1 on the evening shift. The fluid balance chart, observation chart and morning bloods are provided; the examiner gives examination findings on request and speaks for the nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Mrs Hilda Brockbank, 84, was admitted yesterday with vomiting and diarrhoea. The nurse asks you to review her fluid balance chart because her urine output has dropped. Interpret the chart aloud, assess her by asking the examiner for findings, and give a plan.
cpsa.scenario: Mrs Brockbank weighs 62 kg. Usual medication: ramipril 5 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily (both given at 08:00 today). Fluid chart 08:00–20:00: oral 400 mL; IV sodium chloride 0.9% 500 mL (1 litre prescribed over 8 hours from 08:00; the cannula tissued at 12:00 and the infusion was stopped, not resited); total in 900 mL. Urine 150 mL (80 mL 08:00–12:00, 50 mL 12:00–16:00, 20 mL 16:00–20:00); vomit 300 mL; stool column: 'BO ×3, type 7 — not measured'; total out recorded 450 mL; balance written as '+450'. Observations at 20:00: HR 108, BP 96/60 (138/76 on admission), RR 22, SpO₂ 97% on air, temperature 37.2 °C, alert (NEWS2 5). Bloods this morning: Na 136, K 3.3, urea 14.8, creatinine 141 µmol/L (79 three months ago). Examination (on request): dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, cool hands, JVP not visible lying flat, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft and mildly tender. The nurse says: 'The day team said she's 450 positive, so she doesn't need any more drip — I should just encourage oral, shouldn't I?' At about 4 minutes the nurse adds: 'Actually, her pad has been changed twice more for large watery stools, and she vomited into a bowl at lunchtime that got emptied before anyone measured it.'

markingGrid.domain: Totals intake (900 mL) and recorded output (450 mL) and states the recorded balance of +450 mL
Calculates urine output (150 mL over 12 hours in a 62 kg woman ≈ 0.2 mL/kg/hour, falling to about 0.08 in the last 4 hours) and names oliguria
Identifies what the chart misses — unmeasured diarrhoea, the IV that stopped at 12:00, insensible losses — and states the true balance is probably negative
Integrates the chart with tachycardia, falling blood pressure, prolonged capillary refill and dry mucous membranes as hypovolaemia
Identifies AKI and stages it by the higher criterion — creatinine about 1.8 times baseline is stage 1, but urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours is stage 2 — and notes the low potassium
Resites IV access and gives a 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes per NICE CG174, then reassesses
Withholds ramipril and amlodipine and reviews other nephrotoxic or hypotensive drugs
Escalates the NEWS2 of 5 for urgent review by the registrar
Makes the chart reliable: hourly urine output, stool chart with weighed pads, measured vomit, daily weights, and a replacement plus maintenance prescription including potassium
Uses the unmeasured losses to correct the plan rather than invent a precise balance, and teaches the nurse why 'positive' does not mean 'full'

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The day team said she's 450 positive, so she doesn't need any more drip — I should just encourage oral, shouldn't I?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Looks at the chart.) 900 in, 450 out — yes, she's positive. That's fine.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Urine's a bit low but she's 84, they don't drink much. Keep encouraging fluids.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Actually, her pad has been changed twice more for large watery stools, and a bowl of vomit got thrown away.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: OK, add that to the chart if you can. Maybe some loperamide. I'll check her bloods in the morning.

fail.examinerNote: Read the arithmetic and stopped. Did not calculate the urine output, did not look at the observations or examine her, and accepted a positive balance as proof of adequate hydration in a tachycardic, hypotensive, oliguric 84-year-old with AKI. Ignored the stopped infusion and the unmeasured losses, continued the antihypertensives by default and planned nothing until the morning.
fail.summary: Balance read as reassuring; oliguria, hypovolaemia and AKI missed; no fluid, no drug review, no escalation.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The day team said she's 450 positive, so she doesn't need any more drip — I should just encourage oral, shouldn't I?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: On paper, 900 in and 450 out, so plus 450. But urine is 150 mL in 12 hours — about 0.2 mL per kilo per hour. That's oliguria.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Can I examine her?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, cool hands, JVP not seen, chest clear.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: With a pulse of 108 and a pressure of 96 from 138, she's dry. Her creatinine is 141 from 79, and her urine has been under half a mL per kilo per hour for 12 hours — that's AKI, stage 2 on urine output. I'll put in a new cannula and give 500 mL of crystalloid over 15 minutes, then reassess. I'll hold the ramipril and amlodipine and ask the registrar to review.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Actually, her pad has been changed twice more for large watery stools, and a bowl of vomit got thrown away.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Then she's lost even more than the chart shows. Let's start hourly urine and a stool chart.

pass.examinerNote: Calculated the balance and the urine output, examined, recognised hypovolaemia and AKI, gave a protocol bolus with reassessment, held the antihypertensives and escalated. Did not explicitly identify the stopped infusion as a reason the 'given' fluid was lower than planned, did not address potassium or a replacement prescription, and did not explain to the nurse why the balance was misleading.
pass.summary: Balance and oliguria calculated; hypovolaemia and AKI recognised; bolus, drug hold and escalation; chart reliability and replacement plan partial.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The day team said she's 450 positive, so she doesn't need any more drip — I should just encourage oral, shouldn't I?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Let's read it together. In: 400 oral, 500 IV — 900. Out recorded: 150 urine, 300 vomit — 450. So plus 450 on paper.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: But look at what isn't counted. Three type 7 stools with no volume. The drip stopped at 12:00 when the cannula tissued — she only got half the litre. And nothing for sweat and breathing. Her real balance is almost certainly negative.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Urine: 150 mL over 12 hours at 62 kilos is about 0.2 mL per kilo per hour, and only 20 mL in the last four hours. That's oliguria, and it's getting worse.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) May I examine her and check the obs trend?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, cool hands, JVP not seen, chest clear, no oedema. BP was 138/76 on admission.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Pulse 108, pressure 96 from 138, cool and dry — she's hypovolaemic. Creatinine 141 from 79 is stage 1 on its own, but under 0.5 mL per kilo per hour for 12 hours makes this AKI stage 2 — and potassium is 3.3. NEWS2 is 5, so she needs urgent review — I'll call the registrar now.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: New cannula, then 500 mL of balanced crystalloid over less than 15 minutes per NICE CG174, and I'll reassess pulse, pressure, refill and urine straight after. I'm holding the ramipril and amlodipine.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Actually, her pad has been changed twice more for large watery stools, and she vomited into a bowl at lunchtime that got emptied before anyone measured it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you — that's important. It doesn't change what she needs now, because I'm treating her, not the number. Let's not try to guess a precise balance. From now: hourly urine, weigh the pads, measure every vomit, a stool chart and a stool sample, daily weights. After the bolus I'll write a prescription to replace her ongoing losses plus maintenance, with potassium, and an antiemetic.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) 'Positive' only means more was written going in than coming out. The patient tells us whether she's full — and right now she's dry.

distinction.examinerNote: Did the arithmetic, then dismantled it: identified the unmeasured stools, the infusion that stopped at 12:00 and insensible losses, and calculated a worsening urine output per kilo per hour. Confirmed hypovolaemia at the bedside, recognised AKI and hypokalaemia, escalated the NEWS2 score, gave a CG174 bolus with reassessment and held the antihypertensives. Treated the new information about unmeasured losses as a reason to fix the chart, not to invent a figure, and taught the nurse the principle.
distinction.summary: Chart totalled and deconstructed; oliguria per kg per hour; hypovolaemia, AKI and low potassium; CG174 bolus; drugs held; NEWS2 escalated; chart made reliable; nurse taught.

cpsa.hook: A fluid balance chart records what was written down, not what happened to the patient. 'Positive' on paper with a pulse of 108, a falling pressure and 0.2 mL/kg/hour of urine is a dry patient with an incomplete chart.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The arithmetic is deliberately easy, and the trap is stopping there. The recorded +450 mL omits three unmeasured type 7 stools, a litre of saline that stopped at 12:00 after only 500 mL, and insensible losses. Urine output of 150 mL over 12 hours in a 62 kg woman is about 0.2 mL/kg/hour — below the 0.5 mL/kg/hour used in AKI definitions — and falling. NICE CG174 indicators that fluid resuscitation is needed (systolic below 100, heart rate above 90, capillary refill over 2 seconds, RR over 20, NEWS2 5 or more) are all present; the response is a 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes with reassessment, not 'encourage oral'. Creatinine 141 from 79 meets stage 1, and urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours meets stage 2 — the higher stage applies — so the ACE inhibitor and the calcium-channel blocker are held. The late information about discarded vomit should not tempt the candidate to recalculate a precise figure: the chart is unreliable, and the patient is the measurement.

thinkSayDo.think: Do the sum — then ask what the sum leaves out.
thinkSayDo.say: Plus 450 on paper, but the stools, the stopped drip and insensible losses aren't counted.
thinkSayDo.do: Total in and out · identify unmeasured losses · infusion stopped at 12:00

thinkSayDo.think: Urine output is per kilo per hour, and the trend matters.
thinkSayDo.say: About 0.2 mL per kilo per hour, and only 20 mL in the last four hours.
thinkSayDo.do: Calculate · name oliguria · compare with 0.5 mL/kg/h

thinkSayDo.think: The patient settles the question the chart cannot.
thinkSayDo.say: Pulse 108, pressure 96 from 138, cool and dry — she's hypovolaemic with AKI.
thinkSayDo.do: Examine · NEWS2 5 → registrar · new cannula · 500 mL crystalloid < 15 min · reassess · hold ramipril and amlodipine

thinkSayDo.think: Fix the record so tomorrow's chart can be trusted.
thinkSayDo.say: From now: hourly urine, weighed pads, measured vomit, daily weights.
thinkSayDo.do: Stool chart and sample · replacement plus maintenance with potassium · antiemetic

markTriggers: States totals: 900 in, 450 out, +450 recorded
Calculates urine output ≈ 0.2 mL/kg/h and names oliguria
Notes the infusion stopped at 12:00 when the cannula tissued
Identifies unmeasured diarrhoea and insensible losses
Concludes the true balance is probably negative
Links tachycardia, falling BP and capillary refill to hypovolaemia
Stages AKI correctly (stage 2 on urine output) and notes potassium 3.3
Gives 500 mL crystalloid over less than 15 minutes and reassesses
Holds ramipril and amlodipine
Escalates NEWS2 5 and puts accurate monitoring in place

cpsa.title: Preparing and Giving an IV Antibiotic Injection / A Blank Allergy Box Is Not 'No Allergies'
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Medicines safety · Procedure: preparing and giving an IV antibiotic by slow injection through a peripheral cannula on a manikin; the drug chart allergy box is blank and the drug name hides a penicillin
cpsa.capabilities: Checking that a prescription is complete before preparing an IV medicine; treating a blank allergy box as unknown, not as no allergy; asking specifically about reactions to antibiotics and naming the drug to the patient; recognising that co-amoxiclav contains a penicillin; preparing a reconstituted IV injection using aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT); checking the cannula with a saline flush before giving a drug; giving a slow IV injection at the rate in the product information; safe sharps practice and disposal of an unused prepared dose; escalating promptly so that treatment of infection is not delayed; documenting an allergy with the reaction
cpsa.setting: Surgical assessment unit, 14:00. You are the FY1. A manikin arm with a peripheral cannula and a drug trolley are provided; the role-player speaks for the patient.
cpsa.yourRole: Mrs Margaret Haverstock, 61, was admitted this morning with acute cholecystitis. The registrar has prescribed IV co-amoxiclav and asked you to give the first dose now. Prepare the dose and give it through her cannula on the manikin, talking the examiner through your checks.
cpsa.scenario: Drug chart: co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV every 8 hours, first dose 14:00, signed and dated by the registrar; the allergy box has been left blank. Her wristband name, date of birth and hospital number match the chart. On the trolley: co-amoxiclav 1.2 g vial (in date), 20 mL water for injections, syringes, drawing-up needles, two 10 mL sodium chloride 0.9% flushes, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol wipes, a clean tray, gloves, apron, syringe labels, a sharps bin and the product information: reconstitute with 20 mL water for injections; give by slow IV injection over 3–4 minutes; give promptly after reconstitution. A 20 G cannula in the right forearm was sited this morning; the site is clean and flushes without pain. Observations: temperature 38.0 °C, HR 98, BP 132/78, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% on air. If asked only 'Any allergies?', she says 'No, I don't think so.' If asked about antibiotics or penicillin, or told the drug's name, she says: 'Penicillin — years ago I came out in a lumpy rash all over and my lips swelled up. Is this one of those?' Once the candidate has stopped and decided to contact the registrar, the examiner says: 'The registrar has reviewed her, recorded the allergy and prescribed a non-penicillin IV antibiotic. The simulated vial and its product information are on the tray: reconstitute with 10 mL water for injections and give by slow IV injection over 3–5 minutes. Please prepare and give it.'

markingGrid.domain: Introduces, explains the injection and gains consent; confirms identity against the wristband and chart
Checks the prescription is complete — drug, dose, route, time, signature — and that the dose has not already been given
Notices the blank allergy box, asks specifically about reactions to antibiotics, and names the drug to the patient before giving it
Recognises that co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, a penicillin, and does not give it
Contacts the prescriber promptly so an alternative is prescribed — the infection is not left untreated
Hand hygiene, clean tray and ANTT; checks vial, diluent and expiry; reconstitutes exactly as the product information states
Checks the cannula site and flushes with sodium chloride 0.9% before giving the drug
Gives the injection slowly over the stated time, flushes after, watches the patient for a reaction and disposes of sharps at the point of use
Asks about allergy before reconstituting, so no penicillin is drawn up; if a dose was prepared, labels it and discards it rather than leaving an unlabelled syringe
Documents the allergy with drug, reaction and date, tells the patient it is recorded, and reports the blank allergy box as a near miss

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Hello, I'm one of the doctors. I'm going to give you an antibiotic through your drip. Any allergies?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: No, I don't think so.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Reconstitutes without a word, carries the syringe to the bedside and connects it without a flush.) Here we go.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: What is it, love? Is it penicillin? I had a funny reaction to penicillin once.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: No, it's co-amoxiclav — a different one. It'll be fine.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Pushes the full 20 mL in under a minute, then leaves the needle on the tray.)

fail.examinerNote: Accepted 'no allergies' at face value with the allergy box blank, did not name the drug until asked, and then dismissed a penicillin reaction with lip swelling because the drug name did not contain the word 'penicillin'. The cannula was not checked, the injection was pushed far faster than stated and a sharp was left on the tray. A patient with a likely immediate-type penicillin allergy received a penicillin.
fail.summary: Blank allergy box accepted; penicillin inside co-amoxiclav missed; patient's warning dismissed; no flush; injection too fast; sharp left out.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mrs Haverstock, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your full name and date of birth? Thank you — that matches your wristband and chart. The team has prescribed an antibiotic into the drip for your gallbladder. Is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, go ahead.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (At the trolley, hand hygiene, ANTT, checks vial and expiry, reconstitutes with 20 mL water, labels the syringe.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (At the bedside.) Before I give it — this is co-amoxiclav. Have you ever reacted to an antibiotic?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Penicillin — I came out in a lumpy rash and my lips swelled up. Is this one of those?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: It is — co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, which is a penicillin. I'm not going to give it. I'll put this syringe aside to be discarded and speak to the registrar now so you get a different antibiotic without delay.

pass.examinerNote: Identity, consent, preparation and asepsis were sound, and the final bedside check — naming the drug and asking about antibiotic reactions — stopped the error before any drug was given. The candidate recognised the hidden penicillin and escalated promptly. However, the blank allergy box was not noticed at the start, so a penicillin dose was prepared that should never have been drawn up, and the allergy was not documented.
pass.summary: Prepared safely; caught the penicillin at the bedside check; escalated; blank allergy box not noticed at the start; allergy not documented.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mrs Haverstock, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your full name, date of birth and hospital number? Thank you — that matches. The prescription is complete: co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV at 14:00, signed, not yet given. But the allergy box is blank, so I need to ask you myself.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Have you ever had a reaction to any medicine — especially an antibiotic like penicillin?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Oh — penicillin. Years ago I came out in a lumpy rash all over and my lips swelled up. Is this one of those?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you, that's really important. This antibiotic is co-amoxiclav, and it contains amoxicillin, which is a penicillin. With lip swelling last time, I won't give it. I'll ask the registrar to choose a different antibiotic now — your infection still needs treating today.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'd bleep the registrar now: 'Mrs Haverstock has a penicillin allergy with urticaria and lip swelling — the allergy box was blank and co-amoxiclav is prescribed. Please review and prescribe an alternative.' I'll fill in the allergy box with the drug, the reaction and roughly when.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The registrar has reviewed her, recorded the allergy and prescribed a non-penicillin IV antibiotic. The simulated vial and its product information are on the tray: reconstitute with 10 mL water for injections and give by slow IV injection over 3–5 minutes. Please prepare and give it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Checks the new prescription against the wristband, checks the vial and expiry. Hand hygiene, apron, cleans the tray, ANTT — key parts not touched. Reconstitutes with 10 mL water, swirls until clear, checks for particles, labels the syringe.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (At the bedside.) The cannula site looks clean. Cleaning the port, letting it dry. Flushing with saline first — any pain? No swelling, flushing freely. Now the antibiotic, slowly, over about four minutes. Tell me straight away if you feel itchy, hot, wheezy or your lips tingle.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Finishes, flushes again, sharps straight into the bin.) All given. I'll check on you over the next few minutes. Your penicillin allergy is now on your chart and in your notes, so nobody gives it to you again.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll sign the administration with the time and document the allergy, the conversation with the registrar, and that no co-amoxiclav was given. A blank allergy box on a signed antibiotic prescription is a near miss, so I'll report it through the local system.

distinction.examinerNote: Saw the blank allergy box before preparing anything, asked specifically about antibiotics, recognised the penicillin hidden in a combination product and stopped before a dose was drawn up. Escalated with a clear SBAR so treatment was not delayed, then prepared and gave the replacement drug with ANTT, a pre-flush, the correct slow rate, observation for a reaction, a post-flush and safe sharps. The allergy was documented with the reaction, and the system failure was reported as a near miss.
distinction.summary: Blank box spotted early; penicillin recognised before drawing up; prompt escalation; replacement given with ANTT at correct rate; allergy documented; near miss reported.

cpsa.hook: A blank allergy box means nobody has asked — it does not mean there is no allergy. Name the drug to the patient before you give it: patients who say 'no allergies' often remember the penicillin only when they hear the name, and 'co-amoxiclav' does not sound like penicillin.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The patient's first answer — 'No, I don't think so' — invites the candidate to move on. The trap is twofold: a blank allergy box treated as 'none', and a drug whose name hides its penicillin. Weak candidates either never name the drug or reassure the patient that co-amoxiclav is 'a different one'. A second trap is stopping the drug and then walking away: she has acute cholecystitis and a fever, so the prescriber must be contacted promptly for an alternative. NICE CG183 asks for the drug, the reaction and its date to be documented. Once the replacement is prescribed, the station still tests the procedure itself: ANTT, reconstitution exactly as stated, a saline flush to check the cannula, the slow rate in the product information, watching for a reaction and sharps at the point of use.

thinkSayDo.think: The allergy box is blank — that is a question nobody has asked yet.
thinkSayDo.say: Have you ever reacted to any medicine, especially an antibiotic like penicillin?
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · prescription complete and not already given · allergy asked specifically, before preparing

thinkSayDo.think: Co-amoxiclav is amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid — it is a penicillin.
thinkSayDo.say: This contains a penicillin, so I won't give it. I'll get the registrar to choose another antibiotic now.
thinkSayDo.do: Do not prepare or give · prompt SBAR to prescriber · allergy box completed with drug, reaction and date

thinkSayDo.think: The replacement still needs a safe procedure.
thinkSayDo.say: Flushing first — tell me if it hurts. Now slowly, over about four minutes.
thinkSayDo.do: ANTT · reconstitute as stated · label · pre-flush · slow injection · post-flush · watch for reaction · sharps · document · report near miss

markTriggers: Confirms identity and gains consent
Checks the prescription is complete and not already given
Treats a blank allergy box as unknown and asks about antibiotic reactions
Names the drug to the patient before giving it
Recognises co-amoxiclav as a penicillin and withholds it
Escalates promptly so the infection is still treated
Uses ANTT and reconstitutes exactly as instructed
Flushes the cannula before and after the drug
Gives the injection at the slow rate stated and watches for a reaction
Documents the allergy with the reaction and reports the near miss

cpsa.title: Wound Swab / Clean the Surface, Sample the Wound Bed, Label at the Bedside
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Infection · Procedure: wound swab for culture and sensitivity on a simulated lower-leg wound; a pre-labelled specimen tube is offered mid-procedure
cpsa.capabilities: Confirming that a swab is indicated by clinical signs of infection rather than taken routinely; explaining the test and obtaining consent; hand hygiene, apron, gloves and an aseptic non-touch technique; removing surface exudate, slough and old dressing material with sterile saline before sampling; sampling viable tissue in the wound bed (or sending pus if any can be collected) without touching the surrounding skin; placing the swab straight into the correct transport medium; reading and refusing a pre-labelled tube and labelling at the bedside against the wristband; giving the site, clinical signs and antibiotic history on the request; re-dressing the wound; explaining that a positive culture is interpreted alongside the clinical picture; reporting a near miss; documentation
cpsa.setting: Surgical ward, 11:00. You are the FY1. A simulated wound on a lower-leg model is provided; the role-player speaks for the patient and for a healthcare assistant.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Clifford Dunstable, 71, was admitted four days ago with adhesional small bowel obstruction, which has settled without surgery. The nurse is worried about a wound on his left shin, and the registrar has asked you to take a wound swab before she reviews him on the afternoon round. Explain, obtain consent and take the swab on the model.
cpsa.scenario: Mr Dunstable caught his left shin on a car door a week before admission; his practice nurse cleaned it and closed it with adhesive strips. Over two days it has become sorer, and yellow-green exudate has soaked through the dressing. The obstruction has resolved and he is eating. Observations: temperature 37.9 °C, HR 92, BP 134/80, RR 16, SpO₂ 97% on air, alert (NEWS2 1). Type 2 diabetes on metformin; capillary glucose 9.8. No antibiotics this admission; no allergies. With the dressing off: a 4 cm partly separated linear wound with yellow slough and exudate on its surface; erythema about 2 cm around it, warm and tender; no fluctuance, no crepitus, no collection of pus that could be aspirated. He asks: 'Does this mean I need antibiotics now?' At about 4 minutes, once the candidate has cleaned the wound and is about to sample, a healthcare assistant holds out a transport tube: 'I've stuck a label on to save you time.' If the candidate reads it, the label carries the name and hospital number of the patient in the next bed.

markingGrid.domain: Confirms identity against the wristband, checks the indication and asks about antibiotics, allergies and diabetes
Explains the purpose and what to expect in plain language, obtains consent and provides privacy
Hand hygiene, apron and gloves; removes the old dressing, disposes of it and inspects the wound and surrounding skin
Cleans surface exudate and slough off with sterile saline before sampling — does not swab the old dressing or pooled exudate
Samples viable tissue in the wound bed, rotating the swab with enough pressure to collect tissue fluid, without touching the surrounding skin
Places the swab straight into the transport medium without touching the tip or contaminating the tube
Reads the offered label, refuses the pre-labelled tube and labels at the bedside against the wristband
Re-dresses the wound, disposes of waste safely and performs hand hygiene
Completes the request with site, clinical signs, diabetes and 'no antibiotics yet', sends it promptly (refrigerated if transport is delayed) and tells the registrar it is pending
Explains that a wound will grow bacteria whatever happens and that treatment decisions rest on the clinical signs; documents the wound, marks the erythema edge and reports the labelling near miss

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Hi, I just need to swab your leg.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Does that mean I need antibiotics now?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Probably, yes. (Peels off the dressing and rolls the swab through the green fluid on it.) That's the infection there.

dialogue.speaker: HCA
dialogue.text: I've stuck a label on to save you time.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Brilliant, thanks. (Puts the swab in the tube without reading the label.) Can you send that off?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Leaves the wound uncovered.) All done.

fail.examinerNote: No identity check or consent. The candidate sampled the old dressing — skin and environmental flora, not the wound — and promised antibiotics on the strength of a swab. The pre-labelled tube was accepted without reading it, so another patient's name was attached to this sample: a wrong-patient specimen. The wound was left uncovered and nothing was documented. This is a wrong-patient specimen, not a labelling slip: the laboratory will reject a mislabelled sample, and the near-miss is reportable.
fail.summary: No identity check or consent; dressing swabbed instead of wound; pre-labelled tube accepted — wrong patient; wound left open.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Dunstable, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth against your wristband? The nurse is worried your shin wound is infected, so the registrar would like a swab to see which germs are there. It's a cotton bud rubbed on the wound — it may sting a little. Is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Fine. Does this mean I need antibiotics?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The registrar will decide that when she sees you this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, apron, gloves. Removes the dressing, cleans the surface with saline.) I'm cleaning off the surface first so we sample the wound itself.

dialogue.speaker: HCA
dialogue.text: I've stuck a label on to save you time.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks, but I'll label it here once I've taken it. (Samples the wound bed, swab into the tube, labels at the bedside.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Re-dresses.) I'll send it with the request form and write it in your notes.

pass.examinerNote: Safe and correctly sampled: identity, consent, surface cleaning, wound-bed sampling and bedside labelling were all done. The candidate refused the pre-labelled tube by habit but did not read it, so missed the fact that it carried another patient's details and did not report the near miss. The antibiotics question was deflected rather than answered, and the request gave no clinical details.
pass.summary: Correct technique and bedside labelling; did not read or report the wrong label; question deflected; sparse request details.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Dunstable, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth against your wristband? Thank you. Any allergies? Have you had any antibiotics since you came in? And you have diabetes — on metformin?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Your shin is red, sore and leaking, which are signs of infection. The registrar would like a swab so that, if you need antibiotics, we choose the right one. I'll clean the surface first and then roll a swab over the wound. It may sting. Is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Go on. Does this mean I need antibiotics now?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Not automatically. Almost every open wound grows some bacteria, so the swab alone doesn't decide it — the redness, the warmth and how you are in yourself do. The registrar will look at all of that this afternoon, and the swab will tell her which antibiotic would work if she starts one.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, apron, gloves. Removes the dressing into the clinical waste.) Redness about two centimetres around, warm, slough and exudate on the surface, no fluctuance, nothing to drain. I'm cleaning off the surface with saline — the fluid on the dressing would mostly grow skin germs.

dialogue.speaker: HCA
dialogue.text: I've stuck a label on to save you time.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you — can I see it? (Reads.) This has a different name and number on it. That's the gentleman in the next bed. I won't use any pre-labelled tube. Could you bin this one, please? I'll label mine here.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Samples the clean wound bed, rotating the swab with firm pressure over a small area, avoiding the skin edge. Swab straight into the transport medium.) Labelling now against your wristband: name, date of birth, hospital number, left shin wound, date and time.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Re-dresses, disposes, hand hygiene. Marks the edge of the erythema.) I've drawn around the redness so we can see if it spreads.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) On the request: left shin traumatic wound, spreading erythema, temperature 37.9, diabetic, no antibiotics. I'll send it now, tell the registrar it's pending and document the findings. I'll also report the wrongly labelled tube as a near miss — next time it might not be read.

distinction.examinerNote: Confirmed identity, the indication and the antibiotic and diabetic history. Cleaned the surface before sampling the wound bed, and explained why. Read the offered label, found the wrong patient's details, refused it and labelled at the bedside. Answered the antibiotics question honestly: a wound will grow bacteria regardless, so the clinical picture decides. The request carried useful clinical details, the erythema was marked, and the near miss was reported.
distinction.summary: Indication checked; surface cleaned; wound bed sampled; wrong label read and refused; bedside labelling; full request; honest explanation; near miss reported.

cpsa.hook: A swab is only as good as where it came from and whose name is on it. Exudate on a dressing grows skin flora, and a pre-printed label can carry another patient's name. Clean the surface, sample the wound bed, label at the bedside.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Two traps sit in the same minute. First, the instinct to swab the obvious coloured fluid on the dressing or wound surface: the UK Standards for Microbiology Investigations (UK SMI B 11) note that surface swabs often give misleading mixed growth, and advise removing surface debris with saline and sampling a representative part of the lesion. If pus can be collected, it is preferred to a swab. Second, the 'helpful' pre-labelled tube. Labelling away from the patient is how wrong-patient specimens happen; only the candidate who reads the label finds another patient's name. The antibiotics question is a distractor: a swab does not diagnose infection — the clinical signs do — and the result guides the choice of treatment rather than triggering it.

thinkSayDo.think: Is this swab indicated, and what will the lab need to know?
thinkSayDo.say: Any antibiotics since you came in? Any allergies?
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · indication · antibiotics · diabetes · consent · privacy

thinkSayDo.think: The fluid on the dressing grows skin germs — I need the wound itself.
thinkSayDo.say: I'm cleaning the surface first so we sample the wound, not the dressing.
thinkSayDo.do: Hand hygiene · gloves · saline clean · wound bed sampled · straight into transport medium

thinkSayDo.think: Never trust a label I didn't write at the bedside.
thinkSayDo.say: This has another patient's name — I'll label mine here.
thinkSayDo.do: Refuse pre-labelled tube · label against wristband · clinical details · send · document · report near miss

markTriggers: Confirms identity against the wristband
Checks the indication, antibiotics, allergies and diabetes
Explains and obtains consent
Hand hygiene, apron, gloves and an aseptic non-touch technique
Cleans surface exudate and slough with saline before sampling
Samples the wound bed without touching the surrounding skin
Places the swab straight into transport medium
Reads and refuses the pre-labelled tube; labels at the bedside
Gives site, clinical signs and antibiotic history on the request
Explains that the clinical picture, not the swab, decides treatment; documents and reports the near miss

cpsa.title: Setting Up an IV Fluid Infusion / Look at the Cannula Before You Connect the Bag
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Medicines and fluids safety · Procedure: checking, priming and connecting a prescribed IV fluid through a volumetric pump on a manikin; the existing cannula has infiltrated
cpsa.capabilities: Checking a fluid prescription and the bag against it; inspecting and flushing an existing cannula before use; recognising infiltration (swelling, coolness, pallor, pain and resistance on flushing); stopping, removing the cannula and arranging new access rather than running fluid into the tissues; priming a giving set with ANTT and without air; programming a volumetric pump with rate and volume to be infused; confirming the infusion is running and the site comfortable; labelling the line; documentation and site monitoring
cpsa.setting: Acute medical ward, 10:00. You are the FY1. A manikin arm, drug trolley, fluid bag, giving set and volumetric pump are provided; the role-player speaks for the patient.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Ronald Thackwray, 76, was admitted yesterday with diarrhoea and vomiting and an acute kidney injury. His next bag of IV fluid is due now and the nurse has asked you to put it up because she is with another patient. Set up the infusion on the manikin, talking the examiner through your checks.
cpsa.scenario: Fluid chart: sodium chloride 0.9% 1000 mL IV over 8 hours, start 10:00, signed and dated; no known allergies. His wristband matches the chart. On the trolley: a 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% bag (in date, clear, outer wrap intact), an infusion-pump giving set, a volumetric pump, 10 mL sodium chloride 0.9% flushes, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol wipes, a clean tray, gloves, apron, tape, a line label and a sharps bin. Observations: HR 92, BP 118/70, RR 16, SpO₂ 97% on air, temperature 37.1 °C, alert. A 20 G cannula in the left forearm was sited in ED 18 hours ago; the last bag finished an hour ago and the line was disconnected. If asked how the drip arm feels, he says: 'It's been aching since early this morning and it feels tight.' If the candidate inspects the site, the examiner says: 'The skin around the cannula tip is swollen for about 4 cm, cool, pale and taut, and tender to touch.' If the candidate flushes it: 'There is resistance; he winces and the swelling increases.' If the candidate says the cannula will be removed and new access obtained, the examiner says: 'The cannula has been removed. A colleague has sited a new 20 G cannula in the right forearm; it flushes easily with no pain or swelling.'

markingGrid.domain: Introduces, explains and gains consent; confirms identity against the wristband and fluid chart
Checks the prescription — fluid, volume, duration or rate, route, start time, signature — and allergies
Checks the bag against the prescription: fluid, concentration, volume, expiry, clarity, leaks and outer wrap
Asks about the drip arm and inspects and flushes the cannula before connecting anything
Recognises infiltration and does not connect the infusion to that cannula
Removes the cannula, elevates the arm and arranges new access in a different site
Primes the giving set with ANTT — clamp closed, spikes without touching key parts, drip chamber part-filled, line free of air
Connects to the new cannula after a patency flush; sets the pump at 125 mL/hour with 1000 mL to be infused; confirms it is running and the site is comfortable
Documents the infiltration and cannula removal, labels the line with date and time, signs the fluid chart with start time and batch number, and updates the fluid balance chart
Asks the patient to report pain, swelling or leaking at the new site and plans regular site checks with a phlebitis score, reviewing the old site

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Morning, I'm just putting your next bag of fluid up.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: OK. This arm's been aching, mind.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's normal with a drip. (Spikes the bag with fingers on the spike, runs fluid through with bubbles still in the line.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Connects straight to the left cannula without looking at it, sets the pump and walks to the trolley.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The pump is alarming 'occlusion downstream'. He says his arm is getting tighter.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'll just restart it and see if it settles.

fail.examinerNote: No identity, prescription or bag checks. The patient's aching, tight arm was dismissed and the cannula was never inspected or flushed. The key part of the spike was touched, air was left in the line, and the infusion was connected to an infiltrated cannula. The occlusion alarm and worsening tightness were treated as a pump problem rather than a warning sign.
fail.summary: No checks; patient's complaint dismissed; asepsis broken; air in line; fluid run into an infiltrated cannula; alarm overridden.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Thackwray, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth? Thank you. It's time for your next bag of fluid — is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Checks the chart: 0.9% saline, 1 litre over 8 hours, signed, no allergies. Checks the bag: right fluid, volume, in date, clear, no leaks.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, ANTT, closes the roller clamp, spikes the bag, fills the drip chamber halfway, primes the line free of air.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Before I connect it, let me look at your drip. Is it comfortable?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: It's been aching since early this morning and it feels tight.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The skin around the cannula tip is swollen for about 4 cm, cool, pale and taut, and tender to touch.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: This cannula has come out of the vein — the fluid is going into the tissues. I won't use it. I'll take it out, raise your arm on a pillow, and get a new one put in the other arm.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The cannula has been removed. A colleague has sited a new 20 G cannula in the right forearm; it flushes easily with no pain or swelling.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Flushes the new cannula, connects, sets the pump to 125 mL an hour, 1000 mL to be infused, starts it and checks it is dripping.)

pass.examinerNote: Identity, prescription and bag checks were complete, priming was aseptic and air-free, and the candidate examined the cannula before connecting it, recognised infiltration and did not use it. The new cannula was flushed and the pump correctly programmed. However, the site was checked only after priming rather than first, and there was no documentation of the infiltration, line label or plan for monitoring the new site.
pass.summary: Full checks; ANTT priming; infiltration recognised and not used; pump set correctly; documentation and site monitoring missing.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Thackwray, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your full name, date of birth and hospital number against your wristband? Thank you. Your next bag of fluid is due — before I set anything up, can I look at your drip arm? How does it feel?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: It's been aching since early this morning and it feels tight.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The skin around the cannula tip is swollen for about 4 cm, cool, pale and taut, and tender to touch.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you — I'm glad you told me. The drip has slipped out of the vein and the last fluid has gone under the skin. I won't use it. I'm taking it out now, pressing gently and raising your arm on a pillow; the swelling should settle as the fluid is absorbed. We'll put a new one in the other arm.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) Saline is not a vesicant, so elevation and observation are enough here. I'll mark the edge of the swelling, record it, and ask for a new cannula in the right arm — not below the old site.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The cannula has been removed. A colleague has sited a new 20 G cannula in the right forearm; it flushes easily with no pain or swelling.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Checks the chart: sodium chloride 0.9%, 1000 mL over 8 hours from 10:00, signed; no allergies. Checks the bag: same fluid and strength, 1000 mL, in date, clear, squeezed for leaks, wrap intact.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, apron, cleaned tray, ANTT. Roller clamp closed; spike in without touching it; drip chamber half full; primes slowly, tapping out bubbles; cap kept on.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (At the bedside.) Cleaning the port and letting it dry. Flushing first — any pain? No. Connecting. Pump set to 125 mL an hour, volume to be infused 1000 mL — that's 8 hours. Clamp open, it's dripping, and the site looks fine.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Thackwray, if this new arm aches, swells or leaks, press your buzzer straight away — don't wait.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll label the giving set with the date and time, sign the fluid chart with the start time and batch number, update his fluid balance chart, and document the infiltration, removal and new cannula. I'll ask the nurse to check both sites with each set of observations using the phlebitis score.

distinction.examinerNote: Looked at the patient and the cannula before preparing anything, recognised infiltration from the history and examination, removed the cannula and managed the site appropriately for a non-vesicant fluid. Prescription and bag checks were complete, priming was aseptic and air-free, the new cannula was flushed before connection and the pump was programmed with both rate and volume. Line labelling, documentation, fluid balance and a monitoring plan for both sites were all in place, and the patient was told what to report.
distinction.summary: Cannula checked first; infiltration managed; full prescription and bag checks; aseptic air-free priming; pump correctly set; complete documentation and monitoring plan.

cpsa.hook: The infusion is only as safe as the cannula it runs into. Ask how the arm feels, look, then flush — before you spike the bag. A tight, cool, swollen arm means the last litre has gone into the tissues, and the pump will happily push the next one there too.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Most candidates focus on the bag and the giving set and treat the cannula as a given because 'it was working yesterday'. The patient offers the clue — an aching, tight arm — and the trap is to call it normal. Infiltration (swelling, coolness, pallor, pain and resistance on flushing) means the cannula must not be used: stop, remove, elevate, re-site elsewhere and document. A second trap is the pump: an 'occlusion' alarm on a tight arm is a warning, not a nuisance to be silenced. The station is not testing fluid prescribing — the candidate must not change the fluid or rate — but it does test that the rate and the volume to be infused are both programmed and that the infusion is seen to run.

thinkSayDo.think: Before the bag, the patient and the cannula.
thinkSayDo.say: Before I set anything up, how does your drip arm feel?
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · ask · look · flush gently — before priming

thinkSayDo.think: Swollen, cool, pale and tender — this cannula has infiltrated.
thinkSayDo.say: This drip has come out of the vein, so I won't use it. I'll take it out and we'll put a new one in the other arm.
thinkSayDo.do: Do not connect · remove · elevate · mark and document · re-site elsewhere

thinkSayDo.think: Now the infusion itself, done properly.
thinkSayDo.say: Pump set to 125 mL an hour, 1000 mL to be infused — it's running and the site is comfortable.
thinkSayDo.do: Prescription and bag checks · ANTT priming without air · flush · connect · rate and volume · label line · sign chart · fluid balance · site checks
