cpsa.title: Scrubbing Up for Theatre / A Breach You Declare Costs a Minute — One You Hide Costs a Wound
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Surgery and infection prevention · Procedure: surgical hand antisepsis, sterile gowning and closed gloving before the first case of a list; glove contamination after gloving
cpsa.capabilities: Preparing to scrub (jewellery and watch off, nails short and unpolished, skin intact, hat and mask on); checking the sterile pack and glove size; surgical hand antisepsis before the first case with an antiseptic surgical solution and a single-use nail pick, covering all surfaces for the product's contact time; keeping hands above the elbows; drying with a sterile towel from fingertips to elbow; donning a sterile gown and gloves without contamination; keeping the hands in the sterile zone; declaring and correcting contamination immediately; knowing how hand preparation differs for subsequent cases and when to consider double gloving
cpsa.setting: Day surgery theatre, 08:20. You are the FY1, scrubbing to assist. A scrub sink, antiseptic surgical solution, single-use nail picks and a sterile towel, gown and gloves are provided; the role-player is the scrub practitioner.
cpsa.yourRole: The first case on the list is an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for Mrs Eileen Ollerenshaw, 52. The consultant has asked you to scrub and assist. Prepare yourself and demonstrate surgical hand antisepsis, gowning and gloving, talking the examiner through what you are doing.
cpsa.scenario: This is the first scrub of the day. The candidate is in theatre scrubs, hat and mask, and is wearing a wedding ring and a smartwatch. Nails are short and unpolished; the skin of both hands is intact (the examiner confirms if asked). The antiseptic surgical solution is chlorhexidine-based, and its label states the contact time. The scrub practitioner opens the sterile towel, gown and gloves (the candidate's size) onto a separate trolley when asked. At about 5 minutes, after the candidate has gowned and gloved, the scrub practitioner says: 'Your left glove just brushed the edge of the non-sterile trolley as you turned.' If the candidate starts to wipe the glove or moves towards the table, the practitioner adds: 'The consultant is ready to start.'

markingGrid.domain: Removes ring and watch; checks nails and skin integrity, and that hat and mask are on, before starting
Checks the sterile pack is intact and in date and the glove size is correct; asks the scrub practitioner to open it
Before the first case, uses the antiseptic surgical solution with a single-use nail pick until hands and nails are visibly clean
Covers all surfaces — palms, backs, fingers, thumbs, between the fingers, wrists and forearms — for the product's contact time, with hands above the elbows and taps operated without the hands
Dries with a sterile towel from fingertips to elbow, a different part of the towel for each arm, never returning to the hand
Dons the gown touching only the inside, has it tied by the non-scrubbed practitioner, and uses a closed gloving technique
Keeps hands in the sterile zone — in front, between waist and shoulders — and does not touch mask, hat or any non-sterile surface
Declares the glove contamination at once, steps back from the field and has the glove changed — does not wipe it or carry on

Changes the contaminated glove by assisted gloving, or the gown and gloves if the cuff or sleeve may also be contaminated; knows alcohol cannot make a glove sterile again; tells the consultant briefly
States what changes before the next case (alcohol-based surgical rub or antiseptic solution if hands are clean; antiseptic solution again if soiled) and when to consider two pairs of gloves

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Starts washing with the ring and watch still on. Scrubs hands only, quickly, with hands pointing down.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Dries both arms with the same part of the towel, then pulls on the gown and gloves with bare hands.)

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Your left glove just brushed the edge of the non-sterile trolley as you turned.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: It was only the edge — it's fine. (Wipes the glove on the gown.)

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The consultant is ready to start.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: OK, I'm ready. (Walks to the table.)

fail.examinerNote: Jewellery and watch were left on, forearms and nails were missed, and the hands were held below the elbows so water ran back onto clean skin. The towel was reused across both arms and the gloves were pulled on with bare hands. When told about the contamination, the candidate dismissed it and wiped the glove on the gown, then went to the sterile field. Sterility was never achieved, and the breach was concealed rather than corrected.
fail.summary: Jewellery on; incomplete scrub; poor drying and gloving; contamination dismissed; entered the field contaminated.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Before I start: ring and watch off, nails short, no cuts, hat and mask on. Could you open a size 7 gown and gloves for me, please? The pack is intact and in date.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Wets hands and forearms, cleans under the nails with a pick, then scrubs systematically up to the elbows, hands above the elbows.) I'm following the contact time on the product.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Dries with the sterile towel, fingertips to elbow, one side per arm. Gowns and closes gloves.)

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Your left glove just brushed the edge of the non-sterile trolley as you turned.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you. That glove is contaminated — I'll step back. Could you help me change it, please?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Glove changed.) I'm ready now.

pass.examinerNote: Well prepared, with a systematic first-case scrub, correct drying, gowning and closed gloving. The contamination was accepted and the glove was changed. However, the candidate did not consider whether the gown cuff was exposed or touched during the change, did not tell the consultant why there was a delay, and could not say how preparation changes for the next case.
pass.summary: Correct scrub, gowning and gloving; contamination declared and glove changed; cuff not considered; next-case rules not known.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Before I scrub: ring and watch off — I'll put them in my locker tray. Nails short, no polish, no cuts or skin lesions on my hands. Hat and mask on, mask fitted before I start, because I can't touch it afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Could you open a gown and size 7 gloves onto the trolley, please? The pack is intact, the indicator has changed and it's in date.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Elbow-operated tap.) First case of the day, so it's the antiseptic surgical solution with a single-use nail pick. Nails under running water first, then hands and forearms systematically: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists, forearms to just above the elbow. Hands always above my elbows so the water runs away from the clean hands. I'm timing it to the product's contact time.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Into theatre, hands up and in front.) Sterile towel: one hand dries fingertips to elbow with one corner, never going back; the other arm uses the other side.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Gowns, touching only the inside; the practitioner ties the back; closed gloving.) Hands now stay in front of me, between waist and shoulders.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Your left glove just brushed the edge of the non-sterile trolley as you turned.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you for telling me. That glove is contaminated. I'm stepping back from the field. Did my sleeve touch the trolley as well?

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Just the glove.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Then could you assist-glove me? I won't pull the cuff down myself, because it would come into contact with the outside. If the cuff had touched, I'd change the gown as well. Wiping it with alcohol won't make it sterile again.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To the consultant.) Sorry — one minute, I've contaminated a glove and I'm changing it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) For the next case, if my hands are clean I can use an alcohol-based surgical rub or the antiseptic solution; if they're soiled, I wash again with antiseptic solution. If a case carries a high risk of glove perforation, two pairs of gloves are worth considering.

distinction.examinerNote: Prepared fully, including fitting the mask before scrubbing. A systematic first-case scrub with a nail pick, correct hand position and correct drying, followed by aseptic gowning and closed gloving. The breach was declared and the candidate stepped away, checked whether the sleeve had also been touched, and used assisted gloving, knowing that a gown change would be needed if the cuff were involved and that alcohol cannot restore sterility. The delay was explained to the consultant, and the candidate knew the NICE rules for subsequent cases and double gloving.
distinction.summary: Full preparation; systematic scrub; correct drying, gowning and gloving; breach declared and corrected properly; team informed; next-case rules known.

cpsa.hook: Clean hands are not the finish line — sterility has to survive every movement after the sink. A contaminated glove that you declare costs a minute; one that you hide may cost a surgical site infection.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Candidates rehearse the hand-washing sequence and forget that marks are lost after the sink: dripping water back over clean hands, reusing the towel across both arms, pulling gloves on with bare hands, touching the mask. The planted trap is the brushed glove followed by social pressure ('the consultant is ready'). Weak candidates say it was only the edge, or wipe the glove, and carry on. The safe response is to declare, step back and change it. NICE NG125 sets the framework: remove hand jewellery, artificial nails and nail polish; before the first case, use an aqueous antiseptic surgical solution with a single-use brush or pick; before later cases, an alcoholic hand rub or antiseptic solution, with antiseptic solution again if hands are soiled; consider two pairs of sterile gloves where there is a high risk of perforation. The exact contact time follows the product and local policy, so the station tests the principle rather than a number of minutes.

thinkSayDo.think: Anything I can't clean or can't touch later has to be sorted before I start.
thinkSayDo.say: Ring and watch off, nails short, no cuts — mask fitted now.
thinkSayDo.do: Jewellery off · nails · skin · hat and mask · pack checked · glove size

thinkSayDo.think: First case: antiseptic solution and a nail pick; water runs away from my hands.
thinkSayDo.say: Nails, palms, backs, fingers, thumbs, wrists, forearms — hands above elbows.
thinkSayDo.do: Systematic scrub for contact time · sterile towel fingertip to elbow · gown · closed gloves

thinkSayDo.think: A touched glove is a contaminated glove, however small the touch.
thinkSayDo.say: That glove's contaminated — I'm stepping back. Could you assist-glove me?
thinkSayDo.do: Declare · step back · check sleeve · assisted glove change (gown if cuff involved) · tell the consultant

markTriggers: Removes ring and watch; checks nails and skin
Hat and mask fitted before scrubbing
Checks the sterile pack and glove size
Antiseptic surgical solution with a nail pick before the first case
Covers all surfaces for the product's contact time, hands above elbows
Dries fingertip to elbow with a sterile towel, one side per arm
Aseptic gowning and closed gloving
Keeps hands between waist and shoulders, in front
Declares the glove contamination, steps back and has it changed
Knows the rules for subsequent cases and double gloving

cpsa.title: Cervical Screening Sample / Look Before You Brush
cpsa.mlaTheme: Readiness for safe practice / Delivering patient-centred care
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Women's health and screening · Procedure: cervical screening sample on a pelvic manikin; abnormal bleeding disclosed and a cervix that looks suspicious on speculum examination
cpsa.capabilities: Confirming identity with three identifiers and checking that a screening test is due and appropriate; asking about abnormal bleeding and discharge before an intimate examination; explaining HPV primary screening, the procedure and the right to stop; offering a chaperone and protecting privacy; preparing equipment, including checking the sample vial is in date; inserting a speculum gently and visualising the whole cervix; recognising a cervix whose appearance is consistent with cancer and not taking a screening sample; explaining an abnormal finding honestly without diagnosing; urgent suspected cancer pathway referral; documentation of consent, chaperone and findings
cpsa.setting: GP surgery, morning clinic. You are the FY1 on a GP placement. A pelvic manikin and sampling equipment are provided; the role-player speaks for the patient.
cpsa.yourRole: Ms Rhiannon Tregaskis, 44, has booked a cervical screening appointment after a reminder letter. Explain the test, obtain consent and take the sample on the manikin, talking the examiner through each step and telling the patient what happens next.
cpsa.scenario: Ms Tregaskis is a self-employed bookkeeper. Her last cervical screening test was 8 years ago (HPV negative); she ignored two reminders because she was 'too busy'. Last period 11 days ago, regular cycle, uses condoms, not pregnant, no children, no recent procedures, no latex or other allergies. Only if asked directly about bleeding or discharge: for about 3 months she has had bleeding between periods and 'now and again' after sex, and a thin, watery discharge with a smell for a few weeks — she has put it down to 'the change'. She is otherwise well. A practice nurse is available to chaperone. The tray holds metal and plastic specula in two sizes, water-based lubricant, a cervical sampling broom, an in-date liquid-based cytology vial and a request form. When the candidate has inserted the speculum and asks what they see, the examiner says: 'The cervix is irregular and enlarged, with a raised, friable area on the anterior lip that bleeds on contact. There is a thin, offensive, watery discharge.'

markingGrid.domain: Confirms identity with three identifiers and checks the test is due: age, date and result of last test, last period, pregnancy and recent procedures
Asks specifically about bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, and about unusual discharge, before examining
Explains HPV primary screening, what the procedure involves and that she can ask to stop at any time; obtains consent
Offers a chaperone, provides privacy and covering, and positions her comfortably
Hand hygiene and gloves; checks the vial is in date; uses a small amount of water-based lubricant kept off the speculum tip
Inserts the speculum gently, warning first, and opens it to visualise the whole cervix
Recognises a cervix whose appearance is consistent with cancer and does not take the screening sample
Removes the speculum gently, restores dignity and explains the finding honestly without giving a diagnosis
Arranges an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral and discusses with the GP supervisor the same day

Explains that screening is for people without symptoms, so even a normal-looking cervix would not have made the test an investigation of her bleeding; documents consent, chaperone identity, findings, the decision not to sample and the referral, and safety-nets

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Hello, you're here for your smear. Pop your things off and lie on the couch for me.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Okay. It's been a while, sorry.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: No problem. (Inserts the speculum.) Just relax.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The cervix is irregular and enlarged, with a raised, friable area on the anterior lip that bleeds on contact. There is a thin, offensive, watery discharge.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: A bit of bleeding there — that's quite common. I'll take the sample and the lab will tell us if there's anything to worry about. (Takes the sample.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: All done. You'll get a letter in a few weeks.

fail.examinerNote: No identity or eligibility check, no consent, no chaperone offer and no question about symptoms, so the intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding were never uncovered. Faced with a cervix that looked malignant, the candidate took a screening sample and promised the laboratory would sort it out — the false reassurance the sample-taker guidance warns against — and made no urgent referral.
fail.summary: No consent or chaperone; symptoms not asked; suspicious cervix sampled instead of referred; false reassurance; no urgent referral.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Tregaskis, I'm one of the FY1 doctors. Can I check your full name, date of birth and address? Thank you. When was your last test and your last period? Any chance you could be pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: About eight years ago, it was fine. My last period started about a week and a half ago. Not pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Any bleeding between periods or after sex, or any unusual discharge?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Actually, yes — bleeding between periods and after sex for a few months, and a smelly watery discharge. I thought it was the change.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you for telling me. I'd like to look at your cervix with a speculum. You can ask me to stop at any time, and a nurse will be with us as a chaperone. Is that okay? (Checks vial date, lubricant on the sides, inserts gently, visualises.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The cervix is irregular and enlarged, with a raised, friable area on the anterior lip that bleeds on contact. There is a thin, offensive, watery discharge.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) With that appearance I would not take a screening sample. (Removes speculum, covers patient.) Ms Tregaskis, your cervix doesn't look as it should, and with your bleeding it needs to be seen urgently by a specialist. I'll discuss it with my GP supervisor and make an urgent referral today.

pass.examinerNote: Checked identity and eligibility, asked about symptoms and uncovered the bleeding, obtained consent with a chaperone, checked the vial and visualised the cervix properly. Recognised a suspicious cervix, did not sample it and arranged an urgent referral. Did not explain why the screening test could not be used to investigate her bleeding, and documentation and safety-netting were not addressed.
pass.summary: Symptoms uncovered; consent and chaperone; cervix visualised; suspicious cervix not sampled; urgent referral.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Tregaskis, I'm one of the FY1 doctors working with the practice today. Can I check your full name, date of birth and address? Thanks. When was your last test, and what did it show? When was your last period, and is there any chance you're pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Eight years ago, normal. Period finished about a week ago. Not pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Before we start, I ask everyone this: any bleeding between periods, after sex, or any discharge that's unusual for you?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Well — yes. Bleeding between periods and after sex, on and off for three months. And a watery discharge that smells. I assumed it was the menopause starting.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'm really glad you told me. The screening test is designed for people without symptoms, so it isn't the right test to explain bleeding — a normal result could falsely reassure us. What I'd like to do is look carefully at your cervix with a speculum, then decide with you what's needed. It may be a little uncomfortable, you can ask me to stop at any time, and the practice nurse will be here as a chaperone. Is that okay?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, okay.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, gloves. Checks the vial is in date. Small amount of water-based lubricant on the blades, away from the tip.) I'm going to touch your inner thigh, then insert the speculum. (Inserts side-on, rotates, opens.) I can see the whole cervix now.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: The cervix is irregular and enlarged, with a raised, friable area on the anterior lip that bleeds on contact. There is a thin, offensive, watery discharge.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) That appearance is consistent with cervical cancer, so I will not take a screening sample — the sample-taker guidance is to refer urgently instead. (Closes the blades slightly and removes the speculum gently; covers the patient.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To patient, once she is dressed.) Ms Tregaskis, the surface of your cervix doesn't look healthy, and with the bleeding you've described, it needs a specialist to look at it closely and take tests. I can't tell you what it is today, and it may not be cancer, but because cancer is one possibility I'm making an urgent suspected cancer referral, so you'll be seen quickly and should have an answer within four weeks. I'll speak to my GP supervisor now. What worries you most?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll document consent, the chaperone's name, the bleeding history, the cervical appearance, that no screening sample was taken and why, and the urgent referral. I'll ask her to contact us if she hasn't heard about an appointment within a few days or if the bleeding becomes heavy.

distinction.examinerNote: Built the safety check into the routine: eligibility, then symptoms, before touching the patient. Explained clearly why a screening test cannot investigate symptoms, examined with consent, a chaperone and good technique, and on seeing a suspicious cervix stopped short of sampling — exactly as the NHS Cervical Screening Programme sample-taker guidance requires — and made an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12). Explained honestly without diagnosing, invited her concerns, documented the decision not to sample and safety-netted the referral.
distinction.summary: Symptoms sought; screening versus diagnosis explained; excellent technique with chaperone; suspicious cervix not sampled; urgent referral; honest explanation; full documentation.

cpsa.hook: Cervical screening is for people without symptoms. Abnormal bleeding needs its own investigation whatever a screening result shows — and if the cervix looks suspicious, the broom stays in the packet: urgent referral, not a screening result in a few weeks.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The patient booked 'a smear', the tray is laid out and the momentum is to sample. The bleeding between periods and after sex only emerges if the candidate asks, and the patient has already explained it away as the menopause. NHS Cervical Screening Programme sample-taker guidance states that the screening test is not a diagnostic tool and that a normal result can falsely reassure; people with abnormal bleeding are referred for investigation without waiting for a result, and if the cervix looks suspicious of malignancy (enlarged, irregular, friable, offensive watery discharge) the sample taker refers urgently and does not take a sample. NICE NG12 recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral when the appearance of the cervix is consistent with cervical cancer. Technique still earns marks: three identifiers, vial checked in date, lubricant kept off the speculum tip, and the whole cervix seen before any decision. The diagnosis is not the candidate's to make; the honest explanation and the referral are.

thinkSayDo.think: Screening assumes no symptoms — I have to ask before I examine.
thinkSayDo.say: Any bleeding between periods, after sex, or any unusual discharge?
thinkSayDo.do: Three identifiers · last test and result · last period · pregnancy · symptoms

thinkSayDo.think: Intimate examination: explanation, consent, chaperone, dignity.
thinkSayDo.say: You can ask me to stop at any time; the nurse will be here as a chaperone.
thinkSayDo.do: Vial in date · hand hygiene and gloves · lubricant off the tip · gentle insertion · whole cervix seen

thinkSayDo.think: This cervix looks malignant — a screening sample is now the wrong test.
thinkSayDo.say: I won't take the screening sample; this needs a specialist urgently.
thinkSayDo.do: Remove speculum · restore dignity · honest explanation · urgent suspected cancer referral

thinkSayDo.think: The decision not to sample must be visible to the next person.
thinkSayDo.say: I'll record what I saw, why I didn't take the sample, and the referral.
thinkSayDo.do: Document consent, chaperone, findings, referral · safety-net

markTriggers: Confirms three patient identifiers
Checks the last test, last period and pregnancy before starting
Asks about intermenstrual, postcoital and postmenopausal bleeding and discharge
Explains that she can stop the examination at any time; obtains consent
Offers a chaperone and maintains privacy
Checks the vial is in date and keeps lubricant off the speculum tip
Visualises the whole cervix before any sampling decision
Does not take a screening sample from a suspicious cervix
Makes an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral
Documents consent, chaperone, findings and the reason no sample was taken

cpsa.title: Postoperative Dressing Change / The Swelling Under the Dressing Matters More Than the Dressing
cpsa.mlaTheme: Readiness for safe practice / Acute and emergency care
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Surgery · Procedure: removing and replacing a postoperative wound dressing with an aseptic non-touch technique; an expanding wound haematoma in an anticoagulated patient
cpsa.capabilities: Checking the operation, postoperative day and anticoagulant history before touching a wound; explaining and consenting; hand hygiene, apron, gloves and an aseptic non-touch technique; removing a dressing gently while supporting the skin; inspecting the wound systematically before re-dressing; recognising an expanding haematoma as distinct from infection or dehiscence; applying pressure, repeating observations and escalating to the surgical registrar; flagging a recently restarted anticoagulant for a senior decision; using sterile saline only if cleansing is needed in the first 48 hours; applying a sterile dressing without hiding the problem; honest explanation; documentation
cpsa.setting: Surgical ward, 07:30. You are the FY1. A wound model with skin clips and a blood-stained island dressing is provided; the role-player speaks for the patient.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Graham Pellow, 66, is on the second day after an elective open incisional hernia repair with mesh. The nurse says: 'His dressing has blood through it — could you change it before the ward round?' Explain, obtain consent and change the dressing on the model.
cpsa.scenario: The operation was 40 hours ago through a 12 cm midline incision closed with clips. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation; the operation note restarted it last night at 22:00. Overnight observations were stable (HR 76, BP 136/82). He says the wound 'feels tight and is throbbing more than yesterday'. The island dressing has a 6 cm patch of fresh red blood soaked through. No allergies. Once the dressing is removed, the examiner reveals: clips intact, wound edges together, no erythema or discharge; a tense, tender, bluish swelling about 6 × 5 cm beside the lower third of the wound, with fresh blood oozing between two clips. Observations if requested: HR 104, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% on air, temperature 37.2 °C, alert. He asks: 'Is it infected? Can you just put a bigger dressing on?'

markingGrid.domain: Confirms identity, the operation, the postoperative day and anticoagulant use before starting
Explains the procedure, obtains consent, provides privacy and offers analgesia
Hand hygiene, apron and gloves; prepares a clean surface and sterile equipment using an aseptic non-touch technique
Removes the old dressing gently, supporting the skin, and disposes of it before inspecting the wound
Inspects systematically — edges, clips, bleeding, swelling, erythema, discharge — and recognises an expanding haematoma
Stops treating it as a routine dressing: applies firm pressure with sterile gauze; does not squeeze the swelling or remove clips
Requests observations, notices the rise in heart rate, and escalates promptly to the surgical registrar with a clear summary
Flags the apixaban for a senior decision on the next dose; asks for FBC, clotting, U&E and group and save, and IV access
Cleanses only if needed, with sterile saline because it is within 48 hours; applies a sterile dressing that does not hide the swelling; marks its edge for comparison
Explains honestly that this is bleeding under the wound, not infection; documents findings, observations, time of escalation and the anticoagulant question; increases observation frequency

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Morning, I'm just going to change this dressing.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Pulls the dressing off quickly.) Bit of blood. That's normal after surgery.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: It feels really tight. Is it infected? Can you just put a bigger dressing on?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: It's not infected. (Wipes the area with gauze and presses on the swelling to see if anything comes out.) There. (Applies a larger dressing.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: All done — the team will see you on the round.

fail.examinerNote: No identity check, consent or hand hygiene, and the dressing was ripped off. The candidate saw blood and called it normal, did not look at the swelling properly, squeezed it, and covered it with a bigger dressing. There were no observations, no escalation and no question about the apixaban that was restarted last night. An expanding haematoma was hidden under a fresh dressing.
fail.summary: No consent or asepsis; haematoma not recognised; swelling squeezed and covered; no observations or escalation; apixaban missed.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Pellow, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth? You had your hernia repaired two days ago — are you on any blood thinners? I'd like to change your dressing and look at the wound. Is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Apixaban — they restarted it last night. It feels tight.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, apron, gloves; removes the dressing gently.) There's a firm, bluish swelling beside the lower part of the wound and fresh blood coming between two clips. I'm going to press on it with sterile gauze.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Could the nurse do a set of observations, please?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: His heart rate has gone up. I'm going to call the surgical registrar to review him now. (Applies a clean dressing.)

pass.examinerNote: Safe: checked the anticoagulant, used a clean technique, removed the dressing gently, recognised the haematoma, applied pressure, checked observations and escalated. However, the candidate did not flag the apixaban dose for a senior decision, did not request bloods or IV access, did not mark the swelling, and did not answer the patient's question about infection.
pass.summary: Haematoma recognised, pressure and escalation; anticoagulant not acted on; no bloods or marking; question not answered.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mr Pellow, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth against your wristband? You had the hernia repaired the day before yesterday. Are you on any blood thinners?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Apixaban. They started it again last night. It feels tight and it's throbbing more than yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thank you — that's important. I'll take the dressing off and look properly before I put anything new on. It may pull a little. Would you like some pain relief first? Is it OK to go ahead?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, apron, gloves; sets out sterile gauze, saline and a dressing using a non-touch technique. Lifts the dressing low and slow, supporting the skin, and bins it.) Clips intact, edges together, no redness or pus. But there's a tense, bluish swelling about six by five centimetres beside the lower third, and fresh blood oozing between two clips. That's a haematoma, and it's getting bigger.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Firm pressure over the ooze with sterile gauze.) I'm pressing here. I won't squeeze it or take clips out — that's for the surgical team. Could someone do a set of observations, please?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: HR 104, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% on air, temperature 37.2 °C.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: His heart rate was 76 overnight. Could you bleep the surgical registrar now, please?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (On the phone.) Mr Pellow, 66, day 2 after open incisional hernia repair with mesh. Apixaban was restarted at 22:00 last night. He has an expanding 6 by 5 centimetre haematoma at the lower wound with fresh ooze, and his heart rate has risen from 76 to 104, BP 122/78. I'm holding pressure. Could you review him now? I'll hold this morning's apixaban until you decide, and I'll send FBC, clotting, U&E and group and save and put in a cannula.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Is it infected? Can you just put a bigger dressing on?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: It isn't infected — there's no redness or pus. It's bleeding under the skin next to the wound, probably helped along by the blood thinner. A bigger dressing would just hide it, so the surgeon is coming to see you now. I'll put a sterile dressing on that we can check easily and mark the edge of the swelling so we can see if it grows.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll document the wound, the observations, the time I escalated and the apixaban question, and ask for observations every 30 minutes until he is reviewed.

distinction.examinerNote: Checked the anticoagulant before touching the wound, used an aseptic non-touch technique, and removed the dressing gently. Inspected before re-dressing and named an expanding haematoma, distinguishing it from infection. Applied pressure without squeezing or removing clips, used the observation trend to set urgency, and gave the registrar a clear summary including the restarted apixaban, holding the next dose for a senior decision with bloods and access ready. Answered the patient honestly, marked the swelling, increased monitoring and documented.
distinction.summary: Anticoagulant checked first; haematoma recognised; pressure; observations trended; clear escalation; apixaban held for senior decision; bloods and access; honest answer; marked and documented.

cpsa.hook: Changing a dressing is also an examination of the wound. A tight, throbbing wound with fresh blood, in a patient whose anticoagulant was restarted last night, is a haematoma until proven otherwise — and a bigger dressing just hides it.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The task says 'change the dressing', so weak candidates finish the task: wipe, re-dress, leave. The tachycardia and expanding swelling under a fresh repair in a patient whose apixaban was restarted last night point to bleeding — not infection, and not a dressing problem. NICE NG125 asks for an aseptic non-touch technique when changing surgical dressings and sterile saline for any cleansing in the first 48 hours, which the candidate should still do. But the marks are for recognising the haematoma, applying pressure, escalating with the observation trend, and flagging the anticoagulant. Holding the next dose pending review is reasonable; reversing anticoagulation, aspirating the swelling or removing clips are senior decisions, and the patient may need to return to theatre.

thinkSayDo.think: Before I touch a wound: what operation, what day, any anticoagulant?
thinkSayDo.say: Are you on any blood thinners? I'll look properly before I put anything new on.
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · operation and day · apixaban · consent · analgesia · aseptic non-touch set-up

thinkSayDo.think: Tense, bluish, growing, oozing — this is bleeding, not infection.
thinkSayDo.say: That's a haematoma and it's getting bigger. I'm pressing here.
thinkSayDo.do: Gentle removal · inspect · firm pressure · no squeezing, no clip removal · observations

thinkSayDo.think: Rising heart rate plus a restarted anticoagulant — the registrar needs this now.
thinkSayDo.say: Expanding haematoma, heart rate 76 to 104, apixaban restarted last night — can you review him now?
thinkSayDo.do: Escalate · hold next dose for senior decision · FBC, clotting, G&S · cannula · mark edge · sterile dressing · document

Explains, consents and offers analgesia
Aseptic non-touch technique with hand hygiene and gloves
Removes the dressing gently, supporting the skin
Inspects before re-dressing and recognises an expanding haematoma
Applies pressure; does not squeeze or remove clips
Requests observations and recognises the rising heart rate
Escalates to the surgical registrar with a clear summary
Flags the apixaban dose for a senior decision; bloods and IV access

cpsa.title: Local Anaesthetic Infiltration / A Small Dose Can Still Cause Toxicity — Stop and Treat the Patient
cpsa.mlaTheme: Readiness for safe practice / Acute and emergency care
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Emergency medicine · Procedure: local anaesthetic infiltration of a laceration before closure; early local anaesthetic systemic toxicity mid-injection
cpsa.capabilities: Confirming identity, indication, allergies and any previous reaction to local anaesthetic; documenting distal sensation and circulation before anaesthetising; explaining and consenting; checking the drug, concentration, expiry and clarity, and stating the dose in milligrams; aseptic non-touch technique; infiltrating through the wound edge, aspirating before each injection and injecting slowly while talking to the patient; recognising early neurological symptoms of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, stopping and calling for help; ABCDE, oxygen, monitoring and IV access; anticipating seizures and arrhythmia and knowing lipid emulsion rescue is senior-led; understanding that toxicity can follow intravascular injection well below the maximum dose; safe sharps practice; documentation and incident reporting
cpsa.setting: Emergency Department minor injuries, 16:00. You are the FY1. A wound model, 1% plain lidocaine ampoules, syringe, needles and a sharps bin are provided; the role-player speaks for the patient.
cpsa.yourRole: Ms Chloe Fairbourne, 24, has a 3 cm clean laceration on the outer aspect of her left calf from a metal bed frame two hours ago. The ED registrar has assessed it as suitable for primary closure and has asked you to anaesthetise it before she sutures it. Explain, obtain consent and infiltrate local anaesthetic on the model. You do not need to suture.
cpsa.scenario: Weight 60 kg. Fit and well, no regular medicines, no allergies; she has had local anaesthetic at the dentist without problems. Tetanus immunisation complete. The wound is clean with no foreign body; sensation and capillary refill distal to the wound are normal (the examiner confirms if asked). Equipment: 1% plain lidocaine (10 mg/mL) in 10 mL ampoules, a 10 mL syringe, a drawing-up needle and a 25G needle. She is anxious about needles. At about 4 minutes, after the candidate has injected roughly 4 mL, the examiner says: 'She says her lips are tingling, she has a metallic taste and her ears are ringing. She looks frightened and is fidgeting.' If the candidate carries on, or only reassures her, the examiner adds: 'She stops answering and starts twitching.' Observations if requested once help has been called: HR 118, BP 146/88, RR 22, SpO₂ 98% on air; capillary glucose 5.4.

markingGrid.domain: Confirms identity, indication, allergies and any previous reaction to local anaesthetic
Checks and documents distal sensation and circulation before injecting
Explains the procedure and the sting, obtains consent, and positions her lying down
Checks drug, concentration, expiry and clarity; states the dose in milligrams (1% = 10 mg/mL) and that it is within the maximum for the preparation
Hand hygiene, gloves and aseptic non-touch technique; draws up without contaminating the needle and changes to the injecting needle
Infiltrates through the wound edge, aspirating before each injection and injecting slowly while talking to her
Stops injecting at the first symptoms and makes the sharp safe
Recognises possible local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, calls for urgent help, and starts ABCDE with oxygen, monitoring and IV access

Explains that toxicity can occur well below the maximum dose after intravascular injection; anticipates seizures (benzodiazepine) and arrhythmia; asks for the lipid emulsion rescue pack per the Association of Anaesthetists guideline
Does not resume the procedure; documents drug, concentration, volume in mL and mg, timing and the reaction; arranges monitored observation and an incident report

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm going to numb your leg. Sharp scratch. (Draws up and injects quickly into the wound without aspirating.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: She says her lips are tingling, she has a metallic taste and her ears are ringing. She looks frightened and is fidgeting.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's just nerves — you're doing really well. Only a bit more. (Keeps injecting.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: She stops answering and starts twitching.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Oh. (Puts the syringe down on the trolley with the needle uncovered.) Can someone get the registrar?

fail.examinerNote: No allergy check, no distal neurovascular assessment and no dose check. The candidate injected rapidly without aspirating, dismissed classic early toxicity as anxiety and kept injecting, so it progressed to reduced consciousness and twitching. The needle was left exposed, and help was called late and without a clear message.
fail.summary: No checks; rapid injection without aspiration; toxicity dismissed as anxiety; kept injecting; needle left exposed; late escalation.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Fairbourne, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth? Any allergies, or problems with local anaesthetic before? I'll check the feeling and circulation in your foot first.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: This is 1% plain lidocaine, in date, clear. I'll use up to 5 mL, which is 50 mg — well within the limit. It'll sting, then go numb. Is that OK? Could you lie back for me?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Aseptic technique; infiltrates through the wound edge.)

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: She says her lips are tingling, she has a metallic taste and her ears are ringing. She looks frightened and is fidgeting.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'm stopping. (Needle into the sharps bin.) This could be local anaesthetic toxicity. Can someone get the registrar urgently and bring the monitoring? Ms Fairbourne, I'm staying with you.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Airway clear, she's talking. I'll give oxygen and get a set of observations.

pass.examinerNote: Thorough checks before injecting, including distal sensation and a dose stated in milligrams. On the first symptoms, the candidate stopped, made the sharp safe, named possible toxicity, called for help and began assessment. However, aspiration was not mentioned, the candidate was puzzled that toxicity could occur at 40 mg, and there was no plan for seizures, IV access or the lipid rescue pack.
pass.summary: Good checks; stopped and escalated on symptoms; no aspiration; low-dose toxicity not understood; no seizure or lipid plan.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Fairbourne, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth? Any allergies? Have you ever reacted to local anaesthetic, at the dentist for example?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: No, the dentist was fine. I just hate needles.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks for telling me — I'll talk you through it. Before I numb it, I'll check you can feel me touching your foot and look at the circulation. (Checks.) Normal, and I'll write that down.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Checks the ampoule with the nurse.) Lidocaine 1% plain, in date, clear: that's 10 mg per mL. I expect to need about 5 mL, so 50 mg — well within the maximum for this preparation. It'll sting for a few seconds, then go numb. Is that OK? I'd like you lying down.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, gloves, non-touch technique; draws up, changes to the 25G needle.) I'm going in through the wound edge, aspirating before each injection to make sure I'm not in a vessel, and injecting slowly. Tell me if you feel anything strange.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: She says her lips are tingling, she has a metallic taste and her ears are ringing. She looks frightened and is fidgeting.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'm stopping now. (Needle straight into the sharps bin.) Tingling lips, metallic taste and ringing ears are early signs of local anaesthetic toxicity. Put out an emergency call and bring the resus trolley and the lipid rescue pack, please.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Airway open, high-flow oxygen on. Can we attach monitoring — ECG, BP and saturations? I'll put a cannula in. If she has a seizure, she'll need a benzodiazepine, and the senior team will lead on lipid emulsion according to the Association of Anaesthetists guideline.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) She has had about 40 mg, well below the maximum, so this is most likely a small intravascular injection rather than an overdose. The total dose isn't the only thing that matters.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Ms Fairbourne, you've had a reaction to the numbing medicine. Help is here and we're watching your heart. I won't give you any more.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I won't restart the procedure. I'll document lidocaine 1%, about 4 mL, 40 mg, the time, the symptoms, and our response. She needs monitored observation, I'll complete an incident report, and the reaction goes in her record for future procedures.

distinction.examinerNote: Complete pre-procedure safety: allergy and previous reaction, distal neurovascular status documented before anaesthesia, ampoule checked with a second person, and dose stated in milligrams. Aspirated before each injection and injected slowly. At the first neurological symptoms, stopped, made the sharp safe, called for help and the lipid rescue pack, and began ABCDE with oxygen, monitoring and IV access, anticipating seizures. Recognised that toxicity at 40 mg points to intravascular injection, did not resume, and documented fully with an incident report.
distinction.summary: Full checks; aspirated and slow; stopped and escalated at first symptoms; oxygen, monitoring, access; seizure and lipid plan; low-dose toxicity understood; documented.

cpsa.hook: Local anaesthetic toxicity is not only an overdose problem. A small dose straight into a vein can cause it. Aspirate, inject slowly, keep talking — and when the lips tingle, stop and treat the patient.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The symptoms arrive at a modest 40 mg, well within any maximum for the preparation, and the patient is anxious about needles. That combination tempts candidates to call it nerves or a faint and carry on. Circumoral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus and agitation are early central nervous system signs of systemic toxicity (listed in the lidocaine product information). The Association of Anaesthetists quick reference guide says: stop injecting, call for help, give 100% oxygen, secure IV access and monitoring, treat seizures with a benzodiazepine, and use 20% lipid emulsion for cardiovascular instability or arrest. An FY1 is not expected to dose lipid but must ask for it. Vasovagal syncope (pale, sweaty, slow pulse) and anaphylaxis (rash, wheeze, hypotension) are the differentials to name. Checking distal sensation before anaesthetising is a separate, routinely dropped mark.

thinkSayDo.think: Know the patient, the nerve function and the milligrams before the needle goes in.
thinkSayDo.say: 1% is 10 mg per mL — about 5 mL is 50 mg, within the maximum.
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · allergies and previous reactions · distal neurovascular check documented · ampoule checked · consent · lying down

thinkSayDo.think: Every injection could enter a vessel.
thinkSayDo.say: I'm aspirating first and going slowly — tell me if you feel anything strange.
thinkSayDo.do: Aseptic non-touch technique · through the wound edge · aspirate · slow injection · keep talking

thinkSayDo.think: Tingling lips and ringing ears mean toxicity, not nerves — and the dose doesn't rule it out.
thinkSayDo.say: I'm stopping. Emergency call, resus trolley and the lipid rescue pack, please.
thinkSayDo.do: Stop · sharp safe · ABCDE · oxygen · monitoring · IV access · benzodiazepine if seizing · lipid per guideline · no restart · document · incident report

Documents distal sensation and circulation before injecting
Explains, consents and positions her lying down
Checks drug, concentration and expiry; states the dose in mg
Aseptic non-touch technique; changes to the injecting needle
Aspirates before each injection and injects slowly
Stops at the first symptoms and makes the sharp safe

cpsa.title: Adding a Drug to an Infusion Bag / A Fresh Bag, Not the One Already Running
cpsa.contentMap: Practical skills / Medicines safety · Procedure: reconstituting an IV antibiotic and adding it to an infusion bag with ANTT, mixing, labelling and setting the rate; the nurse suggests injecting it into the maintenance bag already running
cpsa.capabilities: Reading the product information before preparing an IV medicine; recognising why a drug must not be added to an infusion bag that is already running (unknown final concentration and volume, poor mixing with a risk of a concentrated portion, wrong infusion time, labelling); reconstituting with the correct diluent; adding to a fresh bag through the additive port with ANTT; mixing and inspecting the final infusion; completing an additive label with a second check; setting the pump for the stated infusion time; checking the chart for a serious interaction; documenting and explaining a refusal to a colleague without conflict
cpsa.setting: Respiratory ward, 10:00. You are the FY1. A manikin arm with a running infusion, a drug trolley and a second pump are provided; the role-player is the staff nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Mrs Eileen Cotterill, 67, was admitted overnight with high-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Her first dose of IV clarithromycin is due now. The nurse has asked you to prepare it and add it to an infusion bag. Prepare the infusion and start it on the manikin, talking the examiner through your checks.
cpsa.scenario: Drug chart: clarithromycin 500 mg IV every 12 hours, first dose 10:00, signed; IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g every 8 hours (last given 08:00); simvastatin 40 mg at night, amlodipine 5 mg daily; no known drug allergies. Running: sodium chloride 0.9% 1000 mL over 12 hours via a volumetric pump into a 20 G cannula in the left forearm, about half the bag left. On the trolley: a clarithromycin 500 mg powder vial (in date), 10 mL water for injections, a 250 mL sodium chloride 0.9% bag, syringes, drawing-up needles, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol wipes, an additive label, a giving set, a second volumetric pump, a clean tray, gloves, apron and a sharps bin. Product information: reconstitute the vial with 10 mL water for injections only; add to at least 250 mL sodium chloride 0.9% or glucose 5% (about 2 mg/mL); infuse over 60 minutes into a larger proximal vein; do not give as a bolus or intramuscularly. If asked, the cannula site is clean and comfortable. At about 2 minutes the nurse says: 'It's compatible with saline, isn't it? Just inject it into her bag that's already running — saves a bag and a pump.' Her ECG this morning was reported as normal, QTc 430 ms, if asked.

markingGrid.domain: Confirms identity and allergies, explains and gains consent; checks the prescription — drug, dose, route, time, signature — and that it has not already been given
Reads the product information before preparing: water for injections to reconstitute, at least 250 mL to dilute, 60 minutes to infuse, never as a bolus
Declines to add the drug to the running maintenance bag and explains why — unknown final volume and concentration, poor mixing, wrong infusion time, labelling
Hand hygiene, clean tray and ANTT; checks vial, diluent and the 250 mL bag — fluid, volume, expiry, clarity, leaks
Reconstitutes with water for injections only, dissolves fully and draws up the whole volume; sharps at the point of use
Cleans and dries the additive port, injects through it, inverts the bag several times to mix and inspects for particles or discolouration
Completes and attaches an additive label — patient, drug, dose, diluent, volume, date and time, signatures — with a second check per local policy

Checks the cannula, primes a line and sets the pump to give the whole bag (250 mL plus the 10 mL added, about 260 mL) over 60 minutes; notes the maintenance fluid is the same diluent so both can run together, or pauses it per local policy
Checks the chart for interactions: simvastatin is contraindicated with clarithromycin, so asks the prescriber to withhold it during the course; checks the QTc
Signs the administration with start time, documents, and explains the decision to the nurse calmly without blame

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Morning, I'm doing your antibiotic. (Reconstitutes with saline from a flush because it is nearer.)

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: It's compatible with saline, isn't it? Just inject it into her bag that's already running — saves a bag and a pump.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Good idea. (Wipes nothing, injects the whole vial into the half-empty running bag, does not invert it.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Done — it'll go in with her fluids.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: How long will the clarithromycin take to go in, and at what concentration?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: However long the bag takes, I suppose. It's fine, it's all diluted.

fail.examinerNote: The product information was never read: the drug was reconstituted in sodium chloride rather than water for injections, which risks precipitation. It was then added to a half-used running bag without cleaning the port or mixing, leaving an unknown concentration that could layer and reach the patient as a concentrated portion, and a 60-minute infusion running over about six hours. No label, no second check and no identity or allergy check.
fail.summary: Wrong diluent; added to running bag; no port cleaning or mixing; wrong infusion time; unlabelled; no identity or allergy check.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mrs Cotterill, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your name and date of birth — and do you have any allergies? Thank you. I'm setting up your second antibiotic, which runs over an hour. Is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Checks chart and product information: water for injections, at least 250 mL, over 60 minutes, not as a bolus.)

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: It's compatible with saline, isn't it? Just inject it into her bag that's already running — saves a bag and a pump.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'd rather not — it has to run over an hour, and in that bag it would take hours and I couldn't be sure of the concentration. I'll make up a separate 250 mL bag.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (ANTT, reconstitutes with 10 mL water, swirls until clear, cleans the additive port, injects, inverts the bag several times, checks for particles.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Completes the additive label and asks the nurse to check it. Primes a line, connects, sets the pump to run the whole bag, about 260 mL, over an hour.)

pass.examinerNote: Read the product information first, declined the running-bag shortcut with a correct reason, used the right diluent, cleaned the port, mixed, inspected and labelled the bag with a second check, and set the correct rate. However, the drug chart was not checked for interactions, so simvastatin — contraindicated with clarithromycin — would have been given tonight, and administration was not documented.
pass.summary: Correct preparation, fresh bag, mixing, label and rate; simvastatin interaction missed; no documentation.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Mrs Cotterill, I'm one of the FY1s. Can I check your full name and date of birth against your wristband? Any allergies to medicines? None — that matches the chart. Your second antibiotic, clarithromycin, goes into the drip over an hour. Is that OK?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Reads the chart: clarithromycin 500 mg IV 12-hourly, due 10:00, signed, not given. Reads the product information aloud: water for injections only, at least 250 mL, 60 minutes, larger vein, never a bolus.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Scans the rest of the chart.) She's on simvastatin 40 mg at night — that's contraindicated with clarithromycin. I'll ask the prescriber to withhold it for the course. Is there an ECG today? QTc 430 — fine.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: It's compatible with saline, isn't it? Just inject it into her bag that's already running — saves a bag and a pump.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: It is compatible, but I won't add it to a bag that's already running. Half a litre's left, so I wouldn't know the final concentration, it may not mix evenly, and at her maintenance rate this would take six hours instead of one. It also wouldn't be labelled properly. I'll make a separate bag — can you be my second checker?

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Fair enough.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Hand hygiene, apron, cleans tray, ANTT. Checks vial and water in date; 250 mL saline bag — right fluid, volume, in date, clear, squeezed, no leaks. Reconstitutes with 10 mL water, swirls until fully dissolved, draws up the full volume, needle straight into the sharps bin.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Cleans the additive port with chlorhexidine-alcohol, lets it dry, injects through the additive port — not the giving-set port. Inverts the bag several times, holds it to the light: clear, no particles.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Completes the additive label: name, hospital number, clarithromycin 500 mg, 250 mL sodium chloride 0.9%, date, time, both signatures.)

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (At the bedside.) The cannula's in your forearm and looks fine. Priming a new line without air, connecting through the Y-connector — same diluent as your fluids, so they can run together. Pump set to 260 mL an hour, 260 to be infused — the 250 mL bag plus the 10 mL I added, over one hour. Tell us if the arm becomes sore; this one can irritate the vein.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll sign the chart with the start time, document, and ask the prescriber to suspend the simvastatin during the course. Thanks for checking with me — the separate bag is about getting the dose and the time right.

distinction.examinerNote: Read the product information before touching the vial, found and acted on the simvastatin contraindication, and checked the QTc. Declined the running-bag shortcut with precise reasons while keeping the nurse on side and recruiting her as second checker. Reconstitution, port cleaning, mixing, inspection, labelling and pump programming were all correct, compatibility with the running fluid was reasoned rather than assumed, and the patient was warned about vein irritation.
distinction.summary: Product information read first; interaction caught; running-bag shortcut declined with reasons; flawless ANTT, mixing, label and rate; documented without conflict.

cpsa.hook: Never add a drug to a bag that is already running. You cannot know the final volume or concentration, the drug may not mix evenly, and an infusion that should take 60 minutes will drip in over hours. A fresh bag, mixed, inspected and labelled, is the only way to know what the patient is getting.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The nurse's suggestion sounds reasonable because the drug is compatible with saline — compatibility is the wrong question. A half-used running bag gives an unknown final concentration and volume, an addition that may layer rather than mix, and an infusion time set by the maintenance rate rather than the 60 minutes the product requires. The second trap is the diluent: the product must be reconstituted with water for injections only, not a saline flush. Distinction candidates scan the whole chart: simvastatin is contraindicated with clarithromycin and must be withheld during the course. The candidate should not quote doses or dilutions from memory; everything needed is in the supplied product information.

thinkSayDo.think: Read the product information before I touch the vial.
thinkSayDo.say: Water for injections only, at least 250 mL, over 60 minutes, never as a bolus.
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · allergy · prescription · product information · chart scanned for interactions (simvastatin)

thinkSayDo.think: Compatible is not the same as safe — a running bag gives an unknown dose over an unknown time.
thinkSayDo.say: I won't add it to the bag that's running — I'll make a separate bag. Can you be my second checker?
thinkSayDo.do: Fresh 250 mL bag · ANTT · reconstitute with water · clean and dry additive port · inject · invert · inspect

thinkSayDo.think: The label and the pump are what make the infusion safe for the next person.
thinkSayDo.say: Pump at 260 mL an hour, 260 to be infused — the whole bag over one hour.
thinkSayDo.do: Additive label with second check · primed line · rate and volume · sign start time · document · prescriber asked to withhold simvastatin

cpsa.title: An Incidental Finding Nobody Has Acted On / 'No PE' Is Not the Whole Report
cpsa.contentMap: Professional behaviour and patient safety · unacted significant imaging finding — reading the whole report, ownership of a requested test when the requester is away, suspected cancer referral, telling the patient before discharge, documentation and incident reporting
cpsa.capabilities: Reading an imaging report to the end rather than stopping at the answer to the clinical question; recognising an unexpected significant finding as an action item, not an FYI; understanding that responsibility for acting on a result stays with the requesting team and passes to whoever is covering when the requester is away; declining to hand a significant finding to the GP through a discharge letter; securing an urgent referral to the lung cancer team; making sure a senior tells the patient before he leaves; documenting the plan and reporting the missed result for learning; challenging a senior respectfully and escalating further if needed.
cpsa.setting: Acute medical ward, Thursday 11:30. You are the FY1.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Gordon Alderwick, 71, is due home at 15:00 today. While writing his discharge summary you open the CT pulmonary angiogram report from four days ago. The medical registrar is on the ward. Discuss the report with the registrar and agree what must happen before Mr Alderwick leaves. The examiner holds further details.
cpsa.scenario: Mr Alderwick was admitted 5 days ago with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He is a retired joiner and an ex-smoker of 40 pack-years. A CT pulmonary angiogram was requested by the admitting consultant, who is now on annual leave until Monday. The report, verified 4 days ago, reads: 'No pulmonary embolism. Patchy consolidation right lower lobe. Incidental finding: 31 mm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe, suspicious for primary lung malignancy. Recommend urgent referral to the lung cancer multidisciplinary team.' The ward-round entry the next day says only: 'CTPA — no PE. Treat as community-acquired pneumonia.' Nothing in the notes acknowledges the mass, no referral has been made and Mr Alderwick has not been told. He has finished his antibiotics, his NEWS2 is 0 and he is keen to go; his wife is collecting him at 15:00. If asked: 4 kg weight loss over 2 months, no haemoptysis, no hoarseness. The registrar says: 'The consultant requested it, so it's in her inbox and she's back Monday. Pop "incidental lung lesion — GP to follow up" in the discharge letter and let him go.' If pressed, the registrar agrees the consultant of the week is on site.

markingGrid.domain: Reads the whole report and identifies the unexpected finding and the radiologist's recommendation
Recognises the finding as needing action before discharge, not at the requester's return
Explains that responsibility sits with the team caring for the patient, including cover when the requester is away
Declines to pass the finding to the GP through the discharge letter as the only plan
Arranges an urgent referral to the lung cancer team via the suspected cancer pathway
Ensures a senior tells Mr Alderwick today, honestly and in private, before he leaves
Asks about red-flag symptoms such as weight loss and haemoptysis
Documents the finding, who was informed and the agreed plan, and copies the GP
Escalates to the consultant of the week if the registrar does not agree

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'm doing Mr Alderwick's discharge. His CTPA showed no PE, so pneumonia was right.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: Good. Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: There's something at the bottom about a lung lesion.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: The consultant requested it — it's in her inbox. Put 'GP to follow up' in the letter.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Okay, I'll add it to the letter. He can go at three.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Who will tell Mr Alderwick about the mass?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: His GP will see the letter and arrange whatever's needed.

fail.examinerNote: Stopped at 'no PE', treated a suspected lung cancer as a footnote and handed it to the GP through a letter the patient may not read and the GP may not action for weeks. Nobody took responsibility, the patient was not told, no referral was made and the missed result was not reported. Delegating to the GP via the discharge letter is the fail trigger — the finding is not owned.
fail.summary: Finding noted but not owned; delegated to GP by letter; patient not told; no referral or documentation of responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Before he goes, can I show you his CTPA? There's no PE, but there's an incidental 31 mm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe. The radiologist recommends urgent lung MDT referral, and I can't see that anyone has acted on it.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: The consultant requested it. It's in her inbox; she's back Monday. Put 'GP to follow up' in the letter.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I don't think we can leave it, because he's still our patient and it's suspicious for cancer. Could we refer him to the lung cancer team today and make sure he's told before he goes home?

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: Fine. Who's going to tell him?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Could you speak to him with me before three? I'll complete the urgent referral, document the conversation and the plan, and put it in the discharge summary to the GP as well.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: Okay, I'll see him after the board round.

pass.examinerNote: Read past the first line, recognised an unacted suspicious finding, challenged the 'leave it in the inbox' plan, secured an urgent referral and a senior conversation with the patient before discharge, and documented it. Did not ask about weight loss or haemoptysis, did not mention escalating to the consultant of the week if needed, and did not report the delay as an incident.
pass.summary: Finding owned; urgent lung cancer referral; senior to tell patient before discharge; plan documented and copied to GP.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Have you got two minutes before Mr Alderwick goes? His CTPA excluded a PE, but the last line reports an incidental 31 mm spiculated right upper lobe mass, suspicious for lung cancer, with a recommendation for urgent lung MDT referral. It was verified four days ago and there's no acknowledgement, no referral and he hasn't been told.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: The consultant requested it, so it's her result. She's back Monday. Put 'incidental lesion — GP to follow up' in the letter.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I understand she requested it, but while she's away the result is ours. It's already four days old, and a line in a discharge letter isn't a referral and isn't telling him. I'd like to make the urgent referral today and have one of us senior to me speak to him before three.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: We're full and the board round is in ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'll do the referral and the paperwork now. If you can't see him today, I'll ask the consultant of the week, because I don't think he should go home without knowing. (To examiner.) Has he lost weight or coughed up blood?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Four kilograms in two months. No haemoptysis.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That adds weight to it. He can still go home today if he's told, referred and has a contact number. I'll document the finding, who knew, the conversation and the plan, copy the GP and his consultant, and complete an incident report so we can find out how it was missed. That's about the system, not about anyone.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.text: Fair. I'll see him with you at two.

distinction.examinerNote: Presented the finding precisely, gave a reason why the inbox and the GP letter are not a plan, and explained ownership during the requester's absence. Gathered the weight loss and named a further escalation route without confrontation. Kept discharge possible once the safety steps were in place, and closed the loop with documentation, copies to the GP and consultant, and a no-blame incident report.
distinction.summary: Whole report read; responsibility explained; urgent referral; senior disclosure before discharge; consultant escalation route; documentation and incident report.

cpsa.hook: The scan answered the question it was asked and then told you something nobody asked about. Read the report to the last line. A significant finding belongs to the team caring for the patient today, whoever requested the scan, and a discharge letter is not a referral.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The first line is reassuring ('No pulmonary embolism'), the ward-round note copied it, the requester is on leave and the registrar offers a tidy route through the GP letter. NHS England's imaging-report guidance is explicit: the referrer who requests the test is responsible for reviewing, acting on and communicating the result, and unexpected significant findings must be communicated before the report is released to the patient digitally. When the requester is away, that duty passes to the covering team, not to the inbox. GMC Good medical practice expects the FY1 to act on a risk to a patient and to escalate if a senior disagrees. Marks are for owning the result, the urgent referral, a senior conversation before discharge, documentation and incident reporting. The candidate is not asked to stage the tumour.

thinkSayDo.think: The answer to the question asked is not the whole report.
thinkSayDo.say: There's no PE, but there's an incidental mass suspicious for cancer.
thinkSayDo.do: Read to the last line · note the radiologist's recommendation

thinkSayDo.think: The requester's inbox is not a safety net.

thinkSayDo.do: Own the result · decline 'GP to follow up' as the plan

thinkSayDo.think: He should not leave without knowing.

thinkSayDo.do: Urgent lung cancer referral · senior conversation before discharge

thinkSayDo.think: If it happened once, it can happen again.
thinkSayDo.say: I'll document it and report it so we learn from it.
thinkSayDo.do: Document · copy GP and consultant · incident report · escalate to consultant if needed
