cpsa.title: The Discharge Fit Note He Wants Rewritten / Certify What You Assessed — and Make the True Note Work for Him
cpsa.contentMap: Professional values and behaviours · honesty in certificates and reports (GMC Good medical practice); completing a fit note (Statement of Fitness for Work) on hospital discharge after uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy; patient request for false duration and a false complication for employment and insurance purposes
cpsa.capabilities: Clarifying exactly what a patient wants certified and why; checking the clinical facts and the documented surgical plan before writing; declining to state anything false or misleading in a certificate, calmly and without accusing; explaining the difference between 'not fit for work' and 'may be fit for work' and tailoring functional advice to a manual job; knowing that if an employer cannot make the suggested changes the patient is treated as not fit without a new note; checking a claimed senior instruction rather than accepting or dismissing it; signposting financial worries; documenting the conversation.
cpsa.setting: Day surgery unit, 15:00. You are the FY1 completing discharge paperwork. The role-player is the patient; the examiner may give information from the notes.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Craig Tunnicliffe, 44, is ready for discharge the day after an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The nurse asks you to complete his fit note. He would like to talk to you about it first. Discuss his request and complete the consultation.
cpsa.scenario: Operation note and ward round entry: uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones; four port sites; eating and drinking, mobilising, pain controlled with paracetamol, observations normal. The consultant's documented discharge plan: 'Not fit for work for 2 weeks. Then may be fit for work with amended duties — no heavy lifting — for a further 2 weeks. GP review if slow to recover.' Mr Tunnicliffe is a warehouse operative; his job involves lifting boxes up to 20 kg for much of the shift. He says: 'Can you put me down as not fit for eight weeks, and write that there were complications? My income protection insurance only pays if I'm off over four weeks, and my boss never gives light duties anyway.' He is worried about money: his partner has just been made redundant. If asked, he has no wound problems, fever, jaundice or vomiting. At about 4 minutes he adds: 'The consultant told me this morning I'd need six weeks. Just write that.' (Examiner, if asked to check the notes: the entry from this morning's ward round matches the 2 + 2 week plan above; the registrar is available by phone.)

markingGrid.domain: Establishes exactly what he wants written and why — duration, 'complications', employer and insurance
Checks his recovery and the documented consultant plan before deciding what to certify
Asks about the physical demands of his job
Declines to write 'complications' or a duration not supported by the clinical assessment, explaining that certificates must not be false or misleading
Stays non-judgemental — acknowledges the financial pressure and does not accuse him of dishonesty
Completes an accurate fit note per the plan, with functional advice for a lifting job (no heavy lifting, amended duties, phased return)
Responds to the 'consultant said six weeks' claim by checking the notes or the registrar, not by refusing or complying outright
Explains how to get a further fit note if recovery is slower than expected, with safety-netting for complications
Explains that if his employer cannot provide the amended duties he is treated as not fit for work without needing a new note
Signposts support for the financial worry and documents the request and the reasoning

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Can you put me down as not fit for eight weeks, and write that there were complications? My insurance only pays if I'm off over four weeks.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's insurance fraud. I'm not doing that.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Fraud? I've just had an operation!

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Your operation was routine. You get two weeks, that's what the consultant said.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: The consultant told me this morning I'd need six weeks. Just write that.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Fine — if he said six, I'll put six. (Writes six weeks not fit.)

fail.examinerNote: Accused the patient of fraud before understanding his situation, then reversed under pressure and certified six weeks on an unchecked claim that contradicts the documented plan. Neither outcome was honest or fair: the first damaged trust, the second produced a misleading certificate. No exploration of his job, no functional advice, no explanation of 'may be fit', no safety-netting and no documentation.
fail.summary: Accusatory refusal, then capitulation to an unchecked claim; misleading certificate; no tailored advice or documentation.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Can you put me down as not fit for eight weeks, and write that there were complications? My insurance only pays if I'm off over four weeks.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I can hear money is a real worry. Can I check how you're doing first? Any wound problems, fever, being sick?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: No, I'm fine really, just sore.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's good news. The operation went smoothly, so I can't write that there were complications — a fit note has to be accurate. The consultant's plan is two weeks off, then two weeks on lighter duties with no heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: The consultant told me this morning I'd need six weeks. Just write that.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Let me check the notes rather than guess. (Checks.) This morning's entry says two weeks, then two weeks of amended duties. I'll write that. If you're not recovering as expected, your GP can review you and extend it.

pass.examinerNote: Acknowledged the worry, checked his recovery and the plan, declined the false wording with a clear reason and without accusation, and checked the claimed instruction instead of accepting it. Did not ask about the physical demands of his job, so the functional advice was generic, did not explain what happens if his employer cannot offer light duties, and did not address the financial pressure or document the conversation.
pass.summary: Honest refusal without accusation; claim checked; accurate note per plan; job demands, employer rule and documentation missed.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Can you put me down as not fit for eight weeks, and write that there were complications? My insurance only pays if I'm off over four weeks, and my boss never gives light duties anyway.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks for being straight with me — it sounds like there's a lot of pressure on you at the moment. Can I understand a bit more? What does your job involve?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: Warehouse. Lifting boxes, up to 20 kilos, most of the shift. And my partner's just been made redundant.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's a lot at once. How are you feeling physically — any wound problems, fever, yellowing, vomiting?

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: No, just sore. Paracetamol's doing it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Good. Your operation went smoothly, so I can't write that there were complications, and I can only put a time off work that matches the medical assessment. A fit note is a legal document — if anything on it isn't accurate, it could cause real problems for you with your employer or your insurer, as well as for me. What I can do is make sure it says honestly what your job needs.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: The consultant told me this morning I'd need six weeks. Just write that.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: If he did, I want it to be right, so let me check rather than guess. (Checks the notes.) This morning's plan is two weeks off, then two weeks where you may be fit for work if you avoid heavy lifting. If you'd like, I can ring the registrar to confirm.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: But my boss won't give me light duties.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's useful to know. I'll tick 'may be fit for work' for weeks three and four and write 'amended duties — no lifting over light weights' and 'phased return'. If your employer can't make those changes, you're treated as not fit for work — you don't need to come back for a new note. And if you're slower to recover, or you get a fever, wound redness, yellow skin or worsening pain, see your GP, who can reassess and extend it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: For the insurance, your insurer may ask the hospital for a report, and it will reflect what happened — I'd encourage you to speak to them directly about what you're entitled to. With your partner's redundancy, Citizens Advice can check what other support you can get. I'll write in your notes what we discussed and why the fit note says what it does.

distinction.examinerNote: Explored the request, his job and the money worry before deciding, checked his recovery, and declined the false wording in terms of what a fit note is rather than what he is. Checked the claimed instruction against the notes and offered to confirm with the registrar. Then made the honest note genuinely useful: functional advice tailored to a lifting job, the rule that unavailable amended duties count as not fit without a new note, a route to extend if recovery is slow, safety-netting, signposting and documentation.
distinction.summary: Request and context explored; honest refusal framed around the document; claim checked; tailored 'may be fit' note; employer rule explained; safety-net, signposting and documentation.

cpsa.hook: A fit note certifies your assessment, not the patient's need. Refuse the false parts calmly, check what you are told, then make the true note as useful to him as it can be.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Two opposite failures are planted. One is the moralising refusal — 'that's fraud' — that ends the consultation and abandons the patient. The other is the late claim that 'the consultant said six weeks', which tempts a candidate who has just refused to comply in order to avoid conflict. The right response to an unverified claim is to check. GMC Good medical practice requires doctors to be honest when completing or signing forms, reports and other documents and to make sure they are not false or misleading. The DWP fit note guidance says 'not fit for work' is for when the patient cannot do any work, and 'may be fit for work' requires functional comments; if the employer cannot make the recommended changes, the employee is treated as not fit for work without a new note. That rule answers his strongest objection honestly.

thinkSayDo.think: Understand the request and the pressure behind it before I respond.
thinkSayDo.say: What does your job involve, and what's worrying you most?
thinkSayDo.do: Clarify duration, wording, purpose · job demands · finances

thinkSayDo.think: I can only certify what the assessment supports.
thinkSayDo.say: The operation went smoothly, so I can't write complications — a fit note must be accurate.
thinkSayDo.do: Check recovery · check consultant plan · decline false content without accusation

thinkSayDo.think: A claim about a senior is checked, not obeyed or dismissed.
thinkSayDo.say: Let me check the notes rather than guess.
thinkSayDo.do: Review today's entry · offer to call the registrar

thinkSayDo.think: Make the honest note work for a manual job.
thinkSayDo.say: If your employer can't offer the lighter duties, you're treated as not fit — no new note needed.
thinkSayDo.do: 'May be fit' with amended duties and phased return · GP route to extend · safety-net · signpost · document

cpsa.title: Apixaban on the Morning of a Colonoscopy / The Dose Question Hides the Real One
cpsa.contentMap: Prescribing · peri-procedural management of a direct oral anticoagulant for endoscopy — procedure bleeding risk, indication and thrombotic risk, dose and renal check, BSG/ESGE 2021 timing, no bridging, documented omission and restart plan
cpsa.capabilities: Not answering 'give or omit' before establishing the procedure, its bleeding risk and the last dose; distinguishing low-risk diagnostic endoscopy from high-risk polypectomy or endoscopic mucosal resection; knowing that national endoscopy guidance omits the morning DOAC dose for low-risk procedures and expects the last dose 3 days before high-risk ones; recognising that a booked high-risk procedure is no longer safe as planned; avoiding heparin bridging for a DOAC; checking indication, thrombotic risk and dose appropriateness; escalating to the endoscopist for a decision; documenting the omission and restart plan; explaining honestly to an anxious patient.
cpsa.setting: Gastroenterology ward, 08:00. You are the FY1. A role-player speaks for the nurse and the patient.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Clifford Penhallow, 74, is on this afternoon's colonoscopy list. The nurse doing the drug round asks whether to give his apixaban, which is due now. Ask the examiner for the information you need, decide what to tell the nurse, and agree a plan.
cpsa.scenario: Mr Penhallow was admitted 2 days ago with iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 92 g/L) and no overt bleeding. CT colonography shows a 25 mm caecal polyp. He is listed for colonoscopy at 14:00, and the request states 'for endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) of caecal polyp'. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation; he had a TIA 5 years ago and has hypertension (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4). No mechanical valve, no VTE history. His last apixaban dose was at 20:00 last night. Weight 82 kg, creatinine 104 micromol/L, eGFR 61. He also takes amlodipine and ferrous sulfate; no antiplatelets. There is no peri-procedural anticoagulation plan in the notes. The nurse says: 'It's prescribed, so I'll give it unless you say otherwise.' Only if the plan to hold is explained to him, Mr Penhallow says: 'I had a mini-stroke once. I'm frightened to stop my blood thinner.'

markingGrid.domain: Does not answer 'give' or 'omit' before establishing the procedure and last dose
Identifies EMR of a 25 mm polyp as a high-bleeding-risk procedure
Checks the indication, thrombotic risk and that the apixaban dose is appropriate for age, weight and renal function
Asks the nurse to withhold this morning's dose pending the endoscopist's decision
Recognises that a high-risk procedure today does not fit the recommended interval since the last dose
Escalates to the endoscopist or gastroenterology registrar for a decision before the list
Does not bridge with low molecular weight heparin
Documents the omission with a reason and a restart plan on the chart and in the notes
Explains the plan to Mr Penhallow and addresses his stroke fear honestly
States the BSG/ESGE rule: omit the morning dose for low-risk, last dose 3 days before high-risk

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: His apixaban's due. It's prescribed, so I'll give it unless you say otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: He's having a procedure, so stop the apixaban.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Just today, or until when?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Stop it for now and give him a dose of enoxaparin instead to cover him.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: I had a mini-stroke once — is it safe to stop?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The enoxaparin will protect you. The endoscopy team will sort out the rest.

fail.examinerNote: Answered reflexively without establishing the procedure, its bleeding risk or the last dose, then added heparin bridging, which is not recommended for DOACs and increases bleeding. Missed that the booked EMR cannot safely go ahead today, gave no restart plan and did not involve the endoscopist.
fail.summary: Reflex stop; LMWH bridging added; procedure risk and timing ignored; no escalation or restart plan.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: His apixaban's due. It's prescribed, so I'll give it unless you say otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Can you hold it for a few minutes while I check? (To examiner.) What procedure is planned, and when was his last dose?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: Colonoscopy at 14:00 for EMR of a 25 mm caecal polyp. Last dose 20:00 last night.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: EMR is a high-bleeding-risk procedure, so this morning's dose shouldn't be given. And with a dose last night, I'm not sure EMR can be done safely today. (To examiner.) Why is he anticoagulated, and what are his renal function and weight?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: AF, previous TIA. eGFR 61, weight 82 kg, age 74.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: His dose is right. (To nurse.) Please don't give it — record it as withheld for the procedure. I'll speak to the endoscopist now about whether EMR goes ahead today, and I'll write the plan and the restart time in the notes. He won't need heparin bridging.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: I had a mini-stroke once. I'm frightened to stop it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: That's understandable. Missing a dose or two around a procedure carries a small risk, and the endoscopy doctor will plan exactly when to restart it.

pass.examinerNote: Paused the reflex, established the procedure, bleeding risk, last dose and dose appropriateness, withheld this morning's dose, identified the timing problem, ruled out bridging, escalated and documented. Did not state the national interval for high-risk procedures or propose what the endoscopist might do, and the reassurance was brief.
pass.summary: Procedure and last dose established; dose withheld; timing problem flagged; no bridging; escalated and documented.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: His apixaban's due. It's prescribed, so I'll give it unless you say otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks for checking. Please hold it for now; it's due, but there's no plan written for the procedure. (To examiner.) What procedure is booked, when was his last dose, and why is he on apixaban?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: EMR of a 25 mm caecal polyp at 14:00. Last dose 20:00 yesterday. AF with a previous TIA and hypertension.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: And his age, weight and renal function, plus any antiplatelets?

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: 74, 82 kg, creatinine 104, eGFR 61. No antiplatelets.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: So 5 mg twice daily is the right dose. The BSG/ESGE guidance says that for a low-risk procedure such as a diagnostic colonoscopy you omit the morning DOAC dose, and for a high-risk one such as EMR the last dose should be taken 3 days before. He had a dose 12 hours ago, so the EMR as booked isn't safe today. That's the endoscopist's decision — perhaps a diagnostic colonoscopy with the polyp marked, and the EMR rebooked after a planned break.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To nurse.) Please withhold this morning's dose and code it as withheld for a procedure, not 'refused'. No enoxaparin bridging — for DOACs it adds bleeding without reducing strokes. I'm bleeping the endoscopist now, well before the list, and I'll document the agreed plan and restart time on the chart and in the notes.

dialogue.speaker: PATIENT
dialogue.text: I had a mini-stroke once. I'm frightened to stop it.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I understand. Your stroke protection matters, which is why we don't stop it without a plan. A short planned break around a procedure has been studied carefully and the stroke risk is low, while bleeding from removing a large polyp is a real danger. The endoscopy doctor will tell you exactly when to restart, and I'll come back once I've spoken to them.

distinction.examinerNote: Paused without a reflex answer, gathered the procedure, bleeding risk, last dose, indication, dose appropriateness and antiplatelets, applied BSG/ESGE 2021 correctly, recognised that the booking no longer fits the guidance and offered sensible options for the endoscopist to decide. Avoided bridging with a reason, coded the omission correctly, escalated well before the list and addressed the stroke fear with an honest balance.
distinction.summary: Full information gathered; BSG/ESGE timing applied; unsafe booking identified; no bridging; omission coded; endoscopist decides; fear addressed honestly.

cpsa.hook: 'Should I give his apixaban?' is the easy question. The real question is what procedure he is having and when he last took it — because if the procedure is high-risk, this morning's dose is not the problem; last night's was.
cpsa.examinerTrap: Candidates answer the nurse's binary question and stop. Reflex 'give' risks bleeding at polypectomy; reflex 'stop and cover with enoxaparin' adds bridging, which BSG/ESGE 2021 and the PAUSE data do not support for DOACs. The guidance is specific: omit the morning DOAC dose for low-risk endoscopy; for high-risk procedures such as EMR, the last dose of apixaban, rivaroxaban or edoxaban should be taken 3 days before. A dose 12 hours earlier means the EMR as booked does not meet that, so the decision belongs to the endoscopist before the list. Marks are for gathering the right information, withholding safely with a documented reason, avoiding bridging, escalating, setting a restart plan and reassuring honestly.

thinkSayDo.think: Don't answer give-or-omit until I know what the procedure is.
thinkSayDo.say: Hold it for now — what procedure, and when was his last dose?
thinkSayDo.do: Procedure · bleeding risk · last dose · indication

thinkSayDo.think: Is the dose itself right?
thinkSayDo.say: Age 74, 82 kg, creatinine 104 — 5 mg twice daily is correct.
thinkSayDo.do: Check dose criteria · antiplatelets · renal function

thinkSayDo.think: EMR is high risk; last dose 12 hours ago doesn't fit 3 days.
thinkSayDo.say: The EMR as booked isn't safe today — that's the endoscopist's call.
thinkSayDo.do: Withhold the morning dose · no bridging · bleep endoscopist

thinkSayDo.think: A gap without a restart plan becomes a forgotten anticoagulant.
thinkSayDo.say: I'll write the plan and restart time, and come back to explain.
thinkSayDo.do: Code omission · document restart · reassure honestly

Recognises the booked EMR does not fit the interval since the last dose
Escalates to the endoscopist before the list
States that LMWH bridging is not used for DOACs
Documents the omission reason and restart plan
Addresses the patient's stroke concern honestly

cpsa.title: Liquid Dose Calculation / Prescribe in Milligrams, Calculate From the Bottle in Your Hand
cpsa.contentMap: Prescribing / Medicines safety · Calculating a liquid dose from the strength supplied; a prescription written in millilitres with no strength; an under-dose already given from a different-strength bottle
cpsa.capabilities: Recognising that a liquid prescription written only in millilitres is unsafe; finding the intended dose in milligrams from the clinical plan rather than guessing; calculating volume from the strength actually supplied (dose required ÷ strength × volume) and sense-checking it; independent second checking; rewriting a prescription with the dose in milligrams, formulation, frequency and duration; working out what was actually given after a strength mix-up; reporting a medication incident and being open with the patient; considering whether other medicines suit a patient with dysphagia, including time-critical Parkinson's medicines
cpsa.setting: Medical ward, 09:00. You are the FY1. The drug chart, the admission clerking and two bottles are provided; the role-player is the staff nurse.
cpsa.yourRole: Mr Walter Ledsham, 74, has Parkinson's disease with swallowing difficulty and was admitted overnight with community-acquired pneumonia. The nurse asks you to check his antibiotic prescription before the 10:00 dose because she is not sure how much to give. Work out the dose, make the prescription safe, and explain your reasoning to the nurse.
cpsa.scenario: The drug chart, written overnight, reads: 'Amoxicillin oral suspension 10 mL three times a day', with no strength and no dose in milligrams. The clerking says: 'CURB-65 1, low-severity CAP. Plan: amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for 5 days (liquid — SALT advice).' No known drug allergies, confirmed with the patient. Weight 68 kg; eGFR 64. Also on the chart: co-careldopa tablets at 07:00, 11:00, 15:00 and 19:00. The ward bottle is amoxicillin oral suspension 125 mg in 5 mL; the night team used a 250 mg in 5 mL bottle that has now been returned to pharmacy. The nurse says: 'The chart says 10 mL. The bottle here is 125 in 5. Do I just give 10 mL?' At about 4 minutes the nurse adds: 'Looking at the night notes, his 02:00 dose was given as 10 mL from this 125 mg in 5 mL bottle.' If asked, Mr Ledsham's 07:00 Parkinson's tablet was not given because he could not swallow it.

markingGrid.domain: Confirms identity and allergy status against the wristband and chart
Recognises that a liquid prescription in millilitres with no strength is unsafe and does not answer 'just give 10 mL'
Finds the intended dose — amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day — from the clinical plan rather than guessing
Reads the strength from the bottle in hand and calculates aloud: 500 mg ÷ 125 mg × 5 mL = 20 mL
Sense-checks the answer (125 mg per 5 mL, so 500 mg is four 5 mL measures) and asks for an independent second check
Rewrites the prescription: amoxicillin 500 mg oral three times a day, oral suspension, 5 days with a stop date, signed — old entry cancelled correctly
Works out that the 02:00 dose was 10 mL of 125 mg in 5 mL = 250 mg, half the intended dose — an under-dose, not a toxicity risk
Escalates and reports: informs the registrar or pharmacist about the missed half-dose, reports the incident locally, and is open with the patient
Notices the missed 07:00 co-careldopa and treats it as time-critical — urgent pharmacist and team review for a form he can take
Explains the system fix to the nurse without blame — doses in milligrams, strength confirmed from the bottle — and documents

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The chart says 10 mL. The bottle here is 125 in 5. Do I just give 10 mL?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: If the chart says 10 mL, give 10 mL. It's been signed.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Looking at the night notes, his 02:00 dose was given as 10 mL from this 125 mg in 5 mL bottle.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Then that's consistent. Carry on as written.

dialogue.speaker: EXAMINER
dialogue.text: How many milligrams is he getting per dose?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: It's 10 mL… so about 125? I'm not sure — the prescriber chose it.

fail.examinerNote: Accepted a millilitre-only prescription as if it were a dose, never looked for the intended dose in milligrams, and could not calculate what 10 mL of the supplied strength contains. The patient would continue on half the intended antibiotic dose for pneumonia, the earlier under-dose went unrecognised and unreported, and the prescription was left unsafe for the next shift.
fail.summary: mL-only prescription accepted; intended dose not sought; calculation wrong; under-dose not recognised; nothing corrected or reported.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The chart says 10 mL. The bottle here is 125 in 5. Do I just give 10 mL?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Let's not — 10 mL means nothing without the strength. The clerking says 500 mg three times a day. This bottle is 125 mg in 5 mL, so 500 divided by 125 is 4, times 5 mL is 20 mL. Can you check that independently?

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: I get 20 mL too.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: I'll cross off the old entry and rewrite it: amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times a day, oral suspension, five days, with a stop date.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Looking at the night notes, his 02:00 dose was given as 10 mL from this 125 mg in 5 mL bottle.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: So he had 250 mg — half a dose. That's not dangerous, but he's under-treated. I'll tell the registrar and pharmacist, and report it through the incident system.

pass.examinerNote: Refused to give a millilitre-only dose, found the intended dose from the plan, calculated correctly aloud, used an independent check, rewrote the prescription properly and recognised the under-dose, escalating and reporting it. However, the candidate did not explain the error to the patient and missed that his time-critical Parkinson's medicine had not been given because he cannot swallow tablets.
pass.summary: Correct dose found and calculated; independent check; prescription rewritten; under-dose escalated and reported; candour and Parkinson's medicine missed.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Thanks for checking before giving it — that's exactly right. Let me confirm Mr Ledsham's identity and allergies first: name, date of birth, wristband, no known allergies — matches.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: The chart says 10 mL. The bottle here is 125 in 5. Do I just give 10 mL?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Not yet. 10 mL is a volume, not a dose — it depends entirely on the strength. The clerking says 500 mg three times a day for five days. Strength in your hand: 125 mg in 5 mL, which is 25 mg per mL. 500 divided by 25 is 20 mL. Sense check: 500 mg is four lots of 125, so four 5 mL measures — 20 mL. Please work it out yourself before you look at mine.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: 20 mL.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Agreed. I'll cancel the old entry and rewrite it: amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times a day, oral suspension, five days, stop date, signed. The dose in milligrams means it's right whatever bottle turns up.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.text: Looking at the night notes, his 02:00 dose was given as 10 mL from this 125 mg in 5 mL bottle.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Then he received 250 mg — half the intended dose. That's an under-dose, not a toxicity risk. I'll ask the pharmacist and registrar whether to give the missing amount now or simply continue from 10:00; I won't decide that from memory. I'll report it as a medication incident, and I'll explain to Mr Ledsham what happened.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: One more thing — his 07:00 co-careldopa wasn't given because he couldn't swallow it. Parkinson's medicines are time-critical; missing doses can make him rigid and worsen his swallow. I'll ask the pharmacist and the team now for a form he can take — a dispersible preparation or another route — rather than waiting for the 11:00 dose to be missed too.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To Mr Ledsham.) Your antibiotic prescription wasn't written clearly overnight and your early dose was half what it should have been. It's corrected now and I'm sorry. We're also sorting your Parkinson's tablets so you don't miss them.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll document the calculation, the rewritten prescription, the under-dose, the advice received and the incident report. The learning is system-wide: liquid doses in milligrams, strength confirmed from the bottle.

distinction.examinerNote: Showed the calculation, the sense check and an independent check. Found the intended dose in the plan, rewrote the prescription so it no longer depends on the bottle, correctly characterised the 02:00 dose as a half-dose rather than an overdose, and referred the replacement decision to the pharmacist and registrar instead of guessing. Was open with the patient, reported the incident, and spotted that a time-critical Parkinson's medicine had been missed because of the same swallowing problem.
distinction.summary: Shown, sense-checked and independently checked calculation; prescription rewritten in mg; under-dose escalated and reported; candour; missed Parkinson's medicine caught.

cpsa.hook: A liquid prescribed in millilitres is not a dose — 10 mL of one bottle is twice 10 mL of another. Find the dose in milligrams, calculate from the strength in your hand, sense-check, have it checked independently, and rewrite the prescription so it no longer depends on which bottle arrives.
cpsa.examinerTrap: The nurse's question invites a one-word answer: 'yes, give 10 mL'. The trap is treating a signed volume as a safe dose. The candidate must look for the intended dose in milligrams (500 mg three times a day in the plan), calculate from the 125 mg in 5 mL bottle (20 mL) and fix the prescription. When the 02:00 dose is revealed, weaker candidates either miss that it was half a dose or panic as if it were an overdose; the correct response is to recognise under-treatment, seek pharmacist and registrar advice on replacing the missing amount, report it and be open with the patient. Distinction candidates read the whole chart: the same swallowing problem has stopped his time-critical Parkinson's medicine.

thinkSayDo.think: 10 mL is a volume, not a dose.
thinkSayDo.say: What dose in milligrams did the team intend? The plan says 500 mg three times a day.
thinkSayDo.do: Identity · allergy · do not give a mL-only dose · find the intended mg dose

thinkSayDo.think: Calculate from the bottle in my hand, then check it a second way.
thinkSayDo.say: 125 mg in 5 mL, so 500 mg is 20 mL — please check it independently.
thinkSayDo.do: Dose ÷ strength × volume · sense check · independent check · rewrite in mg with formulation and duration

thinkSayDo.think: The 02:00 dose was half; and what else has his swallow stopped?
thinkSayDo.say: He's had 250 mg — I'll ask the pharmacist and registrar how to make up the dose, and report it.
thinkSayDo.do: Escalate · incident report · open with patient · time-critical Parkinson's medicine reviewed · document

markTriggers: Confirms identity and allergy status
Refuses to give a millilitre-only prescription
Finds the intended dose in milligrams from the plan
Calculates 20 mL aloud from the strength supplied
Sense-checks and asks for an independent second check
Rewrites the prescription in milligrams with formulation and duration
Recognises the 02:00 dose as a half-dose under-dose
Seeks pharmacist or registrar advice and reports the incident
Is open with the patient about the error
Spots the missed time-critical Parkinson's medicine

plab2.title: A Kidney Mass She Read About on the NHS App — Say Sorry, Say It Straight, Then Refer Today
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in the general surgical ambulatory clinic. Mrs Lorna Fenchurch, 58, a school office manager, was admitted 5 weeks ago with biliary colic and had a contrast CT of the abdomen; she was discharged with a plan for an elective cholecystectomy. She has come back today, upset, because last week her CT report appeared on the NHS App. She shows you the line: 'Incidental 38 mm solid enhancing mass, lower pole of left kidney, suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. Recommend urology referral.' The report was verified 5 weeks ago. You check the record: the finding was never acknowledged, no urology referral has been made and nobody has contacted her. Role-player facts: no visible blood in the urine, no loin pain apart from her gallstone pain, no weight loss; she is the main carer for her mother, who has dementia; her father died of 'kidney cancer' 15 years ago. She asks: 'Is it cancer? And why did I have to find out from my phone?' Your consultant is in theatre next door and can be contacted.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, sit down and acknowledge her distress. Ask what she has read and what she understands by it before explaining anything.
Explore ideas, concerns and expectations: her father's kidney cancer, her fear, her caring role for her mother. Let silences happen.

Be open: tell her you have checked her record and the finding should have been acted on and discussed with her weeks ago, and it was not. Say sorry plainly and without excuses — that is the professional duty of candour, and it does not need a finding of fault first.

Explain the finding honestly: a solid lump in the kidney that may be a cancer and needs further assessment by the kidney specialists. Do not say 'it's probably nothing' and do not say 'it is cancer'. Many kidney cancers found this way are found early.
Brief symptom check: blood in the urine, loin pain, weight loss, fatigue. Mention that you will check her kidney function results.

The plan: you will discuss her with your consultant today and make an urgent referral to urology through the suspected cancer pathway before she leaves the building. Tell her what happens next and roughly when she should hear.

Accountability: you will report the delay through the hospital's incident system so it is investigated and she can be told what happened; give her the PALS details if she wants to raise a concern. Ask whether this affects her gallbladder operation plan — the surgeons and urologists will coordinate.

Support and safety-netting: a named contact number, written information, offer of the cancer nurse specialist once the urology team is involved, support for her caring role. Tell her to seek help urgently for visible blood in the urine or severe loin pain.
Check understanding, summarise and document the conversation, the apology, the referral and the incident report.

self_audit: Asked what she had read and understood before explaining
Explored her fears, including her father's kidney cancer
Acknowledged that the result should have been acted on and was not
Apologised clearly without blaming colleagues or making excuses
Explained that the mass may be cancer and needs specialist assessment, without false reassurance
Asked about haematuria, loin pain and weight loss
Agreed to discuss with the consultant today
Made an urgent urology referral before she left
Explained the timescale and how she will be contacted
Reported the delay through the incident system
Offered PALS information without being defensive
Gave a named contact, written information and safety-netting
Addressed her caring responsibilities
Documented the conversation and the plan
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate can be honest about a system failure while delivering uncertain, frightening news. A top-band candidate finds out what she already knows, says sorry plainly, explains the finding without minimising or catastrophising, and closes the loop before she leaves: consultant informed, urgent referral made, incident reported, contact number given.
plab2.gold_close: Mrs Fenchurch, thank you for coming in and for showing me this. I've looked at your record, and I have to be honest with you: this result should have been acted on and talked through with you five weeks ago, and it wasn't. I'm very sorry that you found out from your phone. The scan shows a solid lump in your left kidney. It may be a cancer, and that's why it needs to be looked at properly by the kidney specialists. I can't tell you today what it is, but lumps like this found by chance are often found at an early stage, when treatment works well. Here's what I'm doing before you leave: I'm speaking to my consultant, who's next door, and I'm making an urgent referral to the urology team through the fast-track cancer pathway, so you should hear from them soon. I'm also reporting what happened through the hospital's safety system so it's properly looked into, and you'll be told what they find. This is my direct number, and here's some written information. If you see blood in your urine or get severe pain in your side, please get urgent help. How are you feeling about everything I've said?
scripts: Before I explain, can you tell me what you've read and what's going through your mind?
This should have been acted on and discussed with you weeks ago, and it wasn't. I'm sorry.
It's a solid lump in the kidney. It may be a cancer, and that's why it needs the specialists.
I won't tell you it's nothing, because I don't know that — but I'll make sure you're seen quickly.
I'm making the urgent referral today, before you leave.
I'm reporting what happened so it's looked into properly, and you'll be told the outcome.
critical_fails: Fails to acknowledge or apologise for the delay
Falsely reassures her that it is probably nothing
States that it is definitely cancer
Leaves the referral to the GP or the consultant 'later' with no action today
Blames radiology or a named colleague
No safety-netting or contact route
Dismissive of her distress or her father's history
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: false reassurance ('these are usually benign') or defending the system instead of apologising. Top-band mark: finding out what she knows first, saying sorry for the delay without excuses, explaining 'may be a cancer — needs specialists' honestly, and making the urgent urology referral, informing the consultant and reporting the incident before she leaves, with a named contact and safety-netting.

plab2.title: Dizzy Seven Hours After a Gallbladder Operation — A Pulse of 88 on Bisoprolol Is Not Reassurance
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on the surgical ward at 20:00. Mr Keith Brannagh, 62, a bus driver, had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy at 13:00 for recurrent biliary colic; the operation note says 'difficult dissection, adhesions; haemostasis achieved'; no drain. He takes bisoprolol 5 mg each morning for angina, and amlodipine; no anticoagulants. The nurse asks you to see him: 'His NEWS2 is only 4 and his pulse is fine. He went light-headed walking to the toilet — probably vasovagal. Can I give him some oral morphine for his tummy?' Role-player facts: he felt faint and had to sit on the bathroom floor; the pain across his upper abdomen has become steadily worse over two hours and is now constant; he feels thirsty and sick; he has not passed urine since the operation. Observations: RR 22, SpO₂ 97% on air, BP 92/58 (146/84 at pre-assessment and 138/80 in recovery), HR 88 regular, temperature 36.6 °C, alert. Examination (examiner gives on request): pale, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen distended and diffusely tender with guarding in the right upper quadrant; port sites dry. Venous gas on request: Hb 104 g/L (138 g/L pre-op), lactate 3.1 mmol/L. One cannula in situ.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm identity and tell Mr Brannagh you are going to check him over straight away. Ask for the observation chart.

A and B: talking in full sentences, RR 22, saturations 97% — oxygen to target saturations if needed. C: BP 92/58 against a baseline of 140s, pulse 88 on bisoprolol, cool peripheries, capillary refill, urine output since theatre. Ask about the faint, pain, thirst, nausea.

Interpret aloud: a 50 mmHg fall from his baseline, no urine for seven hours, rising pain and pallor. Bisoprolol blunts the heart-rate rise, so a pulse of 88 does not reassure, and a NEWS2 of 4 does not override clinical concern. This is shock — postoperative bleeding until proven otherwise.

D and E: alert; examine the abdomen and port sites. Get help now: ask the nurse to call the surgical registrar urgently and critical care outreach. Pain relief is appropriate, but not instead of finding the cause: decline oral morphine as the plan, and give small titrated doses of IV analgesia with close monitoring because of his blood pressure — analgesia does not mask the diagnosis.

Second wide-bore cannula; FBC, clotting, fibrinogen, U&E, LFT, crossmatch; venous gas for haemoglobin and lactate. Give 500 mL crystalloid over less than 15 minutes and reassess. Catheterise or bladder scan and start hourly urine output.

Venous gas: Hb 104 from 138, lactate 3.1. SBAR to the registrar: 'Seven hours after a difficult laparoscopic cholecystectomy, BP 92/58 from 140s, pulse 88 on bisoprolol, no urine passed since theatre, distended tender abdomen, Hb down 34, lactate 3.1 — I think he is bleeding and I need you to see him now.' Anticipate imaging or return to theatre and the major haemorrhage protocol if he worsens.

Explain to Mr Brannagh honestly: his blood pressure is low and you are concerned he may be bleeding inside; the surgeons are coming, and he may need a scan or to go back to theatre. Keep him nil by mouth; hold his antihypertensives and any VTE prophylaxis until reviewed.
Reassess after the bolus; repeat observations every 15 minutes; review his pain after titrated analgesia. Answer his questions; offer to contact his family.
Summarise and document: time called, findings, NEWS2 with the beta-blocker caveat, actions, response and who was informed.

self_audit: Assessed with a structured ABCDE approach
Compared the blood pressure with his own baseline
Identified that bisoprolol masks a tachycardia
Did not accept a NEWS2 of 4 as reassurance in the face of clinical concern
Asked about urine output since surgery
Examined the abdomen and port sites
Named postoperative bleeding as the working diagnosis
Called the surgical registrar urgently and critical care outreach
Inserted a second wide-bore cannula and sent bloods including crossmatch
Gave a 500 mL crystalloid bolus and reassessed
Monitored urine output hourly
Kept him nil by mouth and held antihypertensives
Explained honestly what was happening
Documented findings, actions and escalation
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate looks past a reassuring number. A top-band candidate compares the blood pressure with the patient's own baseline, knows that a beta-blocker hides the tachycardia, treats a NEWS2 of 4 with rising pain and no urine as shock, and gets a surgeon to the bedside with an SBAR that makes the bleeding case.
plab2.gold_close: Mr Brannagh, I'm worried about you. Your blood pressure is much lower than it normally is, you haven't passed urine since the operation and your tummy is getting more painful. Your heart tablet keeps your pulse slow, so it can hide how hard your body is working. I think there may be some bleeding inside after the operation. I've put in another drip, taken blood to check your blood count and to have blood ready if you need it, and I'm giving you fluid now. The surgical registrar is on the way to see you, and they may want a scan or to take another look in theatre. Please don't eat or drink for now. We'll keep a close eye on you every few minutes, and I'm giving you something for the pain now, in small doses so it is safe with your blood pressure. Is there anyone you'd like us to call?
scripts: I'm going to check you over properly right now.
Your blood pressure is about 50 points lower than it usually is.
Your heart tablet slows your pulse, so a normal pulse doesn't mean everything is all right.
I'm worried there may be some bleeding inside after the operation.
The surgical team is coming to see you now.
Please don't eat or drink anything until the surgeon has seen you.
critical_fails: Accepts 'vasovagal' without assessing circulation and the abdomen
Reassured by the pulse or NEWS2 despite bisoprolol and a large fall in blood pressure
Gives morphine and leaves without a plan
No crossmatch or haemoglobin check
Repeated fluid boluses without reassessment or escalation
Does not call the surgical registrar urgently
Gives VTE prophylaxis before a surgical review
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: agreeing it is 'just vasovagal' because the pulse is 88 and NEWS2 is 4. Top-band mark: ABCDE, comparison with his own baseline blood pressure, naming the bisoprolol effect, recognising no urine since theatre and rising pain as shock, second cannula with crossmatch, a 500 mL bolus with reassessment, and an urgent SBAR to the surgical registrar naming postoperative bleeding.

plab2.title: Gram-Negative Bacilli in a Man Sent Home With 'a Virus' — Bring Him Back Today, Wedding or Not
plab2.scenario: Telephone consultation. You are the FY2 on the acute medical unit (AMU). Mr Raymond Haskett, 70, a retired electrician, came in two nights ago with fever and rigors and was discharged yesterday morning with a diagnosis of 'probable viral illness'; no antibiotics were given. His respiratory viral swab was negative. Blood cultures from admission have now grown Gram-negative bacilli; sensitivities are awaited. His notes show type 2 diabetes on metformin and a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) 3 weeks ago; no allergies. You phone him. Role-player facts: he says, 'I'm alright, doctor — a bit shivery last night, that's all.' If asked: two shivering episodes last night, burning when passing urine since yesterday, passing less urine than usual, a dull ache low in his tummy, eating less; no confusion, no breathlessness, no rash; his wife is with him. He has a thermometer: 38.4 °C this morning. He says: 'My granddaughter's getting married tomorrow — can't I just get some tablets from my GP?' Your registrar is on the AMU.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself and where you are calling from. Confirm his identity with two identifiers and check it is a good time and that he can speak privately or is happy for his wife to listen.
Explain why you are calling: one of the blood tests taken when he was in hospital has come back and needs action. Ask how he is now before giving detail.

Structured telephone sepsis screen: rigors, temperature, confusion (ask his wife), breathlessness, urine output, rash, mottled skin, dizziness. Focus the source: dysuria, lower abdominal pain, catheter or recent procedure — the TURP 3 weeks ago. Diabetes control.

Interpret: Gram-negative bacilli in the blood, a fever of 38.4, rigors, reduced urine and surgery within 6 weeks — a likely urinary source with a bloodstream infection; surgery within 6 weeks is a moderate-to-high risk criterion under NICE NG253. He has had no antibiotic, and a confirmed Gram-negative bacteraemia cannot be treated safely at home. This needs face-to-face assessment and treatment in hospital today, not tablets from the GP.

Explain to him in plain words; acknowledge the wedding; explain that untreated bloodstream infections can make people very ill quickly and that the best chance of being at the wedding is treatment now. NICE NG253 says people in the community with moderate-to-high risk criteria who cannot be treated safely outside hospital should be referred urgently for emergency care. Arrange immediate safe transfer and pre-alert the receiving team. He must not drive himself, and should call 999 if he becomes confused, breathless, faint or mottled.
If he declines: check capacity, explore the reason, give clear information about risks, and keep the door open — never 'fine, see your GP'. Agree a time to call back, and involve the registrar.

Close the loop internally: tell the registrar, alert the AMU nurse in charge to expect him, ask microbiology for advice on empirical treatment while sensitivities are awaited, and ensure antibiotics are given promptly on arrival. Flag his diabetes and metformin to the admitting team.

Summarise, check understanding with teach-back, and document the result, the call, his symptoms, advice, plan and who was informed; update his GP and the discharge record; report the absent pending-result plan for learning.

self_audit: Confirmed identity and privacy before discussing results
Asked how he was before giving the result
Explained the result in plain language
Screened for confusion, breathlessness, urine output, rash and dizziness
Asked his wife about confusion
Identified the recent TURP as the likely source and a moderate-to-high risk feature
Recognised that he has had no antibiotic
Advised hospital assessment today and declined GP tablets as the plan
Acknowledged the wedding with empathy
Arranged immediate safe transport to hospital (ambulance by default) and told him not to drive
Informed the registrar and alerted the AMU
Sought microbiology advice
Used teach-back to check understanding
Documented and updated the GP
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate can turn a positive blood culture into a safe recall over the telephone. A top-band candidate confirms identity, screens for sepsis systematically, links the bacteraemia to the recent TURP, recognises that he has had no treatment, and negotiates an immediate admission with empathy for the wedding, while closing every loop inside the hospital.
plab2.gold_close: Mr Haskett, thank you for talking this through with me. The blood test we took when you came in has grown bacteria — the kind that usually come from the waterworks, and your operation three weeks ago makes that more likely. The shivers, the temperature and the burning fit with that. Because the infection is in your bloodstream and you haven't had any antibiotics yet, I need you to come back to the AMU now so we can examine you, start antibiotics through a drip and check your kidneys. I know how much tomorrow matters, and I'm sorry this has come at such a bad time — but treating it today gives you the best chance of being there. The safest way in is by ambulance, so please call 999 as soon as we finish and tell them the hospital has asked you to come in with a blood infection. Please don't drive yourself. If you feel confused, very breathless or faint while you wait, tell the call handler straight away. I'm telling my registrar and the nurse in charge now, so they're expecting you. Can you tell me back what you're going to do?
scripts: Before I go on, can you confirm your full name and date of birth?
One of the blood tests from when you were in hospital has come back, and it needs acting on today.
Have you had any shivering, felt muddled, or passed less urine than usual?
Because the infection is in your bloodstream and you haven't had antibiotics yet, tablets from your GP aren't enough.
I know tomorrow matters — treating it today is your best chance of being there.
Please call 999 when we finish and tell them the hospital has asked you to come in.
critical_fails: Accepts 'I'm alright' and arranges GP follow-up or oral antibiotics without assessment
Does not confirm identity before giving results
No sepsis screen
Misses the recent TURP as a likely source
Allows him to drive himself or to delay coming in until after the wedding
No arrangement for immediate transfer or no safety-netting
Does not inform the registrar or the AMU
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: agreeing to oral antibiotics from the GP so he can attend the wedding. Top-band mark: identity check, structured sepsis screen including confusion via his wife, linking Gram-negative bacteraemia to the TURP, explaining the need for hospital treatment today with empathy, immediate transfer (ambulance by default) with a pre-alert, and informing the registrar, AMU and microbiology with documentation. Transfer route: an ambulance is the safest default for a 70-year-old with an untreated bacteraemia; if his wife can bring him straight in, that is a reasonable alternative only while he has no high-risk features and the receiving team is pre-alerted — he must never drive himself.

plab2.title: Stop My Blood Thinner Two Days Before Surgery? — Seven Weeks After a PE, Ask Whether to Operate Yet
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in the surgical pre-operative assessment clinic. Ms Anita Rawcliffe, 52, a pharmacy dispenser, is booked for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 9 days after three episodes of biliary colic. She started rivaroxaban 7 weeks ago for an unprovoked pulmonary embolism diagnosed in the emergency department; she now takes 20 mg once daily with her evening meal. The surgical listing was made before the PE. Role-player facts: her GP told her to 'just stop the tablet two days before the operation'. She stopped HRT tablets when the PE was diagnosed. Her last gallstone attack was 2 weeks ago and settled at home within 3 hours; no fever, jaundice or dark urine since. No bleeding, no missed doses, no new breathlessness or leg swelling. She weighs 74 kg; renal function last week was normal. She says: 'I just want it done — I've booked the time off work and arranged care for my dog.' The consultant surgeon is operating today but can be contacted; there is an anticoagulation clinic in the hospital.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm identity and the purpose of the visit. Ask what she knows about the plan for her blood thinner around the operation.

Anticoagulant history: why rivaroxaban, when the PE was diagnosed, provoked or unprovoked, dose and timing, adherence, bleeding, current breathlessness or leg symptoms, HRT and other drugs, kidney function and weight, any antiplatelets.
Gallbladder history: frequency and severity of attacks, last attack, fever, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pancreatitis — how urgent is the operation really?

Recognise the issue: a PE 7 weeks ago puts her in the highest-risk period for another clot, and surgery adds to that risk. Stopping rivaroxaban now is not a simple 'two days before' decision. Do not give her stop instructions yourself.

Explain honestly: the timing of an elective operation so soon after a PE needs a senior decision. Options the team will weigh include postponing until she has had a longer period of anticoagulation, or proceeding with a specialist plan for stopping and restarting. You will discuss her with the consultant surgeon and the anticoagulation service today.

Address her frustration: acknowledge the time off work and her arrangements; explain that the delay, if advised, is to protect her from another clot. Until told otherwise, she should keep taking rivaroxaban as normal.

Safety-netting: seek urgent help for gallstone complications (fever with pain, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, severe constant pain) or clot symptoms (new breathlessness, chest pain, a swollen painful leg) or bleeding. Tell her when and how she will hear about the decision.

Summarise with teach-back, document the history, the risk, the advice to continue rivaroxaban and the plan to discuss with the consultant and anticoagulation service; inform the GP so the 'stop two days before' advice is updated.

self_audit: Asked what she had been told about her blood thinner
Established the indication and date of the PE
Checked dose, adherence, bleeding, renal function and weight
Asked about HRT and other relevant drugs
Assessed the frequency and severity of gallstone attacks
Asked about jaundice, fever and pancreatitis
Recognised a PE within 3 months as a high thrombotic risk
Did not give independent stop instructions
Explained that postponing surgery may be advised
Advised her to continue rivaroxaban until a plan is agreed
Agreed to discuss with the consultant surgeon and the anticoagulation service
Acknowledged her frustration about the plans she had made
Safety-netted for gallstone complications, new clots and bleeding
Documented and informed the GP
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate recognises the question behind the question. A top-band candidate does not just fix the timing of the last dose; they notice that the PE was only 7 weeks ago, treat the timing of elective surgery as a senior decision, keep her anticoagulated until then, and handle her disappointment honestly.
plab2.gold_close: Ms Rawcliffe, thank you — that's really helpful. The usual advice to stop a blood thinner a couple of days before an operation is for people who've been on it for a long time. You had a clot in your lung only seven weeks ago, and the first few months after a clot are when you're most at risk of another one; an operation adds to that risk. So I don't want you to stop your rivaroxaban on the basis of the advice you were given. I'm going to speak to the consultant surgeon and our anticoagulation team today. They may advise moving your operation until you've been on treatment for longer, or they may give you a specific plan for stopping and restarting. I know you've arranged time off work and care for your dog, and I'm sorry if this changes things — but the aim is to make the operation as safe as possible for you. Keep taking your rivaroxaban as usual until we tell you otherwise. If you get pain with a fever, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or severe constant pain, or if you become breathless, have chest pain or a swollen painful leg, please seek urgent help. We'll call you by tomorrow with the decision. Can you tell me back what you'll do in the meantime?
scripts: What have you been told about your blood thinner and the operation?
When exactly was the clot in your lung diagnosed?
The first few months after a clot are when the risk of another one is highest.
Please don't stop your rivaroxaban until we give you a plan.
The consultant may suggest moving the operation to make it safer for you.
I know that's frustrating when you've made arrangements — I'm sorry.
critical_fails: Endorses stopping rivaroxaban 2 days before without senior input
Fails to identify that the PE was only 7 weeks ago
Advises heparin bridging or a stop-and-restart regimen without senior or specialist input
Tells her to stop rivaroxaban now
No discussion with the consultant or anticoagulation service
No safety-netting for gallstone complications or new VTE
Dismissive of her frustration
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: confirming the GP's 'stop two days before' advice for a patient 7 weeks after a PE. Top-band mark: identifying the recent PE as the highest thrombotic risk period, checking how urgent the gallbladder surgery really is, continuing rivaroxaban until a senior plan exists, discussing with the consultant surgeon and anticoagulation service, explaining possible postponement with empathy, and safety-netting for gallstone complications, clots and bleeding.

plab2.title: IV Flucloxacillin Injection — 'It's Not Penicillin, Is It?'
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on a medical ward at 18:00. Mr Daniel Lisowski, 44, a bus driver, was admitted this afternoon with cellulitis of the left lower leg that has spread despite two days of oral clarithromycin from his GP. The medical registrar has prescribed flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 6 hours, first dose now. The drug chart allergy box says 'NKDA', signed in the emergency department. Prepare and give the first dose through his cannula on the manikin, explaining your checks to the examiner. Equipment: flucloxacillin 1 g vials ×2 (in date), water for injections, syringes, drawing-up needles, 10 mL sodium chloride 0.9% flushes, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol wipes, a clean tray, gloves, apron, syringe labels, sharps bin, and product information: reconstitute each vial with 20 mL water for injections; give by slow IV injection over 3–4 minutes. A 20 G cannula is in his right forearm, sited at 14:00, site clean and flushing freely. Role-player facts: if asked only 'Any allergies?', he says 'No, nothing.' If asked about antibiotics, or when the drug is named, he says: 'Amoxicillin — when I was 20 I came out in hives and my face swelled up. But this isn't amoxicillin, is it? The GP gave me a different one because of that.' Temperature 37.9 °C, HR 96, BP 134/80, RR 16, SpO₂ 98% on air. Once the candidate has withheld the drug and decided to contact the registrar, the examiner says: 'The registrar has updated the allergy record and prescribed a non-penicillin IV antibiotic. Its simulated vial and product information are on the tray: reconstitute with 10 mL water for injections; slow IV injection over 3–5 minutes. Please give it.'

timeline.content: Introduce, confirm identity with three identifiers against the wristband and chart, explain the injection and gain consent. Check the prescription: drug, dose, route, time, signature, not already given.

Allergy check in your own words, even though the chart says NKDA: 'Have you ever reacted to any medicine, especially an antibiotic?' Name the drug: 'This is flucloxacillin.' He recalls hives and facial swelling with amoxicillin and asks: 'This isn't amoxicillin, is it?'

Name the hinge: flucloxacillin is a penicillin, just like amoxicillin. With hives and facial swelling, he must not receive any penicillin. Do not prepare or give it. Reassure him: 'You did the right thing telling me.'

Escalate promptly — the cellulitis is spreading and needs treatment today: SBAR to the registrar. Correct the allergy record with the drug, the reaction and when it happened; the chart said NKDA, so report it as a near miss.
Replacement prescribed: check the new prescription and the vial. Hand hygiene, apron, clean tray, ANTT — key parts untouched. Reconstitute exactly as stated, check for particles, label the syringe.

At the bedside: re-confirm identity and allergy, inspect the cannula site, clean the port and let it dry, flush with sodium chloride 0.9% asking about pain. Give the injection slowly over the stated time while watching and talking to him; flush after.
Safety-net the reaction: ask him to report itch, flushing, lip or tongue tingling, wheeze or feeling faint; stay with him for the first few minutes. Sharps straight into the bin.

Sign the chart with the time. Document the allergy, the conversation with the registrar, that no flucloxacillin was given, and the replacement. Mark the edge of the cellulitis if not done. Tell him the allergy is now recorded and he should mention it whenever he is offered an antibiotic.

self_audit: Confirms identity with three identifiers
Explains the injection and gains consent
Checks the prescription is complete and not already given
Asks about allergies in own words despite 'NKDA'
Names the drug to the patient before giving
Recognises flucloxacillin as a penicillin
Withholds the drug and does not prepare it
Escalates promptly for an alternative antibiotic
Corrects the allergy record with the reaction
Uses ANTT and reconstitutes as instructed
Flushes the cannula before and after
Gives the injection slowly over the stated time
Observes for a reaction and safety-nets
Disposes of sharps at the point of use and documents
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate's allergy check is real or a box already ticked by someone else. A top-band candidate asks about antibiotic reactions in their own words, names the drug, recognises that flucloxacillin is a penicillin despite a chart that says NKDA, withholds it, escalates so the cellulitis is still treated, corrects the allergy record, and then gives the replacement with a clean, aseptic, correctly paced IV injection and watches for a reaction.
plab2.gold_close: Mr Lisowski, thank you for telling me about the amoxicillin — it really matters. The antibiotic you were prescribed, flucloxacillin, belongs to the same penicillin family, so with the hives and swelling you had before, it isn't safe for you. I didn't give it. The registrar has chosen a different antibiotic that's safe with your allergy, and I've given you the first dose slowly through your drip. If you notice itching, a rash, tingling in your lips, wheeze or feeling faint, press the buzzer straight away. Your allergy is now written clearly in your notes and on your chart, with what happened to you. Whenever you're offered an antibiotic in future, tell them 'I'm allergic to penicillin', not just amoxicillin. What questions do you have?
scripts: Before I give anything — have you ever had a reaction to a medicine, especially an antibiotic?
This one is called flucloxacillin.
Flucloxacillin is in the same penicillin family as amoxicillin, so I'm not going to give it.
I'll speak to the registrar now so you get a safe antibiotic without delay.
I'm just flushing the drip first — tell me if it stings or feels tight.
I'll give this slowly over a few minutes; tell me at once if you feel itchy, hot or wheezy.
From now on, say you're allergic to penicillin, not just amoxicillin.
critical_fails: Gives flucloxacillin to a patient with a penicillin allergy
Relies on 'NKDA' on the chart without asking the patient
Reassures the patient that flucloxacillin is not a penicillin
Withholds the antibiotic but does not escalate — infection left untreated
Breaks asepsis or gives the injection as a rapid push
Does not check the cannula before injecting
Leaves sharps out or does not document the allergy
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: trusting 'NKDA' on the chart, or agreeing with the patient that flucloxacillin 'isn't amoxicillin'. Both are penicillins, and hives with facial swelling suggests an immediate reaction. Top-band mark: own allergy check, drug named aloud, drug withheld before it is drawn up, prompt escalation because the cellulitis still needs treating (NICE NG141 lists non-penicillin options), allergy recorded with the reaction (NICE CG183), and a correctly performed replacement injection — ANTT, saline flush before and after, the slow rate stated, observation for a reaction and sharps at the point of use.

plab2.title: Leg Ulcer Not Improving on Antibiotics — Swab It Now, but Ask Why the Treatment Failed
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in a GP surgery at 10:30. Mrs Winifred Coultas, 76, a retired school cook, has had a venous leg ulcer above her left inner ankle for five months, dressed twice a week by the practice nurse under compression. Four days ago a GP colleague diagnosed infection (more pain, redness and fluid) and prescribed flucloxacillin. The practice nurse says: 'It's no better — can you see her and swab it?' Take a focused history, take a wound swab on the model provided and explain the plan. Role-player facts: she took the capsules for one day, came out in an itchy red rash on her arms and stopped them, but told nobody. 'I had a rash with penicillin years ago, but I thought these were different.' The rash faded within two days; no swelling of the lips or tongue, no wheeze, no breathing difficulty. The ulcer is more painful, redder, wetter and smells. No fever or shivers; eating and feels well in herself. No diabetes. No allergy is recorded in her notes. Examiner holds: temperature 37.4 °C, HR 86, BP 142/84, RR 16, SpO₂ 97% on air. Ulcer: 4 × 3 cm shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus with yellow slough and heavy exudate; erythema extending about 3 cm onto surrounding skin, warm and tender; no fluctuance, crepitus or necrosis; pain in proportion to the findings; no rash now. Foot pulses palpable.

timeline.content: Introduce, confirm identity and consent. Ask how the ulcer has changed since the antibiotic was started.
Ask the question that matters: 'How have you got on with the capsules?' Elicit that she stopped after one day because of a rash, and that she has had a rash with penicillin before.

Characterise the reaction: itchy rash only, faded in two days; no lip or tongue swelling, wheeze or breathing difficulty. Screen for systemic illness: fever, rigors, feeling unwell, severe pain out of proportion.
Ask for observations and examine with consent: size, slough, exudate, extent of erythema (mark the edge), warmth, fluctuance, crepitus, necrosis, foot pulses.

Explain why a swab is now appropriate: NICE NG152 advises against routine swabs at first presentation because ulcers are always colonised, but to consider one when infection is worsening or not improving as expected.

Hand hygiene, apron and gloves. Remove the dressing, clean off surface exudate and loose slough with saline, then sample the clean wound bed, rotating the swab with firm pressure and avoiding the surrounding skin. Swab straight into transport medium; label in front of her.

Request form: left leg venous ulcer, spreading cellulitis, flucloxacillin taken for one day and stopped because of a rash. Re-dress the ulcer; compression is for the nurse to review if the leg is very painful.

Plan: record a penicillin allergy (non-severe rash) so it is never repeated; a non-penicillin antibiotic per NICE NG152 (doxycycline or clarithromycin, or erythromycin in pregnancy) and local guidance, adjusted to the swab result; review in 2–3 days. Let the colleague and practice nurse know.
Safety-net: spreading redness beyond the line, fever, feeling unwell, severe pain or any lip, tongue or breathing symptoms with the new tablets — seek help urgently. Document.

self_audit: Confirms identity and consent
Asks whether she actually took the antibiotic
Elicits the rash and the previous penicillin reaction
Screens for features of anaphylaxis
Screens for systemic illness and pain out of proportion
Requests observations
Examines the ulcer and marks the erythema edge
Explains why a swab is now appropriate
Cleans surface exudate and slough before sampling
Samples the wound bed without touching surrounding skin
Labels at the bedside and gives clinical details
Records the penicillin allergy
Non-penicillin antibiotic per guideline, reviewed with the swab result
Safety-nets and documents
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing two things: correct swab technique, and whether the candidate asks why treatment 'failed' before reaching for a swab and a stronger drug. A top-band candidate discovers that she stopped flucloxacillin after one day because of a rash, recognises flucloxacillin as a penicillin, records the allergy, explains why the swab is now appropriate when it was not at first presentation, cleans before sampling the wound bed, and plans a non-penicillin antibiotic with early review.
plab2.gold_close: Mrs Coultas, thank you for telling me about the rash — that explains a lot. Flucloxacillin is a type of penicillin, so the rash was almost certainly a reaction to it, and it also means the infection has only had one day of treatment. I'm recording a penicillin allergy in your notes so you aren't given one again. I've taken a swab from the ulcer today. When it first got infected, a swab wasn't useful, because every ulcer has germs living on it. Now that it isn't settling, the swab helps us choose the right antibiotic. I cleaned the surface first so the result reflects the ulcer itself. I'll prescribe a different antibiotic that is safe with your allergy, and we'll check whether it needs changing when the result comes back in two or three days. I've drawn around the redness. If it spreads past the line, you get a temperature or shivers, the pain becomes severe, or you notice any swelling of your lips or tongue or difficulty breathing, get help straight away. The nurse will carry on with your dressings. What questions do you have?
scripts: How have you got on with the capsules — did you manage to take them all?
What happened with the rash? Any swelling of your lips or tongue, or trouble breathing?
I'm going to draw around the redness so we can see if it spreads.
Every ulcer has germs on its surface, so we didn't swab it at first. Now that it isn't settling, the swab will help.
I'll clean the surface first so the swab picks up the germs in the ulcer, not just on top of it.
I'm recording a penicillin allergy so you're not given one again.
If the redness passes the line, or you feel unwell, get help the same day.
critical_fails: Does not ask whether she took the antibiotic, so misses the rash
Prescribes or continues a penicillin-based antibiotic
Does not record the penicillin allergy
Swabs the old dressing or surface exudate without cleaning first
Labels the specimen away from the patient or omits clinical details
Does not examine for spreading infection or screen for systemic illness
No safety-netting
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: assuming the antibiotic 'didn't work', swabbing the slough and prescribing a broader penicillin such as co-amoxiclav. Top-band mark: asks whether she took the capsules, uncovers the rash and the earlier penicillin reaction, excludes anaphylaxis, records the allergy, explains why the swab is now appropriate (NICE NG152: not routinely at first presentation; consider if infection is worsening or not improving), cleans before sampling the wound bed, labels at the bedside, and plans a non-penicillin antibiotic per guideline with review in 2–3 days.

plab2.title: Setting Up IV Fluids — The Cannula Is the Source of the Fever
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on a surgical ward at 08:00. Mrs Pauline Rainford, 69, a retired librarian, is on day 2 after a laparotomy and small-bowel resection. She is nil by mouth with a nasogastric tube on free drainage. The fluid chart prescribes Hartmann's solution 1000 mL IV over 10 hours, start 08:00, signed. The nurse asks you to put the bag up. Set up the infusion on the manikin and explain your checks to the examiner. Equipment: 1000 mL Hartmann's bag (in date, clear, wrap intact), pump giving set, volumetric pump, 10 mL sodium chloride 0.9% flushes, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol wipes, clean tray, gloves, apron, tape, line label, sharps bin, swab and blood culture bottles. Her only cannula is a 22 G in the dorsum of the left hand, sited in the emergency department four days ago. Role-player facts: 'The hand with the drip has been sore since last night. I felt shivery in the night.' Abdominal wound comfortable; no cough, no urinary symptoms, no calf pain. No known allergies. Examiner holds: temperature 38.2 °C, HR 104, BP 128/74, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% on air, alert (NEWS2 2). If the site is inspected: redness spreading 3 cm up the vein, tender, a firm cord along the vein, and a bead of pus at the insertion point. Abdomen soft, wound clean and dry. If the candidate says the cannula will be removed and new access obtained, the examiner says: 'The cannula is out. A new 20 G cannula has been sited in the right forearm and flushes easily.'

timeline.content: Introduce, confirm identity against the wristband and chart, explain and gain consent. Check the prescription: Hartmann's, 1000 mL, over 10 hours, start time, signed; allergies.

Look at the patient and the cannula before the bag: 'How has your drip hand been?' She reports soreness and shivers overnight. Ask for observations: temperature 38.2 °C, HR 104 — NEWS2 2, with a new fever.

Inspect the site: spreading redness, tenderness, a firm venous cord and pus at the insertion point in a four-day-old cannula. Name the hinge: this is a cannula-related infection with fever. Do not flush or use it — it may be the source of the fever.

Remove the cannula, swab the pus at the insertion site for culture, and escalate to the surgical registrar. Take blood cultures from a fresh venepuncture site before any antibiotics. Screen briefly for other sources: wound, chest, urine, calf, abdomen.
Access: new cannula in the other arm, away from the infected vein. Confirm it flushes without pain.

Now the infusion: check the bag against the prescription — Hartmann's, 1000 mL, in date, clear, no leaks. Hand hygiene, ANTT: roller clamp closed, spike without touching it, drip chamber part-filled, prime slowly, no air in the line.
Clean the port and let it dry, flush, connect. Pump: 100 mL/hour, 1000 mL to be infused. Open the clamp, confirm it is running and the site is comfortable. Label the giving set with date and time.
Explain to Mrs Rainford: the drip in her hand has become infected, it has been removed, tests have been sent and the registrar is coming to see her about antibiotics.

Document the phlebitis score, removal, swab and cultures, escalation and the new cannula with date and time. Sign the fluid chart with start time and batch number; update fluid balance including NG losses; ask for site checks with each set of observations.

self_audit: Confirms identity and gains consent
Checks the fluid prescription fully
Asks about the drip site before setting up
Requests observations and interprets the fever
Inspects the cannula: redness, cord, pus, age
Does not flush or use the infected cannula
Removes the cannula and swabs the insertion site
Takes blood cultures from a fresh site before antibiotics
