Escalates to the surgical registrar
Checks the bag against the prescription
Primes the giving set with ANTT and no air
Sets the pump rate and volume to be infused
Labels the line and signs the fluid chart
Documents the site findings and arranges site checks
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate looks at the patient before the equipment. A top-band candidate asks about the drip hand, requests observations, finds a four-day-old cannula with spreading redness, a venous cord and pus, recognises it as the likely source of a new fever, removes it rather than running fluid through it, sends a swab and blood cultures, escalates, and only then sets up the prescribed infusion correctly through new access.
plab2.gold_close: Mrs Rainford, the soreness in your hand and the shivers last night have the same cause — the drip in your hand has become infected. I've taken it out, sent a swab from the spot and some blood tests to find out which germ it is, and the surgical registrar is coming to see you about antibiotics. Your tummy and wound look fine, which is reassuring. You now have a fresh drip in your other arm, and your fluids are running through it slowly over the next ten hours because you can't eat or drink yet. The nurses will check the new drip every time they do your observations. If this one gets sore, red or swollen, press your buzzer straight away. What questions do you have?
scripts: Before I put the fluid up, how has your drip hand been?
Could I have her latest observations, please?
This drip has become infected — it may be why you've had a temperature.
I'm not going to use it. I'll take it out and send a swab from the spot.
I'll take blood cultures from a fresh site before any antibiotics.
Pump at 100 mL an hour, 1000 mL to be infused — it's running.
Press the buzzer if the new drip gets sore, red or swollen.
critical_fails: Connects or flushes the infusion through the infected cannula
Does not inspect the cannula before connecting
Ignores the fever or does not ask for observations
No blood cultures or no escalation to a senior
Introduces air into the line or breaks asepsis while priming
Changes the prescribed fluid or rate on own judgement
No documentation of the cannula findings
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: hanging the bag on the existing cannula because 'the job is just the fluids'. A four-day-old hand cannula with spreading redness, a cord and pus in a febrile post-operative patient is a likely source of infection. Top-band mark: ask about the site and get observations first, remove the cannula, swab the insertion site, take blood cultures from a fresh site before antibiotics, escalate to the registrar, briefly screen for other sources, then set up the prescribed Hartmann's through new access with ANTT, air-free priming, correct pump rate and volume, a labelled line and a documented phlebitis score.

plab2.title: Torn Glove and Blood on Your Hand Before the Next Case — Soiled Hands Need a Wash, Not Just Gel
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on the emergency surgical list at 21:40. You have just assisted with incision and drainage of a perianal abscess. As you took your gloves off, you noticed a split in the right glove and the patient's blood on the back of your right hand. The next case is a laparoscopic appendicectomy for Mr Tomasz Wierzbicki, 23, and you are to scrub and assist. The scrub practitioner (role-player) says: 'We're running late. It's your second case, so just use the alcohol rub — no need to scrub.' Tell the scrub practitioner what you will do, then demonstrate your hand preparation, gowning and gloving on the station provided. Role-player facts: the scrub practitioner is under pressure from the registrar and pushes once more ('Gel is fine for second cases, everyone does it'), then accepts a clear explanation. Examiner holds (on inspection of your hand, if you look or ask): blood on intact skin only; no cuts, abrasions, eczema or puncture wounds; no sharps injury; no splash to eyes or mouth. You are not wearing jewellery. If asked, the previous patient has no known blood-borne virus infection. The scrub sink has antiseptic surgical solution, nail picks and elbow taps; a sterile gown and gloves in your size, including indicator underglove, are available.

timeline.content: Acknowledge the time pressure politely. Say what happened: a glove split and blood on your hand. Wash the blood off now with soap and running water.

Check the skin of the hand: any cut, graze, eczema or puncture? Any splash to eyes or mouth? Here there is none, so it is contamination of intact skin, not a sharps or mucocutaneous exposure. If there had been a break in the skin, encourage bleeding, wash, and follow the trust inoculation-injury procedure urgently.

Explain to the scrub practitioner why gel alone is not enough: alcohol rub is acceptable before a later case only when hands are clean. Hands that have been soiled need washing again with antiseptic surgical solution (NICE NG125).
Preparation: no jewellery, nails short, hat and mask on. Ask for a gown and gloves to be opened; check pack integrity, date and size.
Surgical scrub with antiseptic solution: nails, then palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists and forearms, for the product's contact time, hands above elbows, elbow taps.
Dry with a sterile towel, fingertips to elbow, a different part of the towel for each arm.

Gown touching only the inside; practitioner ties the back; closed gloving. A glove has just failed during this list, so consider two pairs of gloves with an indicator underglove (NG125: consider when perforation risk is high).
Hands in front, between waist and shoulders. Change gloves at once if a perforation is noticed during the case.
Close the loop: thank the practitioner, tell the registrar about the short delay, and report the glove failure if the local policy requires it.

self_audit: Stays polite but does not accept the shortcut
Washes the blood off immediately with soap and water
Inspects the hand for cuts, grazes or punctures
Asks about splash to eyes or mouth
Knows what to do if the skin was broken
Explains why soiled hands need antiseptic solution, not alcohol rub alone
Checks jewellery, nails, hat and mask
Checks the sterile pack and glove size
Systematic scrub for the product's contact time
Hands above elbows; elbow taps
Correct drying with a sterile towel
Aseptic gowning and closed gloving
Considers double gloving after a glove failure
Informs the team about the delay
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate applies the rule, not the routine. Alcohol rub before a later case is fine only for clean hands; this candidate's hands were contaminated with blood through a torn glove. A top-band candidate washes the blood off, checks the skin to decide whether this is a reportable exposure, explains the reason to the scrub practitioner without conflict, performs a full antiseptic scrub, gowns and gloves correctly, and considers double gloving.
plab2.gold_close: I know we're behind, and I don't want to hold things up, so I'll be quick. When I took my gloves off, the right one had split and there was blood on the back of my hand. I've washed it off, and I've checked: no cuts, no grazes, no puncture, and nothing in my eyes or mouth, so this isn't a needlestick-type exposure. If the skin had been broken, I'd follow the inoculation-injury procedure now. Alcohol rub is fine for a second case when hands are clean, but mine have been soiled, so I need to scrub again with the antiseptic solution — that's what NICE recommends, and it only takes a few minutes. Could you open a gown and size 7 gloves for me, with an indicator underglove? Because a glove has already failed tonight, I'd like to double glove for this one. I'll let the registrar know I'm two minutes behind. Thank you for opening up for me.
scripts: My glove split in the last case and I had blood on my hand — I'm washing it off now.
There are no cuts or punctures, and nothing went in my eyes or mouth.
Alcohol rub is fine for clean hands, but mine were soiled, so I need to scrub again.
It'll take a few minutes, and I'll let the registrar know.
Could you open an indicator underglove as well? I'd like to double glove after that tear.
Hands above my elbows, fingertips to elbow, one side of the towel for each arm.
critical_fails: Uses alcohol rub alone on hands soiled with blood
Does not wash the blood off promptly
Does not check the skin for a break or ask about splash exposure
Breaks sterility after the scrub and continues
Incorrect gowning or gloving (bare hands touching the outside of the gloves)
Confrontational or dismissive with the scrub practitioner
Keeps jewellery on or does not check nails and skin
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: going along with 'just gel, it's your second case' when the hands have been soiled with blood. NICE NG125 allows an alcoholic hand rub or antiseptic surgical solution before later operations, but if hands are soiled they must be washed again with antiseptic surgical solution. Top-band mark: washes the blood off at once, checks for any break in the skin or splash (and knows the inoculation-injury route if there is one), explains the rule courteously, performs a full systematic scrub, dries, gowns and gloves aseptically, and considers double gloving after a glove failure.

plab2.title: Paracetamol Dose for a Four-Year-Old — Two Strengths, One '10 mL'
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on the paediatric assessment unit at 09:30. Theo Marchetti, 4, weight 17 kg, was admitted overnight with tonsillitis and poor drinking; he is now drinking well. The drug chart prescribes paracetamol 240 mg oral every 4–6 hours when required, maximum 4 doses in 24 hours. The ward stock is paracetamol oral suspension 120 mg in 5 mL. His mother, Ms Gina Marchetti (the role-player), asks why the nurse is getting the medicine ready: 'He's hot again. I always give him 10 mL of mine — it's the same, isn't it?' She has a bottle of paracetamol 250 mg in 5 mL ('6 years plus') from home. The nurse has asked you to check the dose with her before it is given. Role-player facts: on the ward at 07:30, before the ward round, she gave Theo 10 mL from her own bottle without telling the nurses; no other paracetamol in the last 24 hours (the overnight team gave none) and no ibuprofen; she bought the bottle last week because the shop had run out of the infant one. Theo is sitting up watching a tablet, chatting, drinking juice. Examiner holds: temperature 38.4 °C, HR 120, RR 24, SpO₂ 99% on air, capillary refill 2 seconds.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself to Ms Marchetti and Theo, confirm Theo's identity against his wristband and chart, and check allergies. Explain you are checking his medicine with the nurse.

Before any calculation, ask what he has already had: 'When did he last have paracetamol, from which bottle, and how much?' She gave 10 mL of the 250 mg in 5 mL bottle at 07:30. Ask about any other doses or ibuprofen in the last 24 hours.
Calculate aloud. Ward dose: 240 mg ÷ (120 mg per 5 mL) = 10 mL. Home dose: 10 mL of 250 mg in 5 mL = 500 mg — about double his prescribed dose, given two hours ago.

Name the hinge: the same 10 mL holds twice the paracetamol in the stronger bottle. He is not due any paracetamol now — less than four hours since the last dose, and that dose was above the prescribed amount. Do not give the ward dose.

Decide safely, not from memory: tell the paediatric registrar, record the exact dose and time, and check TOXBASE or with the registrar whether any action is needed. Record the time from which the next correct dose may be given.
Treat the child, not the number: he is comfortable, drinking and chatting. NICE NG143 — antipyretics are for distress, not just to lower a temperature. Encourage fluids; recheck observations.

Explain to Ms Marchetti without blame: her bottle is a stronger version for children six and over, so 10 mL of it is double Theo's dose. For his age, the infant 120 mg in 5 mL bottle at 10 mL, up to four times in 24 hours, at least four hours apart, using the syringe supplied. Ask her to check any other medicines at home for paracetamol.

Agree with the nurse to label the home bottle and keep it off the ward supply. Document the calculation, the home dose and time, advice received, and the plan for the next dose. Safety-net: drowsiness, vomiting or abdominal pain must be reported straight away.

self_audit: Confirms identity, weight and allergies
Asks what paracetamol has already been given, when and from which bottle
Asks about other doses and ibuprofen in 24 hours
Calculates 10 mL of 120 mg in 5 mL = 240 mg
Calculates the home dose as 500 mg
Recognises the home dose was about double
Does not give the ward dose now
Informs the registrar and checks TOXBASE or senior advice
Assesses the child and uses antipyretics for distress only
Explains the two strengths to the mother without blame
Teaches the correct bottle, dose, interval and maximum
Uses the oral syringe supplied, not a spoon
Records the next safe dose time
Documents and safety-nets
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate checks what has already been given before calculating what to give. A top-band candidate establishes the exact home dose, recognises that 10 mL of the stronger bottle was double Theo's prescribed dose two hours ago, withholds the ward dose, involves the registrar and TOXBASE rather than guessing, assesses the child rather than the thermometer, and teaches the mother the difference between the two strengths without blame.
plab2.gold_close: Ms Marchetti, thank you for telling me about this morning's dose — it changes what we do. Your bottle at home is the stronger one, made for children aged six and over, so 10 mL of it has twice as much paracetamol as 10 mL of the infant bottle. That means Theo had about double his usual dose at half past seven. He looks well, and I've told the registrar and we're checking with our poisons advice service whether anything else is needed, just to be safe. He won't have any more paracetamol now; the next dose won't be before the time we've written on his chart, and it will be 10 mL of the infant strength, up to four times in 24 hours, at least four hours apart, with the syringe in the box. The temperature itself isn't dangerous — we treat him if he's miserable. Please keep the stronger bottle for when he's six, and tell us straight away if he becomes drowsy, is sick or has tummy pain. What questions do you have?
scripts: Before we give anything, when did Theo last have paracetamol, and from which bottle?
How much did you give, and has he had anything else since yesterday morning?
His dose is 240 mg — that's 10 mL of this infant bottle.
Your bottle is twice as strong, so 10 mL of it is 500 mg — about double.
He isn't due any more now; I'll tell the registrar and check the poisons advice.
We treat him if he's miserable, not just because the number is high.
Use the infant strength and the syringe in the box, at least four hours apart.
critical_fails: Gives the ward dose without asking about the home dose
Confuses the two strengths or calculates the wrong volume
Does not recognise that 10 mL of the stronger bottle was a double dose
Gives further paracetamol before senior or TOXBASE advice
Does not inform a senior
Blames or criticises the mother
No explanation of the correct strength, dose and interval
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: giving the ward 10 mL without asking what Theo had at 07:30. The same 10 mL is 240 mg from the infant bottle and 500 mg from the '6 plus' bottle; the second was double his prescribed dose two hours ago. Top-band mark: establish the exact home dose and time first, calculate both doses aloud, withhold the ward dose, inform the paediatric registrar and check TOXBASE rather than deciding from memory, assess the child rather than the temperature (NICE NG143), and teach the mother the two strengths, the dose for his age, the four-hour interval and the four-dose maximum, without blame.

plab2.title: Cervical Screening Sample With Bleeding After Sex — The Test Is Due, but It Does Not Investigate the Symptom
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in general practice. Ms Amelia Rookwood, 29, a primary school teacher, has come for routine cervical screening. Her only previous test, at 26, was HPV negative. Take the sample on the pelvic manikin, explaining as you go, and tell her what happens next. Role-player facts: last period 10 days ago, regular cycle, on the combined pill, no chance of pregnancy, no children, no procedures in the last 3 months. Only if asked about bleeding: spotting after sex 'four or five times' over the last 2 months with a new partner of 4 months; condoms not always used. No bleeding between periods, no pain, no unusual discharge. She is nervous: her first test 'really hurt', and she asks whether a smaller speculum can be used. She is happy to have a chaperone if offered. Equipment: specula in two sizes, water-based lubricant, a cervical sampling broom, a liquid-based cytology vial, swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing, and a request form. The vial on the tray expired last month (an in-date vial is in the drawer); the candidate finds this only if they check. When the candidate has visualised the cervix and asks, the examiner says: 'The cervix looks healthy. No lesion, no contact bleeding, normal discharge.'

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm three identifiers (name, date of birth, address or NHS number). Acknowledge her nerves about last time and agree she can stop at any point.

Eligibility and suitability: last test and result, last period, contraception, pregnancy, recent childbirth or procedures. Then ask everyone the symptom questions: bleeding between periods, after sex, unusual discharge, pain. The postcoital bleeding emerges here.

Explain the test: a sample of cells is tested first for high-risk HPV, and only if HPV is found are the cells examined. Explain that because she has had bleeding after sex, you will also take swabs for infection, and that the screening test is not designed to explain bleeding.
Consent, chaperone offered and accepted, privacy to undress and a sheet to cover. Offer the smaller speculum, explain she can insert it herself if she prefers, and position her comfortably.

Prepare: hand hygiene, gloves, check the vial expiry — it is out of date; replace it with an in-date vial, because a sample in an expired vial will be rejected and she would need another test. Small amount of water-based lubricant on the blades, away from the tip.

Warn, insert the speculum gently side-on, rotate and open to see the whole cervix. Report what you see. With a healthy-looking cervix and the test due, take the screening sample: broom in the canal, five full clockwise rotations with pencil pressure, then straight into the vial and rinsed firmly; cap to the line. Take swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea as per the kit instructions.

Close the blades slightly and remove the speculum gently. Cover her, let her dress in private. Label the vial with her details at the bedside and check it matches the request form; record symptoms on the form.

Explain results: a letter after the sample is tested. If HPV is not found, her next invitation will be in 5 years; if HPV is found, the cells are checked and she may be recalled in a year or referred for colposcopy. Separately: the bleeding after sex is being looked into in its own right — swab results, review with the GP, and gynaecology referral per the local pathway if it persists or remains unexplained, whatever the screening result.
Safer sex advice and testing for other infections (HIV, syphilis) offered; safety-net: heavier bleeding, bleeding between periods, pain or discharge — come back sooner.
Summarise, check understanding, and document identity check, consent, chaperone, the vial change, full view of the cervix, sample and swabs taken, and the follow-up plan for the bleeding.

self_audit: Confirmed three patient identifiers
Checked last test, last period, pregnancy and recent procedures
Asked about bleeding after sex, between periods and unusual discharge
Explained HPV primary screening in plain language
Explained that screening does not investigate her bleeding
Obtained consent and told her she can stop at any time
Offered a chaperone and protected her privacy
Offered a smaller speculum and positioned her comfortably
Checked the vial expiry and replaced the expired vial
Kept lubricant off the speculum tip and inserted gently
Visualised the whole cervix before sampling
Took the sample with five clockwise rotations and transferred it promptly
Took swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
Labelled the vial at the bedside and matched it to the form
Arranged follow-up of the bleeding independent of the screening result
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate can take a screening sample well while keeping two thinking points alive: an expired vial that would get the sample rejected, and a symptom that the screening test must not be used to answer. A top-band candidate asks about bleeding before examining, treats her anxiety practically, checks and replaces the vial, takes a technically correct sample and infection swabs from a healthy-looking cervix, and makes a separate plan for the postcoital bleeding — with no promise that a normal screening result explains it.
plab2.gold_close: Amelia, that's all done — thank you, I know last time was hard. Your cervix looked healthy today, which is reassuring. The screening sample will be tested for HPV, the virus that causes almost all cervical cancers, and you'll get a letter with the result. If no HPV is found, your next invitation will be in five years. I've also taken swabs to check for infections like chlamydia, which is a common cause of bleeding after sex. The screening test isn't designed to explain bleeding, so even if it comes back normal, we'll look into the bleeding separately: I'll ring you with the swab results, and if the bleeding carries on, we'll arrange for you to see a specialist. Until the swab results are back, using condoms each time is the safest option. If the bleeding gets heavier, happens between periods, or you get pain or an unusual discharge, please come back sooner. Is there anything you'd like to ask?
scripts: Before we start, I ask everyone: any bleeding between periods or after sex, or any unusual discharge?
The screening test looks for HPV — it isn't designed to explain bleeding, so we'll look into that separately.
You can ask me to stop at any point, and we can use a smaller speculum.
I'm just checking the date on this pot — this one's out of date, so I'm using a new one, or the lab would reject the sample.
Your cervix looks healthy, so I'll take the sample now.
I'm also taking swabs for infections like chlamydia, which commonly cause bleeding after sex.
If no HPV is found, you'll be invited again in five years — but the bleeding has its own follow-up.
critical_fails: Uses the expired vial
Does not ask about abnormal bleeding before sampling
Tells her a normal screening result will explain or rule out the cause of her bleeding
No consent or chaperone offer for an intimate examination
Continues after she asks to stop
Samples without visualising the whole cervix
Leaves the vial unlabelled or mismatched to the request form
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: using the out-of-date vial, or reassuring her that 'the smear will pick up anything' when she has postcoital bleeding — NHS Cervical Screening Programme guidance is explicit that screening is not a diagnostic test and samples in expired vials are rejected. Top-band mark: asks about bleeding before examining, explains HPV primary screening and the 5-year recall after an HPV-negative result at 25–49, offers a chaperone and a smaller speculum, checks and replaces the vial, takes a correct sample from a fully visualised healthy cervix, adds chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing, labels at the bedside and plans follow-up of the bleeding independent of the screening result.

plab2.title: A Six-Year-Old Collapses in the Children's Assessment Unit — Breaths First, Then 15:2
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in the paediatric assessment unit at 16:40. Maisie Ravensworth, 6, was brought in an hour ago by her father with two days of vomiting and drowsiness; she was waiting for a senior review. Her father calls out: 'She's gone limp and she's gone blue round the lips!' A child resuscitation manikin represents Maisie; the role-player is her father, Mr Nathan Ravensworth. A nurse is nearby and will do what you ask. Equipment: paediatric bag-valve-mask, oxygen, suction, and a defibrillator with paediatric pads. Your task: manage the situation, talking through what you are doing, until the resuscitation team arrives. Examiner holds: Maisie does not respond to voice or touch; after airway opening there is no normal breathing, no movement and no cough; there is a small amount of vomit in her mouth. After five rescue breaths the chest rises but there are no signs of life. The defibrillator advises 'No shock advised' at the first analysis. At about 5 minutes, during CPR, the examiner says: 'She coughs, moves her arm and starts breathing normally.' Her weight on the chart is 21 kg. The resuscitation team arrives at about 6 minutes 30 seconds.

timeline.content: Check for danger, assess responsiveness ('Maisie, can you hear me?' with a tap on the shoulder), shout for help and press the emergency buzzer. Reassure her father in one sentence and keep him close.

Turn her head to the side briefly to clear the vomit or use suction under direct vision — no blind finger sweep. Open the airway with head tilt and chin lift, without over-extending the neck. Look, listen and feel for breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
Not breathing normally: ask the nurse to put out a 2222 paediatric arrest call and bring the defibrillator.

Give five rescue breaths with the bag-valve-mask and high-flow oxygen, each about one second, just enough to make the chest rise. If the chest does not rise, reposition the airway and check the seal. Then look for signs of life: movement, coughing or normal breathing.

No signs of life: start chest compressions without a prolonged pulse check. Heel of one hand (or two if needed for depth) on the lower half of the sternum, at least one third of the chest depth, 100–120 per minute, full recoil. Ratio 15:2. Ask the nurse to give the two breaths with the bag so pauses stay short.

Defibrillator arrives: attach paediatric pads (or switch to paediatric mode) front and back while compressions continue, stand clear for analysis, and when it advises 'no shock' restart compressions immediately. Swap compressors every couple of minutes if fatigued.

Signs of life return: stop compressions, reassess ABC — airway, breathing rate and effort, colour, pulse and perfusion. Keep the airway open, give high-flow oxygen, attach monitoring, check blood glucose, and place her on her side if she is breathing but not fully awake. Keep the pads on.
Speak to her father briefly and honestly: 'Her heart and breathing stopped and we've got them going again. She is very unwell and the specialist team are coming now.' Do not leave Maisie.

Hand over to the team with a structured summary: age, weight, presentation, time of collapse, five breaths and CPR 15:2, one analysis with no shock, signs of life at about 5 minutes, current observations, glucose, vomit in the airway.
State that you will document times and actions and that the family will be supported and updated by the team.

self_audit: Checked for danger and responsiveness
Shouted for help and pressed the emergency buzzer
Cleared vomit by turning the head or suction under direct vision — no blind finger sweep
Opened the airway with head tilt–chin lift without over-extension
Checked breathing for no more than 10 seconds
Asked for a 2222 paediatric arrest call and the defibrillator
Gave five rescue breaths with a bag-valve-mask and oxygen, watching for chest rise
Started compressions on no signs of life without a prolonged pulse check
Compressed the lower half of the sternum to at least one third of chest depth at 100–120 per minute
Used a 15:2 ratio with minimal interruptions
Attached the defibrillator safely and resumed CPR straight after 'no shock advised'
Stopped CPR when signs of life returned and reassessed ABC
Gave oxygen, monitoring and checked glucose after return of signs of life
Gave a structured handover and spoke honestly to the father
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate can run paediatric — not adult — basic life support under pressure: five rescue breaths before compressions, 15:2, and good-quality compressions for a child's size. A top-band candidate explains that children usually arrest from lack of oxygen, delegates the breaths to keep compressions continuous, uses the defibrillator safely, and recognises when to stop: when clear signs of life return, CPR stops and ABC reassessment begins.
plab2.gold_close: Mr Ravensworth, I need to tell you clearly what has happened. Maisie stopped breathing and her heart stopped pumping properly, probably because she had become very unwell and short of oxygen. We gave her oxygen breaths and pressed on her chest to keep blood going to her brain, and after a few minutes she started breathing and moving again. That is a good sign, but she is still very unwell. The children's emergency team are here now and will look after her, find out why this happened and keep her closely monitored, probably on the high-dependency or intensive care unit. A nurse will stay with you, and someone from the team will come and explain everything as soon as they can. Is there anyone you would like us to call for you?
scripts: Help, please — 2222, paediatric arrest, and bring the defibrillator.
Five rescue breaths first, with oxygen, watching the chest rise.
No signs of life — starting compressions, fifteen to two.
Can you give two breaths after every fifteen compressions?
Pads on — stand clear for analysis. No shock advised — back on the chest.
She's coughing and breathing — stopping compressions to reassess airway, breathing and circulation.
critical_fails: Does not call for help or put out an arrest call
Starts compressions without giving five rescue breaths
Uses the adult 30:2 sequence without adapting to a child
Delays compressions for a prolonged pulse check
Performs a blind finger sweep of the mouth
Touches the child or allows others to touch her during analysis
Continues compressions after clear signs of life return without reassessing
Leaves the child to update the father
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: going straight to 30 compressions as in an adult, or stopping to search for a pulse while a 6-year-old has no signs of life. Top-band mark: help and 2222 call, airway cleared without a blind sweep, five rescue breaths with oxygen, compressions on the lower half of the sternum to a third of chest depth at 100–120 a minute at 15:2, safe defibrillator use, stopping CPR when she coughs and breathes, and a clear handover with the father kept informed.

plab2.title: Dressing Change on Fragile Skin — A Clean Wound Needs Gentle Hands, Not a Swab or Antiseptic Cream
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on a surgical ward at 10:00. Mrs Margaret Fenwright, 81, is on day 3 after an emergency open repair of an incarcerated left femoral hernia; no bowel was resected. She has taken prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for three years. The nurse says: 'Her dressing is lifting at the edges and she wants it changed before her daughter visits. She's also asking for a swab.' Change the dressing on the model provided and address her concerns. Role-player facts: she is anxious: 'My neighbour caught MRSA after her hip operation. Can you swab it to be sure, and put some of that antiseptic cream on it? And when can I have a shower?' She bruises easily, and a plaster tore her skin last year. Pain is mild and improving; no fever; eating and walking. No allergies. Examiner holds: temperature 36.8 °C, HR 78, BP 138/76, RR 14, SpO₂ 97% on air. MRSA screen on admission negative (if asked). Wound (on removal of the dressing): 6 cm left groin incision closed with an absorbable subcuticular suture; edges together; a little dried blood; faint pinkness only along the suture line, no spreading redness, swelling, warmth, discharge or gaping. The surrounding skin is thin and bruised, and the dressing's adhesive border is stuck firmly to it.

timeline.content: Introduce, confirm identity, consent and privacy. Clarify the operation, the day, and her steroid use and fragile skin. Offer analgesia.
Ask about pain, fever, discharge and how she feels in herself. Request observations: normal.
Hand hygiene, apron and gloves; set out equipment using an aseptic non-touch technique (NICE NG125).

Remove the dressing low and slow: support the skin with one finger, peel the border back on itself, and use an adhesive remover or moisten the border if it sticks. Never rip the dressing off thin, steroid-treated skin.
Inspect: edges together, dried blood, faint pinkness along the suture line only, no spreading redness, swelling, discharge or gaping. Say aloud that this is a healing wound.
No routine cleansing of a clean, dry, intact wound; gently remove dried blood if needed. Apply a low-adherence dressing with a gentle (for example silicone) adhesive, avoiding tape on fragile skin.

Address her requests: no swab, because there are no signs of infection and a swab of healthy skin will grow harmless bacteria and may lead to unnecessary antibiotics; her admission MRSA screen was negative. No antiseptic cream — NICE NG125 advises against topical antimicrobials for wounds healing by primary intention.
Shower: she may shower now, as it is more than 48 hours after surgery (NG125); pat dry and avoid soaking the wound in a bath until it has healed. Do not stop the prednisolone.
Safety-net: spreading redness, swelling, discharge, gaping, fever or increasing pain — tell the nurse. Document the wound, her fragile skin and the dressing used.

self_audit: Confirms identity and consent
Clarifies operation, day and steroid use
Offers analgesia
Requests observations
Hand hygiene and an aseptic non-touch technique
Removes the dressing low and slow, supporting the skin
Uses adhesive remover or moistens the border if stuck
Inspects the wound systematically
Recognises a healing wound without infection
Applies a gentle-adhesive dressing; avoids tape
Explains why a swab is not needed
Explains why antiseptic cream is not used
Gives correct showering advice
Safety-nets and documents
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing gentle, safe technique and the judgement to do less. A top-band candidate recognises skin made fragile by long-term steroids and removes the dressing without tearing it, inspects and names a healing wound, declines a swab and topical antimicrobials with clear, kind explanations, gives correct showering advice, and safety-nets for infection.
plab2.gold_close: Mrs Fenwright, the wound is healing well. The edges are together, and the slight pinkness right along the stitch line is normal at this stage. There's no sign of infection: no spreading redness, no swelling and no discharge. I understand why you're worried after what happened to your neighbour. A swab would grow the harmless germs that live on everyone's skin, and that could lead to antibiotics you don't need. Your MRSA test when you came in was clear. Antiseptic creams aren't recommended on a wound that's healing like this — they don't reduce infection and can irritate the skin. Because of your steroid tablets your skin is delicate, so I took the old dressing off slowly and I've used a gentle one without tape; please keep taking the prednisolone as usual. You can shower now: let the water run over it and pat it dry, but don't soak it in the bath yet. If it becomes red, swollen, hot, starts leaking or opening, or you feel feverish, tell the nurse straight away. What questions do you have?
scripts: Your skin is delicate because of the steroids, so I'll take this off slowly.
I'm supporting the skin and peeling the edge back on itself.
The edges are together and there's no sign of infection.
A swab would grow the harmless germs on everyone's skin, and that might lead to antibiotics you don't need.
Antiseptic creams aren't recommended on a wound healing like this.
You can shower now — pat it dry, but no baths yet.
If it gets red, swollen, hot or starts leaking, tell the nurse straight away.
critical_fails: Rips the dressing off fragile skin without support or an adhesive remover
Applies a new dressing without inspecting the wound
Takes a swab or starts antibiotics for a clean wound
Applies a topical antiseptic or antibiotic cream
No hand hygiene or aseptic technique
Dismisses her worry about MRSA without explanation
No safety-netting or documentation
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: tearing her skin while ripping off the dressing, or swabbing a clean wound and adding antiseptic cream 'to be safe'. Top-band mark: links long-term prednisolone to fragile skin, removes the dressing low and slow with support, inspects and names a healing wound, uses a gentle-adhesive dressing without tape, declines the swab and topical antimicrobials (NICE NG125) with clear reasons, advises that she may shower after 48 hours, and safety-nets for infection.

plab2.title: Found Unresponsive With Gurgling Breaths on the Ward — Suction, Airway, Adjunct, and Don't Ever Forget Glucose
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on a medical ward at 07:15. Mrs Doreen Bellingham, 74, was admitted two days ago with a urinary tract infection. She has type 2 diabetes treated with basal insulin and gliclazide; she ate very little yesterday. The healthcare assistant found her unresponsive with noisy, gurgling breathing and has called you. An airway manikin represents Mrs Bellingham; the examiner gives findings and speaks for the nurse. Equipment: Yankauer sucker, oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways of several sizes with lubricant, non-rebreathe mask, bag-valve-mask, oxygen, monitoring, a capillary glucose meter. Your task: assess and manage her airway and breathing, and act on any findings, talking through what you do. Examiner holds: responds to pain only (moans, localises), eyes closed. Gurgling from vomit pooled in the mouth; after suction, snoring remains until the airway is opened manually. RR 18, SpO₂ 89% on air, HR 98, BP 146/82, temperature 37.4 °C. Pupils equal and reactive. No signs of head injury, no facial trauma, not on anticoagulants. If an oropharyngeal airway is inserted, the examiner says: 'She coughs and gags against it.' If a nasopharyngeal airway is then inserted correctly: 'Tolerated; snoring stops; SpO₂ 96% on 15 litres.' Capillary glucose only if checked: 1.9 mmol/L. After glucose treatment per protocol, at about 6 minutes: 'She opens her eyes and asks where she is.'

timeline.content: Approach safely, call her name and assess responsiveness (AVPU: responds to pain). Shout for help, ask for the emergency team or outreach per local policy, and ask for the airway trolley and monitoring.

Airway: look in the mouth — vomit. Turn her onto her side or use the Yankauer under direct vision to clear it; no blind finger sweep. Then head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust and listen: snoring persists when you let go.
High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask at 15 L/min. Breathing: rate, depth, chest movement, saturation — RR 18 and adequate effort, so she needs a clear airway, not ventilation.

Adjunct: explain that an oropharyngeal airway is used only if there is no gag reflex. Size from incisors to angle of the jaw, insert inverted and rotate 180°. She gags — remove it at once to avoid vomiting and laryngospasm.

Switch to a nasopharyngeal airway, which is better tolerated when the gag is present: no suspected base-of-skull fracture or facial trauma here. Size per local kit, lubricate, insert along the floor of the nose with a gentle rotation, never force. Reassess: snoring stops, SpO₂ rises.

Circulation and disability: pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, cannula; pupils; and 'Don't ever forget glucose' — capillary glucose 1.9 mmol/L. This is a likely cause of her reduced consciousness.

Treat severe hypoglycaemia in an unconscious patient per the hospital (JBDS) protocol: IV glucose via a secure cannula, or IM glucagon if there is no IV access. Nothing by mouth while the airway is unprotected. Recheck glucose after 10–15 minutes.
When she wakes she will not tolerate the airway adjunct — remove it if she gags. Reassess ABCDE, keep oxygen titrated to target, keep her on her side until fully alert.

Next steps: long-acting carbohydrate once she can swallow safely; review gliclazide and insulin (likely to recur — sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can be prolonged), frequent glucose monitoring, inform the registrar and diabetes team, sepsis review of the UTI.
Hand over in SBAR to the senior and document the event, airway interventions, glucose readings and treatment.

self_audit: Assessed responsiveness and called for help early
Cleared vomit by suction under direct vision or lateral positioning — no blind finger sweep
Opened the airway with head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust
Gave high-flow oxygen and assessed breathing adequacy
Stated that an oropharyngeal airway is only for patients without a gag reflex
Sized the oropharyngeal airway from incisors to angle of jaw and inserted it correctly
Removed the oropharyngeal airway immediately when she gagged
Checked for head or facial injury before a nasopharyngeal airway
Inserted a lubricated nasopharyngeal airway gently and reassessed
Checked capillary glucose as part of D

plab2.title: The Syringe Someone Else Drew Up — Check the Label and the Milligrams Before You Inject
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in the Emergency Department minors area at 20:15. Mr Kofi Boateng, 45, a delivery driver, has a 7 cm clean laceration across the front of his right thigh from a broken glass table top two hours ago. The registrar has assessed it as suitable for closure; an X-ray shows no retained glass. You have been asked to infiltrate local anaesthetic before the wound is sutured. Explain the procedure, obtain consent and administer the local anaesthetic on the model provided. You do not need to suture. On the tray: a 20 mL syringe full of clear fluid with no label, and two empty 10 mL ampoules of lidocaine 2% plain. The nurse (role-player) says: 'I've drawn up 20 mL of the 2% to save you time.' Unopened 1% plain lidocaine 10 mL ampoules, syringes, needles and a sharps bin are also available. Role-player facts (patient): 'I'm allergic to the dentist's injection.' If explored: years ago, sitting upright in the dentist's chair, he felt hot, sweaty and light-headed straight after the injection, went pale and passed out briefly, and was fine after lying flat for a few minutes. No rash, itching, lip or tongue swelling or wheeze. He has had local anaesthetic since, for a mole removal, lying down, without problems. No regular medicines; no other allergies. Examiner holds: sensation and capillary refill distal to the wound normal; observations normal.

timeline.content: Introduce, confirm identity and consent. Confirm the plan with the patient: numb the wound so it can be stitched.

Explore the 'allergy': hot, sweaty, pale and fainting while sitting upright, with no rash, swelling or wheeze, and later uneventful local anaesthetic. This is a vasovagal episode, not an allergy. Plan to do it with him lying down and record the history accurately.
Check and document distal sensation and circulation before anaesthetising.

Look at the tray. The syringe is unlabelled and was prepared by someone else, so its contents cannot be verified — do not use it. Also, 20 mL of 2% lidocaine is 400 mg, twice the 200 mg single-dose ceiling for plain lidocaine in the BNF and product information. Discard it safely and thank the nurse.

Prepare your own: check 1% plain lidocaine with the nurse (drug, concentration, expiry, clarity). 1% = 10 mg/mL; about 10 mL (100 mg) should be enough. Draw up with a non-touch technique, label the syringe, and change to a fine needle.

Hand hygiene and gloves. With him lying down, infiltrate through the wound edges, aspirating before each injection and injecting slowly while talking to him. Watch for early toxicity: tingling lips, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation.
Sharp straight into the sharps bin. Test for numbness before suturing begins.
Document: drug, concentration, volume in mL and dose in mg, time, site, neurovascular status, and the dentist history recorded accurately as a faint, not an allergy.
Report the near miss through the local incident system so the team can learn from it. Safety-net: tell staff at once if he feels unwell, light-headed or has tingling around the mouth.

plab2.title: Digital Rectal Examination With a 'Normal' PSA — A Prostate That Feels Malignant Is Referred Anyway
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in general practice. Mr Clive Rendall, 66, a retired electrician, has had 4 months of getting up three times a night to pass urine, hesitancy and a weak stream. His PSA last week was 2.6 micrograms/L, which the laboratory reported as within the age-specific reference range. The GP has asked you to examine his prostate today. Explain, obtain consent and perform a digital rectal examination on the manikin; then tell him your findings and plan. Role-player facts: no blood in the urine, no burning, no fever, no retention; no bone pain or back pain; no weight loss; bowels normal. Father had 'prostate trouble' in his 70s. Takes no regular medicines. He says at the start: 'The blood test was fine, so do we even need to do this?' He accepts a chaperone if one is offered and the reason explained. Examiner holds: inspection — normal perianal skin. Palpation — normal tone; no rectal mass; prostate moderately enlarged, the left lobe hard, irregular and nodular, the median sulcus not felt on the left, non-tender; right lobe smooth and rubbery. Glove: brown stool, no blood. Urine dipstick (if asked): negative. Abdomen (if asked): no palpable bladder.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, and acknowledge his question about the normal PSA.
Brief focused check: urinary symptoms and their effect on him, haematuria, retention, infection symptoms, bone or back pain, weight loss, family history. These shape how you interpret what you feel.

Answer the PSA question honestly: PSA is helpful but not perfect — some prostate cancers do not raise it, and the examination tells us about the size, shape and texture of the prostate that the blood test cannot.

Explain the examination: a gloved, lubricated finger in the back passage for about a minute; uncomfortable rather than painful; he can ask to stop at any time. Offer a chaperone and explain their role; it is accepted. Consent.
Privacy to undress, left lateral position with knees drawn up, cover with a sheet. Hand hygiene and gloves. Inspect the perianal area first.

Warn, lubricate, insert gently. Tone and squeeze; sweep the rectal walls; then the prostate: size, consistency, surface, symmetry, median sulcus, tenderness. Withdraw, inspect the glove, offer tissues and cover him.

Present findings: moderately enlarged prostate, left lobe hard, irregular and nodular with loss of the sulcus on that side; right lobe smooth; no rectal mass; brown stool, no blood. State the decision: a prostate that feels malignant is referred on a suspected cancer pathway whatever the PSA (NICE NG12).

Explain to Mr Rendall: one side of the prostate feels firmer and more irregular than expected. Most enlarged prostates are benign, but this needs urgent specialist assessment, usually an MRI scan first and possibly a biopsy. Avoid stating a diagnosis.
Supporting tests per the referral pathway: kidney function and urine dipstick. Safety-net: unable to pass urine, blood in the urine, new bone or back pain, or leg weakness — seek urgent help.
Summarise, check understanding and his concerns, and document consent, chaperone identity, findings and the urgent referral.

Took a brief focused urinary and red-flag history
Explained the examination and that he can stop at any time
Offered a chaperone, explained their role and recorded their identity
Obtained consent

Inspected the perianal area before palpation

Assessed tone and all rectal walls

A top-band candidate explains why the examination still matters, performs it with consent, chaperone and dignity, describes the prostate in full, and refers urgently on the suspected cancer pathway because the prostate feels malignant — not because of the PSA.
plab2.gold_close: Mr Rendall, thank you — I know that wasn't pleasant. Your prostate is a little enlarged, which is common at your age and explains some of the waterworks symptoms. But one side of it feels firmer and more irregular than I'd expect. That can have more than one cause, and I can't tell you what it is from an examination, but it needs a specialist to look at it properly. Even though your PSA was in the normal range, that blood test doesn't pick up every problem, so I'm making an urgent referral to the urology team on the suspected cancer pathway; you'll be seen quickly, with the aim of an answer within four weeks. They'll usually arrange an MRI scan of the prostate first and then decide whether a biopsy is needed. I'll also check your kidney function today. If you can't pass urine, see blood in your urine, or develop new pain in your bones or back, please get help straight away. What questions do you have?

I'll examine with a gloved, lubricated finger for about a minute. You can ask me to stop at any time.
A chaperone will be in the room — they're there for both of us.
I'm going to look first, then you'll feel my finger. Take a slow breath out.
One side of the prostate feels firmer and more irregular than I'd expect.
Even with a normal PSA, what I've felt means you should see the urology team urgently.

No consent or chaperone offer for an intimate examination
Inserts without inspection, warning or lubrication
Does not describe the prostate
No urgent urology referral
States a cancer diagnosis as fact

plab2.title: Bimanual Examination for 'IBS' at 61 — A Pelvic Mass Is an Urgent Referral, Not a Peppermint Oil Trial
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in general practice. Mrs Patricia Venning, 61, a retired dental receptionist, has had 3 months of bloating most days, feeling full quickly and needing to pass urine more often. She has read about irritable bowel syndrome and asks for peppermint oil. The GP has asked you to perform a pelvic examination. Explain, obtain consent and perform a bimanual examination on the manikin; then tell her your findings and plan. Role-player facts: menopause at 52, no postmenopausal bleeding, no HRT. Bowels slightly looser, no rectal bleeding. Appetite reduced; clothes looser at the waist despite eating less. No family history of ovarian or breast cancer that she knows of. No previous abdominal surgery. She says: 'My sister has IBS and it sounds exactly the same. Can't we try the peppermint oil first and do any tests later?' She is happy to have a chaperone if offered. Examiner holds: abdomen — mildly distended, no definite shifting dullness, non-tender, no palpable mass above the pelvis. Vulva — atrophic changes only. Bimanual — uterus small and mobile; a firm, irregular, fixed mass in the left adnexa about 8 cm across, non-tender; right adnexa normal; no cervical motion tenderness. Glove: no blood. Observations normal.

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, and acknowledge her wish to try peppermint oil. Explain you want to examine first so that any treatment is the right one.

Brief focused check: duration and frequency of bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency, change in bowel habit, weight loss, postmenopausal bleeding, family history of ovarian or breast cancer. New, persistent symptoms like these starting after 50 need ovarian cancer considered before an IBS label.

Explain the examination: two gloved, lubricated fingers in the vagina with the other hand on the tummy, for about a minute; uncomfortable rather than painful; she can stop at any time. Offer a chaperone; it is accepted. Consent.
Privacy to undress, sheet over, lying back with heels together and knees apart. Hand hygiene and gloves. Abdominal examination first for distension, ascites and masses. Inspect the vulva.

Warn, lubricate, insert gently. Cervix and cervical motion; uterus between both hands for size, position, mobility, tenderness; then each adnexum in turn for tenderness or a mass. Watch her face. Withdraw, check the glove, cover her.

Present findings: small mobile uterus; a firm, irregular, fixed left adnexal mass about 8 cm; mild abdominal distension without definite ascites. A pelvic mass that is not obviously a fibroid in a postmenopausal woman requires an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral to the gynaecological cancer service (NICE NG12).

Explain to Mrs Venning honestly: the examination found a lump next to the womb, on the left side. It may not be cancer, but it must be checked urgently. The referral does not wait for blood tests; an ultrasound scan and a CA125 blood test may be arranged as part of the pathway but will not delay it.

Address the IBS request kindly: IBS rarely starts for the first time after 50, and peppermint oil would not treat what was found; it would only delay finding out. Ask what she is most worried about and who she has for support.
Safety-net: worsening swelling, breathlessness, vomiting, inability to open the bowels, or pain — seek help the same day. Tell her when to expect the appointment and what to do if she has not heard.
Summarise, check understanding, and document consent, chaperone identity, findings and the urgent referral.

Recognised that new IBS-like symptoms after 50 need ovarian cancer considered

Obtained consent and provided privacy
Examined the abdomen for distension, ascites and masses

Declined to start an IBS trial in place of referral and safety-netted

I can't tell you what it is from an examination — lumps there can have several causes, and not all are serious — but it needs to be checked urgently, and that's more important than trying peppermint oil, which wouldn't treat a lump and would only delay things. I'm referring you today on the urgent pathway to the gynaecology specialists, so you should be contacted quickly — the aim is for you to know within four weeks whether or not this is cancer. plab2.title: 1.3 Litres Positive After a Hip Fracture Repair — The Night Note Says Furosemide, the Patient Says Bleeding
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on the orthopaedic ward at 08:00. Mr Trevor Wakelin, 78, weight 80 kg, had a hip hemiarthroplasty yesterday afternoon for a fractured neck of femur. He has a urinary catheter and a wound drain. The nurse hands you his 24-hour fluid balance chart (07:00 to 07:00): IV Hartmann's solution 2,000 mL (1,000 mL in theatre, 1,000 mL on the ward); oral 350 mL; total in 2,350 mL. Urine 640 mL; drain 380 mL; total out 1,020 mL; balance written as '+1,330 mL'. Hourly urine for the last 6 hours: 30, 20, 15, 10, 10, 5 mL. The night doctor wrote: 'Positive 1.3 L. If urine output < 30 mL/h, give furosemide 40 mg IV.' The nurse asks: 'He's only passing 5 mL an hour — shall I give the furosemide now?' Your task: interpret the chart, tell the examiner your assessment and plan, and explain to the nurse. Examiner holds: Observations at 07:30: HR 106, BP 98/56 (152/84 pre-operatively), RR 20, SpO₂ 95% on 2 L nasal oxygen, temperature 36.9 °C, alert (NEWS2 6). Examination if requested: pale, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, dry mouth, JVP not seen, chest clear, no peripheral oedema; the thigh is tense and more swollen than expected; drain bottle has 380 mL of fresh blood. Catheter: bag and tubing patent, no kinks, a bladder scan shows 40 mL. Bloods at 06:00: Hb 86 g/L (124 pre-op), creatinine 132 µmol/L (88 pre-op), K 4.9, urea 11.2. Drug chart: ramipril 10 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily (started post-operatively), enoxaparin prophylaxis due at 18:00, morphine as required. Anaesthetic record (only if the candidate asks for it): estimated intra-operative blood loss 600 mL, not transferred to the ward chart.

timeline.content: Acknowledge the nurse's concern and say clearly: 'Please don't give the furosemide yet — I want to look at him and the chart first.' Confirm patient identity, operation, time of surgery and weight.
Read the chart aloud: in 2,350 mL, out 1,020 mL, recorded +1,330 mL. Urine 640 mL in 24 hours ≈ 0.33 mL/kg/h; the last 6 hours 90 mL ≈ 0.19 mL/kg/h and falling hour by hour — oliguria.

Ask what the chart leaves out: theatre blood loss (anaesthetic record — 600 mL), insensible losses, fluid shifted into the operated thigh, and fasting before surgery. The true intravascular balance is likely negative despite the positive figure.

Assess the patient: observations and trend (HR 106, BP 98 from 152, NEWS2 6), perfusion, JVP, chest, oedema, wound, thigh swelling and drain. Check the catheter is draining (patent, bladder scan 40 mL) — the problem is not mechanical.
Interpret the bloods: Hb 86 from 124 — significant post-operative blood loss, possibly continuing into the thigh and drain; creatinine 132 from 88 — AKI stage 1; potassium high-normal.

Conclusion: hypovolaemia from blood loss causing oliguria and AKI. Furosemide would lower his blood pressure further and worsen the kidney injury. Plan: 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes per NICE CG174 and reassess; group and save/crossmatch; discuss transfusion with the senior given ongoing bleeding and haemodynamic compromise.

Stop ibuprofen and withhold ramipril; review morphine dose given the kidneys; ask the senior whether this evening's enoxaparin should be held while he may be bleeding. ECG and troponin if indicated — post-operative myocardial injury can also cause hypotension in this age group.

Escalate now: NEWS2 6 and suspected bleeding — orthopaedic registrar to review the thigh and wound, and inform the orthogeriatric team. Hourly urine output and observations, repeat U&E and Hb, and correct the chart to include the theatre losses.

Explain to the nurse: 'A positive chart means more was written going in than coming out — it doesn't tell us where the fluid is. His blood is in his thigh and the drain, not in his circulation. Diuretics are for fluid overload, and he has the opposite.' Ask her to cross out the conditional furosemide instruction pending senior review.
Document the assessment, the decision not to give furosemide with the reason, the plan and the escalation.

Calculated urine output in mL/kg/hour and noted the falling trend
Looked for losses not on the chart, including the anaesthetic record

Examined the wound, thigh and drain for bleeding
Checked the catheter was patent before attributing oliguria to the kidney
Interpreted the haemoglobin fall and AKI stage 1
Gave a crystalloid bolus with reassessment
Arranged group and save/crossmatch and discussed transfusion with a senior

Escalated to the orthopaedic registrar for suspected bleeding
