plab2.title: 'Write Severe Back Pain, Not Stress' — An Honest Fit Note for the Problem He Actually Has
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in a GP surgery. Mr Owen Lathbury, 36, a call-centre team leader, has booked to discuss 'a sick note'. Your task: discuss his request and agree a plan. Role-player facts: he says, 'I need two weeks off. Can you write that I've got severe back pain and I'm unfit for work? HR said stress isn't a proper illness.' On exploration: an occasional dull lower back ache for three months after long shifts, no injury, no leg pain, numbness, weakness, bladder or bowel symptoms, no weight loss or fever; he can do everything at work despite it. The real problem is work: a new manager six months ago, sharply increased targets and public criticism in team meetings. For six weeks he has slept badly (waking at 4 a.m.), dreads Sunday evenings, has felt low most days, has had tearful episodes in the car, and his concentration is poor — he made two errors at work last week. He is drinking 3–4 pints most evenings to 'switch off', up from weekends only. If asked: no thoughts of suicide or self-harm, no plans, supportive partner, no previous mental health history; he is still at work and has not taken any sick leave. He is worried that 'stress' on a fit note will mark him out as weak. If the candidate refuses: 'My colleague got one like this from another doctor. Why won't you just do it?' If the candidate offers an honest fit note, he asks: 'If it says stress, can you at least make it sound less bad?'

timeline.content: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, and ask what he needs and what has led him to ask today. Listen without interrupting.

Clarify the back pain: onset, severity, effect on work and daily life, and red flags (leg symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel change, weight loss, fever, night pain). It is mild and not stopping him working.

Explore what is really going on: the change at work, sleep, mood, anhedonia, anxiety, concentration, errors at work, alcohol intake and why it has increased, support at home. Ask directly and sensitively about thoughts of self-harm or suicide.

Explain honestly: 'I can't write that you have severe back pain, because from what you've told me that isn't what's stopping you. A fit note has to reflect my assessment — I'm not doubting you're struggling, but I need to describe what's actually happening.'
Respond to the colleague comment without criticising the other doctor: you can only certify what you have assessed; an inaccurate note could also cause him problems if it is questioned.

Offer the truthful alternative: his symptoms of work-related stress with low mood and poor concentration are a genuine health problem and a valid reason for a fit note. Discuss whether he cannot work at all ('not fit') or could work with changes ('may be fit' — e.g. temporarily adjusted targets, phased hours, a meeting with his manager or occupational health), and agree the option that fits your assessment and his function.

Address the wording: the condition should be as accurate as possible, but you can use less specific wording if a precise diagnosis would harm his position with his employer — it must still be true. Offer wording such as 'stress-related illness' and agree it with him. Confirm he does not need a fit note for the first 7 days of absence, as he can self-certify.

Treat the underlying problem: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), sleep, reducing alcohol with practical advice, consider a mood questionnaire, occupational health and the employer's employee assistance programme, and review in two weeks.

Safety-net: if he has thoughts of harming himself, contact the surgery urgently, NHS 111 (mental health option) or 999. Summarise, check understanding and document the request, assessment and reasoning.

self_audit: Clarified exactly what he wanted certified and why
Assessed the back pain properly, including red flags
Recognised that the back pain was not limiting his work
Explored stress, mood, sleep, concentration and alcohol
Asked directly about thoughts of self-harm or suicide
Declined to certify severe back pain and explained why
Remained non-judgemental and did not accuse him of lying
Responded to the colleague comment without criticising another doctor
Explained that work-related stress is a legitimate reason for a fit note
Discussed 'not fit' versus 'may be fit' and workplace adjustments
Agreed honest but less specific wording where appropriate
Offered treatment: talking therapies, sleep and alcohol advice
Arranged review and safety-netting
Documented the request and the reasoning
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing honesty under social pressure without loss of compassion. The candidate must not certify a diagnosis or limitation they have not found, and must not stop at 'no'. A top-band candidate rules out serious back pathology, uncovers the work-related stress and low mood, screens for risk and alcohol, explains the refusal in terms of what a fit note is, and then offers a truthful fit note — with wording agreed to protect his position — plus treatment and follow-up.
plab2.gold_close: Owen, thank you for being so open with me. I can't write that you have severe back pain, because the back ache you've described isn't what's stopping you, and a fit note has to match what I've assessed. But what you've told me — six weeks of poor sleep, feeling low, struggling to concentrate and drinking more to cope — is a real health problem caused by the pressure at work, and it is a proper reason for a fit note. Based on what we've discussed, I'll write a fit note for two weeks for a stress-related illness, wording we've agreed together, and I'll suggest that when you go back your employer looks at your targets and a phased return. I'd like you to refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies today — I'll give you the details — and to try to cut back the evening drinking, because it makes sleep and mood worse. Let's meet again in two weeks to see how you are. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, please contact us, NHS 111 or 999 straight away. Does that sound fair?
scripts: Tell me what's been happening that's made you need time off.
How has the back pain affected what you can do at work?
Sometimes when people feel this low, they have thoughts of harming themselves. Has that happened to you?
I can't write severe back pain, because that isn't what I've found — but I'm not doubting that you're struggling.
Stress affecting your sleep, mood and concentration is a genuine reason for a fit note.
The wording has to be true, but we can agree on wording that doesn't feel exposing.
critical_fails: Writes a fit note stating severe back pain or unfitness the assessment does not support
Accuses him of lying or fraud
Refuses and ends the consultation without offering help
Fails to explore the stress, mood and alcohol behind the request
Does not ask about thoughts of self-harm or suicide
Criticises the doctor who issued his colleague's note
Dismisses stress as not a real illness
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: writing 'severe back pain' to help him out, or saying 'that would be fraud' and closing the consultation. Top-band mark: back pain assessed and red flags excluded, the real story of work-related stress with low mood, poor sleep and rising alcohol uncovered, risk asked about directly, the refusal explained in terms of what a fit note certifies, a truthful fit note offered with 'not fit' versus 'may be fit' discussed and wording agreed, and treatment, review and safety-netting arranged.

plab2.title: Drowsy and Confused With Cirrhosis — Score the GCS, Then Stop the Sedation and Find the Precipitant
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on a medical ward at 22:00. Mr Gareth Lowry, 56, has alcohol-related cirrhosis and was admitted 2 days ago with tense ascites. The nurse says: 'He was agitated earlier and the evening doctor gave him lorazepam at 18:00. Now he's really drowsy — I think his GCS is about 11. He keeps trying to get out of bed when he rouses, so can you write him up for some more lorazepam?' Assess his conscious level using the Glasgow Coma Scale on the role-player (demonstrate any physical stimulus; do not apply real pressure), ask the examiner for findings, and start management. Examiner holds: eyes open to voice (E3); confused conversation — thinks it is his flat (V4); does not obey commands; localises to trapezius pinch (M5) — GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive; coarse flapping tremor of outstretched hands when he briefly holds them up. Airway patent, RR 18, SpO₂ 95% on air, HR 104, BP 98/60, temperature 37.9 °C. Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Abdomen distended with ascites, diffusely tender. No melaena reported; bowels not opened for 3 days; lactulose prescribed on admission but marked 'refused' or 'not given' on every round. Last alcoholic drink 10 days ago; no tremor at rest, no sweating. Bloods this morning: sodium 129, creatinine 142 (98 on admission), Hb stable. No diagnostic ascitic tap has been done since admission. No head injury reported; no falls.

timeline.content: Acknowledge the nurse's concern. Before any prescription, you want to assess him yourself.

GCS, structured: check for confounders (sedative given at 18:00, hearing, language); observe; speak; then a safe physical stimulus only if needed. Score each component: E3 to voice, V4 confused, M5 localising — GCS 12. Report the components, not just 'about 11'. Pupils separately; look for a flapping tremor.

ABCDE immediately: airway patent, breathing adequate, oxygen only if saturations fall below target. HR 104, BP 98/60, temperature 37.9 °C — possible infection. Capillary glucose (5.8). Look for bleeding, head injury and focal neurological signs.

Name it: drowsiness, confusion and a flapping tremor in cirrhosis is hepatic encephalopathy until proven otherwise, worsened by a benzodiazepine. Alcohol withdrawal is unlikely 10 days after his last drink, with no tremor at rest or sweating; it is a differential, not the default.

Decline more lorazepam: benzodiazepines worsen hepatic encephalopathy and his conscious level. Keep him safe instead: low bed, close observation, falls precautions; nil by mouth until his swallow is safe.

Find the precipitant: infection — fever and tender ascites mean spontaneous bacterial peritonitis must be excluded with a diagnostic ascitic tap, blood cultures and urine; constipation — lactulose not given for 3 days; sedation; AKI and low sodium; check for GI bleeding. Treat: lactulose to produce two to three soft stools a day (via NG tube or as an enema if he cannot swallow safely); antibiotics per local guideline if SBP or sepsis is suspected — do not wait for the tap result to start them in a septic patient.

Escalate to the medical registrar now; involve the gastroenterology team. Parenteral thiamine per local protocol given his alcohol history. Review nephrotoxic drugs and diuretics with the AKI. If GCS falls further, particularly to 8 or below, he needs urgent airway assessment by an anaesthetist and critical care review.
Explain to the nurse: why no lorazepam, the GCS components to monitor, and to call if GCS falls by 2 or more or the motor score drops. Neurological observations hourly at first.
Document the GCS components with times, the decision not to give further benzodiazepines and why, the precipitant screen, treatment and the escalation.

self_audit: Assessed the patient before prescribing anything
Checked confounders and observed before stimulating
Used speech before a safe physical stimulus
Scored and reported E3 V4 M5 = 12
Examined pupils and looked for a flapping tremor
Performed ABCDE and noticed fever, tachycardia and low blood pressure
Checked capillary glucose
Recognised hepatic encephalopathy and considered alcohol withdrawal
Refused further benzodiazepines and explained why
Identified missed lactulose and constipation as a precipitant
Arranged a diagnostic ascitic tap and septic screen for possible SBP
Started lactulose and antibiotics per guideline where indicated
Escalated to the registrar and gastroenterology
Set a plan for repeat GCS with clear call-back criteria
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate can perform a proper GCS on a confused patient and then refuse the easy prescription. A top-band candidate scores the components accurately, recognises hepatic encephalopathy, declines further lorazepam, searches for and treats the precipitants — missed lactulose, possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, sedation, AKI — escalates, and leaves the ward with clear GCS trigger points.
plab2.gold_close: (To the nurse.) Thank you for calling — you were right to worry. His GCS is 12: eyes open to voice, confused speech, and he localises but doesn't obey commands. With the flapping tremor and his liver disease, I think this is hepatic encephalopathy, and the lorazepam has probably made it worse, so I'm not going to prescribe any more. We need to find what's tipped him over. He's had no lactulose for three days and hasn't opened his bowels, so we'll start that now — by tube or as an enema if he can't swallow safely. He also has a temperature, a fast pulse, low blood pressure and a tender tummy, so I'm worried about an infection in the fluid in his abdomen: I'll take blood cultures, do a diagnostic tap of the fluid and start antibiotics per our guideline. I'm calling the medical registrar now and we'll involve the liver team. Please do neurological observations every hour, keep the bed low, and call me straight away if his GCS drops by two or more, if his motor response gets worse, or if he becomes harder to rouse.
scripts: Before I prescribe anything, I'd like to see him myself.
Mr Lowry, can you open your eyes? Do you know where you are?
I'm going to press on your shoulder. (Demonstrates trapezius pinch.)
Eyes to voice 3, confused 4, localising 5 — GCS 12. Pupils equal and reactive.
Hold your arms out with your hands cocked back for me.
I'm not going to give more lorazepam — it can deepen this kind of confusion in liver disease.
Call me if his GCS falls by two or more, or his motor score drops.
critical_fails: Prescribes further lorazepam or other sedatives
Reports only a total GCS without components
Uses a harmful stimulus on the role-player
Does not perform ABCDE or check glucose
Does not look for a precipitant
Misses possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
No escalation to a senior
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: writing up more lorazepam for a drowsy, confused patient with cirrhosis — benzodiazepines worsen hepatic encephalopathy and can tip him into coma. Top-band mark: structured GCS reported as E3 V4 M5, pupils and asterixis examined, ABCDE with glucose, hepatic encephalopathy recognised and alcohol withdrawal considered, sedation stopped, precipitants hunted (missed lactulose, constipation, possible SBP with diagnostic tap and antibiotics per guideline, AKI), lactulose started, registrar and gastroenterology involved, and clear GCS-based call-back criteria with neurological observations.

plab2.title: Adding Levetiracetam to an Infusion Bag — Not Into the Bag That's Already Up
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 on a surgical ward at 09:45. Mr Graham Tremlett, 58, a joiner, has epilepsy controlled for six years on levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily by mouth. He was admitted yesterday with adhesional small-bowel obstruction and is nil by mouth with a nasogastric tube on free drainage. The team has prescribed levetiracetam 1000 mg IV every 12 hours, first dose 10:00. Prepare the dose, add it to an infusion bag and start it on the manikin, explaining your checks to the examiner. Equipment: three levetiracetam 500 mg in 5 mL vials (in date), a 100 mL sodium chloride 0.9% bag, syringes, drawing-up needles, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol wipes, an additive label, a giving set, a volumetric pump, clean tray, gloves, apron, sharps bin, and product information: dilute the dose in at least 100 mL of sodium chloride 0.9%, Hartmann's or glucose 5%; infuse over 15 minutes. Running: Hartmann's 1000 mL over 10 hours via a pump into a 20 G cannula in the right forearm, about half the bag left. Role-player facts (the patient): 'I'm due my tablet at ten. I haven't had a fit in six years and I don't want one now. Can't I just swallow it?' No known allergies; site comfortable. At about 2 minutes the examiner, as the nurse, says: 'It's compatible with Hartmann's — I checked. Just inject it into the bag that's running and save a line.'

timeline.content: Introduce, confirm identity against the wristband and chart, check allergies, explain and gain consent. Acknowledge his worry about missing a dose.

Check the prescription: levetiracetam 1000 mg IV 12-hourly, due 10:00, signed, not yet given; same as his usual oral dose. Explain why not by mouth: nil by mouth with the NG tube on free drainage, so a tablet would not be absorbed. Antiepileptics are time-critical — he gets it on time, by vein.
Read the product information aloud. Calculate: 1000 mg ÷ 500 mg per 5 mL = 10 mL, two vials. The third vial is not needed — set it aside.

Nurse's suggestion: decline politely and explain. The drug is compatible with Hartmann's, but adding it to a half-used running bag gives an unknown final concentration, may not mix evenly, and at the maintenance rate would take about five hours instead of 15 minutes. A separate 100 mL bag is the only way to give the right dose over the right time, properly labelled.
Hand hygiene, apron, clean tray, ANTT. Check vials, expiry and the 100 mL bag — fluid, volume, expiry, clarity, leaks. Draw up 10 mL accurately, sharps straight into the bin.

Clean the additive port and let it dry; inject through the additive port, not the giving-set port. Invert the bag several times to mix and inspect for particles or discolouration. Complete the additive label — patient, drug, dose, diluent, volume, date, time, signatures — with a second check.

Check the cannula site, prime a line without air, connect and set the pump to deliver the bag over 15 minutes; the maintenance Hartmann's is compatible, so both can run through the Y-connector, or pause it per local policy. Confirm it is running.

Reassure Mr Tremlett: same dose, same time, by vein. Sign the chart with the start time; ask the team to keep his antiepileptic IV until he can absorb by mouth, and to tell him promptly if a dose is delayed. Document.

self_audit: Confirms identity, allergies and consent
Checks the prescription and that the dose is due
Explains why oral is not possible while on free drainage
Treats the antiepileptic dose as time-critical
Reads the product information before preparing
Calculates 10 mL from two vials
Declines to add the drug to the running bag
Explains the reason to the nurse without conflict
Uses ANTT and checks vials and bag
Cleans and dries the additive port
Inverts to mix and inspects the bag
Completes an additive label with a second check
Sets the pump for 15 minutes and confirms flow
Documents and reassures the patient
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate knows why compatibility does not make the running-bag shortcut safe. A top-band candidate reads the product information, calculates the volume correctly, declines to inject into the half-empty maintenance bag and explains the unknown concentration, mixing and timing, prepares a fresh 100 mL bag with ANTT, mixes, inspects and labels it with a second check, and gives the dose on time over 15 minutes while reassuring a patient anxious about seizure control.
plab2.gold_close: Mr Tremlett, you're getting exactly the same dose of levetiracetam as your usual tablets, at the same time — it's just going into the vein, because with the tube draining your stomach a tablet wouldn't be absorbed. I've made it up in its own small bag so it goes in properly over about 15 minutes, rather than slowly mixing into your other drip over several hours. It's labelled so everyone knows what's in it. It's running now. While you can't take tablets, your doses will be given this way every 12 hours, on time. If you notice any warning feelings you sometimes get before a seizure, press your buzzer straight away. What questions do you have?
scripts: You won't miss your dose — we'll give the same amount into the vein, on time.
With the tube draining your stomach, a tablet wouldn't be absorbed.
A thousand milligrams at 500 per 5 mL is 10 mL — two vials.
It is compatible, but I won't add it to the bag that's running — I'll make up a separate bag.
Could you be my second checker for the label?
Pump set to run the 100 mL bag over 15 minutes.
Press the buzzer if you get any of your warning feelings.
critical_fails: Injects the drug into the running maintenance bag
Calculates the wrong volume or uses all three vials
Gives the dose as an undiluted bolus
Gives it orally or via the NG tube on free drainage
Breaks asepsis or does not clean the additive port
No additive label on the bag
Delays the dose without escalating
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: injecting the levetiracetam into the half-full Hartmann's because the nurse says it is compatible. Compatibility is not the issue: the final concentration would be unknown, the drug may not mix evenly, and a 15-minute dose would trickle in over about five hours — in a patient who must not miss an antiepileptic dose. Top-band mark: product information read, 10 mL from two vials calculated aloud, fresh 100 mL bag prepared with ANTT, port cleaned and dried, bag inverted and inspected, additive label with a second check, pump set for 15 minutes, and the patient reassured that his time-critical medicine is on time.

plab2.title: A Visitor Chokes in the Emergency Department Waiting Room — Back Blows, Thrusts, and CPR When He Goes Down
plab2.scenario: You are the FY2 in the emergency department at 13:20. As you walk through the waiting room, Mr Kieran Varley, 52, who is waiting with his mother, stands up suddenly from his chair while eating a takeaway burger, clutching his throat. His mother shouts for help. A role-player plays Mr Varley until he collapses, after which a resuscitation manikin is used. A healthcare assistant is nearby and will do what you ask. Your task: manage the situation, talking through what you do. Examiner holds: when asked 'Are you choking?' he nods but cannot speak; no sound from his cough; lips dusky. After correctly performed back blows: 'No relief.' After correctly performed abdominal thrusts: 'No relief.' If the cycle is repeated, at about 3 minutes: 'He becomes limp and unresponsive.' Once he is on the floor and the airway is opened: no normal breathing. If the candidate looks in the mouth before rescue breaths: 'You can see a piece of food at the back of the mouth that you can reach.' The defibrillator advises 'No shock advised' if attached. The resuscitation team arrives at about 6 minutes 30 seconds.

timeline.content: Go to him and ask: 'Are you choking?' He nods but cannot speak or cough — this is severe obstruction.
Call for help: ask the healthcare assistant to put out an emergency call for the resuscitation team and bring the defibrillator and airway trolley. Tell him: 'I'm going to help you.'

Stand to his side and slightly behind, support his chest with one hand and lean him well forward. Give up to five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand, checking after each to see whether the obstruction has cleared.
No relief: stand behind him, place a clenched fist between the umbilicus and the xiphisternum, grasp it with the other hand and pull sharply inward and upward, up to five times, checking after each.
Still obstructed: alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts. Do not attempt a blind finger sweep.
He becomes unresponsive: support him carefully to the floor, confirm the resuscitation team is coming, open the airway and check for breathing for no more than 10 seconds.

Not breathing normally: start chest compressions at 30:2 — compressions may dislodge the obstruction. Before each set of breaths, look in the mouth and remove any visible object you can reach; no blind sweep. Use a pocket mask or bag-valve-mask with oxygen. Attach the defibrillator as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts.
Continue CPR with minimal interruptions, swapping compressors if available, until he shows signs of life or the team takes over.

Hand over: '52-year-old man, choking on food, severe obstruction from the start; back blows and abdominal thrusts without relief; unresponsive at about 3 minutes; CPR 30:2 since; food removed from the mouth; one analysis, no shock advised.' Mention that he will need examination for abdominal-thrust injury if he survives.
Ensure his mother is supported by a staff member and kept informed; document the event and times.

self_audit: Asked 'Are you choking?' and judged the cough
Recognised severe obstruction from the silent cough and inability to speak
Called for help and the resuscitation team early
Leaned him forward and gave up to five back blows, checking after each
Gave up to five abdominal thrusts with correct hand position, checking after each
Repeated the cycle while he remained conscious
Did not perform a blind finger sweep
Lowered him safely to the floor when he became unresponsive
Checked breathing for no more than 10 seconds
Started CPR at 30:2 without delay
Looked in the mouth and removed only a visible object before breaths
Attached the defibrillator and followed the prompts
Handed over clearly, including the need to check for thrust injury
Arranged support for his mother
plab2.trigger: The examiner is testing whether the candidate recognises severe choking immediately and follows the RCUK sequence without hesitation: help, up to five back blows, up to five abdominal thrusts, repeat — and switches to CPR the moment the patient becomes unresponsive. A top-band candidate explains why compressions help in this situation, looks in the mouth only to remove a visible object, and gives a handover that includes the risk of injury from the thrusts.
plab2.gold_close: (To his mother, once the team has taken over.) Mrs Varley, I'm one of the doctors. Kieran choked on a piece of food and it completely blocked his breathing. We tried to dislodge it with back blows and pushes on his tummy, and when he lost consciousness we started CPR and were able to remove the food from his mouth. The emergency team are looking after him now and are doing everything they can. I don't yet know how he will do — the next few minutes are important, and someone will come and talk to you as soon as there's news. A nurse will stay with you. Is there anyone you'd like us to call?
scripts: Are you choking? Nod if you can't speak.
Help — choking in the waiting room, call the resus team and bring the defibrillator.
I'm going to give you some firm blows on your back.
Now some sharp pushes on your tummy — inward and upward.
He's unresponsive — down to the floor carefully, starting CPR.
I can see food at the back of his mouth — removing only what I can see.
critical_fails: Does not call for help
Tells a patient with a silent, ineffective cough to keep coughing
Goes straight to abdominal thrusts without back blows, or omits abdominal thrusts after failed back blows
Performs a blind finger sweep
Continues back blows and abdominal thrusts after he becomes unresponsive
Delays CPR for a pulse check once he is unresponsive and not breathing normally
Leaves the patient to fetch equipment
plab2.examiner_tip: INSTANT FAIL RISK: still giving back blows to a man who has gone limp on the floor, or telling a silent, dusky patient to keep coughing. Top-band mark: severe obstruction named at once, help called, up to five back blows then up to five abdominal thrusts repeated while conscious, an immediate switch to CPR at 30:2 when he becomes unresponsive, a look in the mouth to remove only a visible object, safe defibrillator use, and a handover that flags the need to examine for injury from the thrusts.
